AS editor writing poetically of the weather says, "The backbone of winter is broken, but its tail wags yet occasionally." THE appearance of Queen Victoria in public helps trade. In other words, the circulation of the sove- reign helps to circulate the sovereign. SA m JONES says, "Live so your children may put their feet in your tracks and be honourable." That is, don't walk all over the road on the way home at nights.

"POOR JOHN—he was a kind and forbearing hus- band I" sobbed John's widow, on her return from the funeral. "Yes," said a sympathising neighbour; "but it is all for the best. You must try to comfort yourself, my dear, with the thought that your hus- band is at peace at last." AMAZING INDEED I—A French count won a great reputation for courage in 1870, during the siege of Paris, when he patriotically mounted guard upon the ramparts. He never ducked his head or threw himself prostrate, when shot or shell whistled by or ex- ploded near. "Amazing I" his comrades used to say. "How wonderfully cool!" The fact was, the count was stone-deaf! AN American mate, on board a ship manned with a crew who had had no nautical experience, took a pack of cards and nailed one card close to where each rope was made fast, and named the rope after the card. The result was such orders as, "Let go the ace of spades!" "Man the nine of hearts and nine of diamonds !" " Haul tight the queen of clubs! " How jaded your horse looks, cabman !" remarked an old lady as she dismounted from the cab. "Ii not the bit uncomfortably large for his mouth?' "It ain't the big bit in his mouth, mum; it's the siaall bit in his stomach; and," looking at the quarter she tendered for her fare, it doesn't seem as if it'll get much larger." "WILL you take a wedding trip 1" said the mother to her son-in-law. I think not," answered the young man looking furtively at the long trail of the wife's dress. "I will erect a bridge over it."

div.head: " CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL" CHAT.
For another year, at least, the Norfolk Broads are safe. In consequence of the present agitation the riparian owners have not deemed it expedient to stop a single boat.

Sir Andrew- Clark, M.D., and Lady Clark, who have been the guests of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone at Hawarden Castle, left, Hawarden on Tuesday morn- ing en route for Leamington, leaving Mr. Gladstone our Chester correspondent says, in excellent health. lie is expected next week to leave Hawarden for Scotland. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Mr. Armitstead are staying at the Castle.

I hear that it has been decided at the Foreign Office, of course with the concurrence of Lord Salis- bury, that there is not sufficient ground for retain- ing the silver transferred from Chili to Monte Video, Pn d still less for handing it over to the con- signee. Directions have accordingly been sent out to restore the bullion to the duly authorised repre- sentatives of the de facto Government, and we may shortly expect to hear that this has been done.

The death took place in Edinburgh on Tuesday of Sir John Steel, 8..5.A., sculptor to the Queen. He had been in delicate health for some time, and had done little work during recent years. He had reached the advanced age of 87. One of his prin- cipal works, and the one for which he received his knighthood, was the equestrian statue of Prince Albert in Charlotte-square, Edinburgh, which was unveiled by the Queen on the 17th August, 187 G.

Accounts from the North tell us that though the weather is fine the migrant birds are leaving rapidly. All the warblers, save a stray willow- wren here and there have departed; and very few ringousels and whinchats are left. The only song- ster save the chirping starling, is the robin, which holds forth well in the mornings and evenings, but otherwise the woodland choir is mute; and though the larks are abundant, they are songless above the fields and meadows.

One of Lord Salisbury's political friends sent him a newspaper containing Lord Randolph Churchill's predictions to a Cape reporter respecting political prospects in this country. " Truth " says the friend received back a slip of paper inscribed with the following extract from " Coningsby " :—" The political grapes were sour for Mr. Rigby; a prophet of evil, he preached only mortification and repent- ance and despair to his late colleagues."

A pretty story is being told in clubland of the graceful way young Lord Dudley announced his engagement to his mother. It is said that he kissed her and told her that he would have wished to lead to the altar the loveliest woman in England, bu this could not be, as it was impossible for a man to marry his mother; and, failing that, he had offered his hand and heart to Miss Gurney. The young peer hardly looks capable of such a felicitous COM:. pliment.

The new Lady Dudley walked down the aisle with a smile on her face,and her antique point lace veil,the bridegroom's gift, thrown back, which caused some speculation as to whether the Prince of Wales had claimed the privilege of the first "chaste salute," and so heightened the bride's becoming colour. Her bridegroom, as he left the chancel, exchanged a " wink-the-other-eye " look with the chums he left behind him. He is an ordinary-featured young man, without a tithe of his mother's good looks.

Mr. and Mrs. Kendal start for America next week During their previous visits they were notable lions in tramatlantic society. It was their emphatic desire to be announced in drawing-rooms and intro- duced to guests as Mr. and Mrs. Hunter Grimstone, Kendal being their nom ds thedtre. This often brought about results not desired, for as Mr. and Mrs. Grimstone they were unknown and attracted no attention, whilst on one occasion at least they were asked by a fellow guest at a crush if they knew or could point out the Kendsls, who were expected to be present.

The Rev. G. Armstrong Bennetts, B.A. (London), who has just been appointed Wesleyan Methodist Connexional Temperance Secretary, is one of the most promising of the younger men in the Wesleyan ministry. He was a Devonshire lad, and passed his early youth in the beautiful country about Dartmoor. He is a man of influence in the Wes- leyan Conference, being a member of the committee of examiners who test the theological status of young divines seeking full admission to that body' He is an effective speaker and an enthusiastic advo- cate of temperance..

Mr. Lecky, the historian, who, is about to publish his first volume of poems, is a distinguished-looking man, above average height and sfender,close shaven save for short auburn whiskers, with a high fore- head and dome-shaped head. He is by birth an Irishman, and graduated in Trinity COHN?, Dublin, but is opposed to Home Rule. He may frequently be seen on Sundays listening with, interest to the various speakers who hold forth on religion and politics in Hyde Park.. He resides in London, and has married a German lady,. who,once held a high position in a foreign court.

"Hockey," says the Cambridge Town Council, "is a dangerous game and a. nuisanceto the public." Very likely it is, and its name somehow prejudices one against it. Yet hockey is a great favourite with the lady students at Newham, wbere, unless we have been greatly mieinformed, it was introduced at the special desire of Miss Clough, the venerable principal, who is certainly one of the last people whom we would expect to recommend any danger- ous sport to the members of her dock. Doubtless the dangers of hockey, like those of other games, depend a good deal on where and how it is played.

The majority of the London. delegates who re- mained for the Saturday's proceedings of the Con- gress returned from N-ewcastle by the 5.15 train, and a very lively party they made. To the official placard" Reserved" which was, placed on the win- dows of their saloon,. a wtig had added" For the Earl of Fifeshire and party,' or some such legend, and passengers on the platform& at York and other stopping places were somewhat surprised at the stentorian lungs of this distinguished party, and at the new departure in aristocratic customs by those of the group who were travelling in their shirt sleeves.

Lord Beaconsfi.ld's memory is, well preserved in the affection of Londoners. A striking illustration of this was afforded the other evening in a small. company, where the conversation turned on oun• leading statesmen. A gentleman holding a respon- sible position at once engaged attention by remark:, "Disraeli spoke to me once." There was a chOrus of inquiries as to what he said. " exclaimed the hero, in the leisurely way of a man who had important information to communicate. "I once opened the door to him, and, being a little flustered, I trod on his gouty toe." "What did he do?" cried .everyone. "He said, Oh, hang the boy," was,the reply.

The statement that Sir Samuel Wilson became the owner of Hughenden may be correct (writes al correspondent), but when the Victorian" raatton- aire " first went to reside there in 1882 it was on an eleven years lease at £2,000 a year. Later. on he was on the point of buying Osmaston Manor in Derbyshire for £206,000, but Sir Andrew Walker,the baronet brewer of Warrington, profiting by at moment of hesitation, stepped in and snatched ths, bargain from him. Sir Samuel Wilson never shows his face in Portsmouth. He made big promises in 1866, and local industries looked forward to im- mense development; but the only thing he as done for the locality has been to work a military i relative on to the Gosport bench.

The Conclave is the burning subject in Rom. just now, because a rumour gained currency that the Pope is in very bad health. The Pope, our readers may be assured, is in excellent health. He leceives visitors, gives audiences, and continues to work with great activity. His memory is prodigious:. names and dates are retained by him with marvell- ous exactitude. He rises at half-past six every morning. and says Mass at seven o'clock, Half-past twelve is the hour of his frugal dinner. Every afternoon his Holiness, when visits and other occupations permit, takes carriage exercise in the gardens. At nine o'clock he takes a very light supper. He then shuts himself in his apartments and writes for two and a half hours.

Mr. T. It. Buchanan,. m M.P., discusses the legal as- pect of rights of way Scotland in a letter to the "Times." Our readers will have seen that in several districts the Scotch people are just now battling to secure rights of way which landlords have seized, and that magistrates and others of the most law- abiding class of citizens have taken part in the de-

struction of fences. The law and landlords in Scotland are the same as in England. When land- lords commit a "grab," they do not have recourse to the law. When the public assert their rights, the landlords become, as they think, the injured and aggrieved persons, but still they shrink from ap- pealing to the law. You can no more expect a grabber to take this course than you can a highway- man to report himself to the police.

We are promised a new potato. But by all accounts it is likely to remain a luxury. There would be a prejudice against a black tuber, however delicate might be the taste or flowery the farina. The new variety has a blackish stalk, the plant grows large, the flower is blue, the potato is a bluish black. Its introduction to these islands reverses popular tradition, for it comes from the East and not from the West. Some officer engaged in the Zulu campaign was its Raleigh, and botanists have consequently called the new potato the Cetewayo. It is said to be waxy rather than flowery, and the enthusiasts of course praise the delicate flavour. Still, waxiness of texture and darkness of colour are on the whole points against it. But a strange future is in store for it. It mixes admirably with truffles, where truffles are used for stuffing poultry.

The " Star " says : —The prolonged discussion no Mahatma mysteries and theosophical miracles has led to a wager, and the wager only lands us in fresh mysteries. Mr. "Stuart Cumberland " has offered £l,OOO for a real miracle, ar.d " Arthur Des- mond, late colonel Madras Engineers," has accepted what has been called the " vainglorious challenge." Mr. Herbert Burrows says his "difficulty with re- gard to Mr. Cumberland is a great one. How do I know there is such a person ?" A precisely similar difficulty will arise with regard to Colonel Arthur Desmond. For all we know, he may be a Mahatma playing larks on the Theosophists, or Mr. Cumber- land's familiar. He wrote to us about a fortnight ago from the address he now gives, " 13, Duke-st., Chelsea," but a letter sent to that address was re- turned through the Dead Letter Office. As there is no "13, Duke-st., Chelsea," in the Post Office Directory, we assume that Arthur Desmond's letters must be precipitated from somewhere in some mysterious way. This " challenge " at present looks as if it would even darken the occult.

A striking illustration of the necessity for con- tinuous and courageous advertising has come under my notice. A firm that manufactures a condiment of world-wide fame had been in the habit of adver- tising to the extent of about £5,000 a year through one of the most eminent advertising agencies in London. They thought they could dispense with advertising, seeing that their speciality was on every table, Accordingly all orders and contracts were stopped. Sales began to lall off, and the de- crease continued until the firm went back to their agents and announced that they intended to adver- tise again. But the decline had become so serious that in order to recover lost ground they have now to spend ..ElO,OOO a year where formerly they spent £5,000. When I expressed to my informant sur- prise that cessation from advertising should so speedily affect business, I was told that there is no doubt of the fact. It is well-known for instance, that wholesale houses reduce their orders when they find that the article they have been dealing in is no longer advertised. They do this to save them- selves from future loss, because their experience teaches them that the public demand declines as advertising declines.

div.head: MRS. BESANT'S INDIAN TOUR.
div.p: MRS. BESANT'S INDIAN TOUR.

While Mrs. Besant will do a fair amount of sight-seeing during her Indian trip it will, nevertheless, be on the'whole so to speak, a business affair. Mrs. Besant will leave in the latter part of November for Bombay, in which city she will speak soon after her arrival. From Bombay she will go to Poonah.,where she is also expected to speak, and thence to Madras, where the Theosophical Convention will be held. From Madras Mrs. Besant will probably go by sea to Calcutta, after which she will visit Benares, Delhi, Agra, and one or two other places. She will return to England from Bombay in the latter part of February.

div.head: HOW NAPOLEON KEPT HIS WORD.
div.p: HOW NAPOLEON KEPT HIS WORD.

(FROM "LITTLE FOLKS.") The Great Napoleon, as is well known, spent part of his youth in the military school at Brienne. 01 what use he made of his time here is shown in the way he commanded and conducted his wars, and by his life in general. Napeleon was very fond of fruit, which is no uncommon taste with young people, and owing to this a poor fruit woman earned many a penny from him. It would happen sometimes that Napoleon had no money to pay for what he bought from the old woman, but she trusted him, and he would always pay as soon as he could. When the time arrived for Napoleon to leave Brienne to put in practice what he had learned, and to show himself the skilled soldier and clever man he became, he still owed the woman a few shillings; for at the last time,. when she brought him some peaches, he said— "Good woman, I am leaving here, and find I cannot pay you for these, but you shall not be forgotten.' " Oh, noble gentleman," she answered,." go away quite easy on that score, and may Heaven keep you safely and make you a good man !" in the midst of such a career as Napoleon's now became, it was not extraordinary that the best memory should forget some little things, and that he forgot the old woman and his debt to her was not wonderful. In a short time Napoleon convered Italy and went into Egypt;. thence he returned to Paris and was made consul ; there he restored peace and order, and was made the French Emperor. All this time the poor old fruit woman in Brienne had still nothing but his promise "You shall not be forgotten." But, as will be shown, Napoleon's word, all ',-..hough life, was as good and better than money. After many years Napoleon again visited Brie/Inc in disguise with a friend. WE.-,11 might he have been moved on, first entering, thinking over the past years and of all the dangers he had passed saf,?..ly through, andliimself now an Emperor. Suddenly, while walking through the town, he stopped in one of the streets, put his hand to his head, as one who thinks of something, and then mentioned the name of the fruit woman. Her home was soon•found out, and there he and his atr•- tendant went..

A narrow door opened into a. small but clean room, and here they found the woman kneeling,:, with two child,ren by the stove„ preparing thei" meagre evening•meal. "Can I get some fruit here ?". said the Emperor.. "Yes, certainly," answered the woman, "melons - are just ripe ";and she brought some. While the two visitors were eating the fruit the Emperor asked-- "Do you know the Emperor who is said to be here to-day ?" "Know him, I should think! did !" answered the- old woman. "Many are the pines and baskets of fruit he has bought of me while he was here at 7 school."

"Did he always pay regularly "Yes, always."..- . Then said the visitor to her, "Woman, either you : do not tell the truth or you must have a bad . memory, for, to begin with, you,do not know the Emperor —for I Um- he; and I did not pay you as regularly as you say; for I owe you how some- • shillings. ' At this moment the attendant louinted out on the table a large sum.of-money. The-woman, on recog, nesing the Emperor and hearing the money jingle on the table, fell at his feet quite overcome with fright, joy, and • thankfulness, while the two child-it ren gazed at each, other not knowing what to do or mt. The Emperor afterwards ordered the old house to he pulled down and another builtiont the same spott "The house shall bear my name;" he said," and promise to look after the children.' True to his word;.liapoleon sawthe daughter well , married, and the son brought. up at his expense., and in the same school from w-hich. came the great.: hero himself.

"By jinks I" exclaimed Mingo. " Yer the best hand at a disguise I ever seed. Blow me, if yez own gal would suspect you. But fire away, an' let me know w'at a-foot to-night." The men sat down on opposite sides of a dirty little table, and, sinking his ,voice to a whisper, Iteybold asked: "When did you see Gilbert last I" "1 aint seed him to speak to since he's been in New York; but I take a peep at him now and then %vithout his knowing it. First time I get hard up, 'm goin' to as him to be my banker; an' if he don't come down quick, you can take my head for a football."
"Mingo:" ire away, Kemal." 'I want thi.l- man sent up again:"
'When 1" 'As soon as it can be.done.° '"lfave you gtt the job set up, Iteinalr 'No ;_I want you to do. that."

"And) you 'll pay big T' 11- pay what is right, Mingo. A hundred &liars in advance, and three times that when the job's finished," said Reybold, handing over the money he had received from his partner. " I 'm (loin' so well now, layin' plans for others to work, anrgittin a divvy of all that comes in, that I can't afford to take no big risks. Oh, Gilbert's a sharp one; I tell you; an' they do say how the young lady w'at he savesl. from drowndit' is dead gone on him," This was said with a malicious wink that stung Reybold like a dagger-thrust. "You can do the work; will: you 7' asked Rey-bold, striking the table to emphasise his. question. "I'd a heap sight rather undertake to have him put out of the-way for good," said Mingo, thought- " You-see, Kemal, it's easier to kill a man outright, if ha-'e up an' down squar'' than it is to kill his- character, an' r guess Gilbert would, a sight rather,die than go up again—" "That 's why I want him to go up," interrupted Reybold. "'Oh, I see. You feel; kinder spiteful." "

" he was dead, it might no help me particit• larly ; bit if it can be shown to the world that he is•-a criminal at heart, why, my end, will be gained." " Oh; yes, I' see: I'll try it; but youal have to•pay bigger." "'How, muclrmore ? "

"Twice as much ; an"when that'b mita mayhave to call on you, To be sure, I can make Gilbert pay to be rid of me-;: a little outside matter of ray own —one of the perquisites, of my acquaintance like—" "I accept your offer, Mingo," broke in Reybold, and he extended his-hand across the table., "Will you do the ; "I'll try."' "You,naust sar Yea.'" "Well, if I must, I must. FB3 And Mingct took Reybold's hand and shook it heartily.
The conference was at an end, and with an under- standing as -to the next place of meeting, Revbolil waO'conducted by Mingo to the street. 'Waste. no. time,. Mingo," ware •Reybokrs ia St words.
And the response was: "If Gilbert aint sent up before the new .3re ar, F then ra a , angte au son of temp'ranne, an.' a u sionary.'!"
CHAPTER X. PLA/13, FOR THE FUTURE.
The itterest shown by Irene Lefferft- d a happy effect, on Allen Gilbert. He worked w ith a lighter heart,. an& every day he felt more-arid 'more like a man.

The new interest he felt indife purified his-heart ot the desire for revenge that had so long s tirred its depths: True, he neveTfor an instanilgave up the tb,iought a abandoning the search for evidence to prove that, he was innocent of the crime for which. lie had so cruelly suffered; but his impulse was . now to show hit- true character in the best light to the world, nether than to punish the unprincipl ed con- spiratom whoi, to save themetives, had:mad.ahim a victim:.

He found inn Florence andilis motherievhng cora. fortem, whoi by keenly interesting him in the pre- sent-,, made him cease brooding over the...past----to forgetrit they knew was impossible. The little family soon made fricrid. with the workers in the crowded tenement, and; at Florence's suggestion,. a night schooli was establisbied in their own quarters.

Sitie-taught the girls reading, writing and sewing, and Allen instructed the boys in such branchea-as. lie thought might be of use to them, These_liids were bootblacks, newsboys, messevAer boas. or. swab boys in stoxes. afl otilaUom had,been forced, by the necessities ot their parents, to , begin the fight for existenc years before they should have left school.

From the very first, .the efforto,.ei the gewrous teachers were crownod with success. Tha poor people were grateful i beyond expression ; anti by way of showing this,, they came constantly to .the brother and sister ~with their confidencts---the stories. ch,f their sore lards and ardent hopes, Great as the change was in Allen, the new.life- wrought a still greater change in Florence. The glow of health came to her cheeks„.and tha light that had distinguished her hopeful girlhood returned to her eyes. The men in the tenemenk never wearied in speaking of her beauty and,goc..2- ness, and, as the„ women shared in this -.spirit of admiration, they endorsed the, views of their. bias- bands and fathers. without a pang of jealousy. Soon after thk.night school. was startek Dr. Putnam heard about it,. and ~as he was. earnest in good things, with the means for gratifying his desires in that way, he at once became interested. Allen never mentioned his ouspicion2,to.his sister. Certain it is she- would hr.vn been pained, had he done so; but :he could not help seeing that the young doctor's. nightly visits were hrgely due to his increasinaadmiration for the beantiful Florence. It required no very keen powers of observation to see the effect of the doLtor's visits on: the; young lady. Had she been lesa natural and more adept in hiding her emotions, she might have saceeeded in keeping back the pleased light that carae to her eyes when she heard his. voice or knock. She was.to.happy to think of analysing her own feelings. Had she fully understood what, these first joyous heart-throbs meant, she would have been on her guard., for she fully realised tbat, no matter how nearly ()ill a level she and the doctor might be by birth and education, wealth removed them, sociall.4,r, very fazapart. But they had another earne3t supporter in their night school work. As soon as irene Lefferts heard of it, he insisted on furnishing all the necessary books and other educational appliances, and great quantities of plain sewing for the girls, the garments being their own after they had made them.

Irene came one afternoon every week, and she wasso gentle and sisterly that Florence felt no em- barrassment in, having her to teL At such times she would remain till "school was out," when the joyous duty a escorting her home would devolve en Allen.

The emotion of love .is.largely the result of asso- oiation. Lot any two people of the opposite sex— between whom the barriers of previous engagementt, or great disparity of age. os social positions do not exist—be much throwa together, and so become dependent ou each other for happiness, and the. chancea are ten to one that they will fall in love.
But, At addition. to this assOciatioa, there was a romantic origin to, the friendship which speedily sprang up between) Allet and th* lady ha had rescued.

We call the. feeling "friendship," as either of there would have frankly called it, if asked for an, explanation of their relationship at this time. Allen worked with an energy and care that, pleased his patrons greatly, and gradually added to, their number, until at length be found that he must, have a little dam and a boy a his own. This messenger boy was a bright lad of fourteens who had grown sickly and sallow making cigars im the tenement house. His. name was Victor Blanc, and he had a sister a year•younger, named. Bertha, who was a great pet of Florence. "Well, Victor,' said Allen, one evening after he had been on his feet ever since daylight, "we are both tired and hungty ; so we'll shut up shop and go home. What say you 7" "Well, sir," laughed Victor, "IV a said yes to that offer if you'd_made_it _three hours ago." _ _ _ _

Allen had incked his desk and was in 'the act a putting the key into his pocket, when he heard a heavy step and a coarse cough behind him, and turning quickly, he found himself face to face with Mingo Pete. "Ha! Good evening, old friend," said Mingo Pete, smiling in a way that showed all his yellow teeth, and reaching out his hand when he caught Allen's eyes. "1 'ye been a sarchin' an' a sarchin' for you for weeks an' weeks. But here you are at last. An' how are you, any way 2" Allen was so taken by surprise that he could not refuse the ruffian's hand; but quickly regaining his self-control, he said: "I do not know why you should want to see me. I have had Lig. desire to huut. You

" well, well!" exclaimed Ming ~,1 " mays the way with some fellers. NV'en they bens to git honours an' wealth then they peer ro have no more use for, the old friends as was under the drag with 'em. But I say, Number 367, is that boy your ion?"

Mingo painted to the boy, who stood near the door, with his big eyes full of wonder. Without replying to this, Allen said: "You can-go home, Victor. I will close up." "Ah, yes, that's better. I never like to let kids into our secrets; they'll learn 'ern soon enough; no fear of that. Curtis that young uns has got to be taught goodness an' virtue an' them kind o' things, but when it comes to t'other side of the question, they don't want no-postin'." Then waving his hand at Victor, Mingo continued: "You run home, sonny, yer boss an' me is goin' to talk over the ale time when him an' me wore the uniform an' served the State," and the wretch threw back his head and laughed as if he had uttered a great joke. "Now,. why de you come here 9" asked -Allen, turning fiercely, upon the intruder, when the-boy had left.

"Oh, come,-Abn't get mad," said Mingo, rising to his feet, for there was a dangerous light in the eyes • of the young man confronting him. "Madi. you 'scoundrel What right—how dare you tome here as if you were a friend of mine? Out of this place at once, or I shall flog you like the cur that you are cried Allen, as, with 'his left hand, he seized Mingo by the collar, and with the right pointed' to the door. "I didn't come to sponge or to make no fuss," whined Mingo, cowed for the moment by the other's . resolute manner. "It's a rule for them as has been in quod together to help each other if they gets . hard up, I chanced to find out that you was a-doin' well; an' as I can't get no work—just coz I've been in limbo—l thought that, as you knowed how it was yerselc you might help me till I cm raise miff money to take me away to some country where I aint knowed, an! where I can make a freak start under a new name."

While -Alien's bitter experience had intensified his horror of crime, it had also deepened and broadened his charity, and he had come tosthink of the training, or want of training, of the-criminal classes, and the temptations that were yielded to for the need of .a helping hand. He had never liked this felibw, Mingo. He felt in his heart, that he was beyond redemption ; yet, as his own case flashed through this mind, Allen reasoned that he might be wrong in his judgment, and that it was his duty to help this.man, it. he could do so without 2empromis- ing himself.. "You-do not took like a man who could tell the truth/'said Allen, scorn in his voice and a softer light, tike pity, in his eyes. "I aint practised it so much as r have the t'other,".Said Mingo, with affected humility. "The truth aint paid, so well; but, if I had a chance, I should like to, try it. I don't pretend to be no better'n I:am When I was sent up, w'ich has been four times, Idesarved it, an' I didn't never w'ine. But no man, as remembers his mother an' them long-ago days when he was a young, innercent kid, wants to think that he aint never goin' to do no better, an' that there aint nothin' -aiore to look for'a'd to than. dyin' in quod an' bein' buried in the paupers'. bone yard; not that the buryin' counts for much;. an' a man that hasn't beea choice 'bout the folks he's kep' comp'ny with when alive, shouldn't kick 'bout them he's going' to lie down 1 alongside of when he's planted with other stiffs." Mingo was so touched with his own speech that • he actually turned his face to the back of his chair, and,, hiding his face in his, hands, sobbed, aloud. It-is-said' that a woman's tears ,is her strongest.. weapon—it is certainly a very ready and a very - effective-weapon—but when a man cries, it implies . &stronger if not a deeper feeling. Often, in the dark days which still came to him in-his-dreams, Allen felt that if he could only cry - Biondi as when he was a boy, and let the tears pour - out in floods, that they would float from his heart - the load of agony that crushed Was if it were in an ever-tightening vice. "lam poor," said Allen, much touched by tfb e . splendid acting of the wretch before him, "but, 541.. faraa.licaza. lam willing to bele Ton. This I will no, not necaabe I cnancea to meet you in teat place. where you went to suffer for your guilt, and I went as the victim of an infamous conspiracy, but because . you are a fellow-man in want, and eager to lead a new life—'

"Yes, that's it! that's it! There you've hit me squar': Help me out of this hole, an' show you . I can do 'bout what's right ;" ai.d Mingo rose and reached out his hands pleadingly. "And you will be advised by me?" asked Allen. "Yes, just as if I was yer,born slave." "Then,',* said Allen, as ...he took the ontlaw's hands, "I will trust you. I: know what it is to be . kicked down when I tried to. crawl up; and with GOd's help, I will never obstruct the way of a man aiming at a beter life." He gave Mingo five dollars, and told him to call on the following evening, promising to try and find ; him some suitable employment the meantime. Mirwo, was so profuse. hi his thanks that Allen did not object to his walking along with him for - some distance on the way home, protesting at every - step his purpose to lea.d.alnaw life. As they walked on, Allen paid no heed to the people they passed, an so did not see, Mott Rey- . bold. Had he done so, he must have noticed the quick;, meaning glances ezohanged between him and,: Mingsk

Alfrar passing, , Reybold stopped an . the nexts4 corner, and waited till joined by Mingo. "Well, Pete," heisaid,, " what's the report ?" "TVs good; eculdn't-be better," was the reply?' "Ton seem to,be„w,osking him Ca Alia friendly's/ racket."
"it's the orkly•way, to strike him. I tried the, bullying, but he'd a thrashed me an' flung me int% the street if It hadn't took the back track."

"What do you no&i r "W'y, mean that I'm a-tryin' to reform. I sigh to lead a better life, an' :to become a morel God-fearit' citizen. I cried so much. we'en I told lim„ this, that I'm, dry as a chip, au' must hurry off for, a drink—" "He gave you money, eh, Mingo T" laughed Boy, bold.
"Just ,enough for a drink but till I';nable to earn a isonest livin'," chucklad Mingo, "ypiumst. help mwsti.th grub an' clothes.* (ro be contirkesed.)

div.head: FLOODS IN SPAIN.
div.p: THE FLOODS IN SPAIN.
QVER 1,500 LIVES LOST: TERRIBLE SUFFERINGS..

MADRID, ALQKDAY. —ln Sau Sebastian the news of the disastrous floods has caused a great sensation. At a Cabinet Council held therete-day, orders were issued to provide funds for the relies of the sufferers. MADRIP,,TtrESDAY.—As. communication with the pro". vinces becomes gradually restored the-appalling extent ef last week's inundations is more audj more apparent. Fresh rspterts are constantly, being, received of ruin, misery, and loss of lifa, The floods are general in the South of Spain, and the amount o 2 damage done there is terrible. At the port of Almeria 400 houses have been destroyed, and 4,ooopfamilies are, ruined, having, lost everything they possessed. Fifteen dead bodies have been found. In CarDellon and in Valencia also thsioods have had most disastrous results. The province of Toledo,. however, had suffered still worse. All the rail- ways-are under water, and many trains he been thrown off the line. The town of: Consuerga, containing 7,0 a ,inhabitants,, is almost entirely in ruins, and more thanl,soo perscne have perished. Almost all,bhe houses were swept away by the flood, the rush of seater being so sudden that, the occupants were taken by surprise when asleep, and were unabls to make theirescape. The aspect of the town is frigh.tful,. So far 40 bodies have been recovered, but hundreds of dead persons and animals areseen floating down the swollen sewers. The Government has sent a delegate to the town to assist the sufferers, and a forma engineers with provisions of all sorts is, expected. Several women have already died of hungem, The Queen, Regent has despatched her steward with instructions to distribute bread, wine, and 50,000 banes in money among the unfortunate inhabit. ants. 41 large body of workmen are actively engaged burying the dead. 'Jibe Government is taking steps to, render assistance, to the sufferers by the floods and a national subscript has been opened. The newspapers also express their neediness to receive money for the re- lief of the distress.. Even now the full extent of the dis- aster is not know.ra,,and no details have yet been received particularly from towns in the neighbourhood of Consuerga, where terrible floods have occurred. The wine and corn, crops have been completely destroyed. Urda, Villefranca, Camanas, and Yebenes, town in tho province of Toledo, as well as Vera in Andalusia, have suffered considerably by the inundation. MADRI. TRUESDAY. —The gendarmerie have been ob. liged to use force in order .to compel men to share in the work of recovering the bodies of the victims of the floods at Consuegra. Sixteen, robbers have been caught red- handed while rifling the clothing of the corpses. Up to yesterday 945 corpses have been recovered. The national subscription now amounts to £20,000. The inhabitants of Consuegra sleep in the open air. They have no means of obtaining food themselves, and the quantity of provisions supplied from outside sources is insufficient
The schooner Morris Wilson has capsized off the coast of Nova Scotia, and 14 of the crew have been drowned.

On the evening of Monday Mr. Foard revised the lists for the townships of Warrington (extra municipal) Poulton-with-Fearnhead, Rixton-with-Glazebrook, and Woolston-with-Martinscroft. The political parties were represented as at Penlieth. The business was mostly of a routine character. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor' appeared on behalf of the Rev. G. Alton, of St. Barnabas Church, to claim a vote in respect of a freehold benefice, of church and laud, of the yearly value of 40s. and upwards. The vote was allowed.—The vote as a freeholder of the Rev. H. V. Pigot, of St. Paul's Church, was also allowed. The Liberals objected to the vote of Joseph Eaves,of Manchester-road, Rixton. The Revising Barrister, addressing,the assistantoverseer,said that when a man moved he did not car is carry h vote with him; it belonged to the premises, and if he moved only next door and into a house belonging to the same land- lord the word successive should be put in. The vote was attached to the premises and not to the voter per- sonally; he did not carry it about with him like personal luggage. The vote was disallowed. NEWTON DIVISION. Mr. James T. div.head: 'THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE 'OF A TUDDLEIL
div.p: 'THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE 'OF A TUDDLEIL
DRIVEN TO DESPERATION BY A DRUNKEN-
WIFE.

At the.magistratee,eourt, Warrington, on Thurs- itiay,'Thomas Worsley, a puddler at Bewsey Forge, and living at 67 Ha dock-st., was charged, he hay- ickg,j ust.recovered from his injuties,with attempting to,commit suicide by cutting his' throat. The Chief Constable said the prisoner had a wife and nine children, four of theca married, and had one of the best.of characters for ,sobriety and industry. About 25 minutes-to six on the morning of the 18th P.S. Zones and P.C. Robinson received information that he had out his throat at his house. Thy went there, and in a bedroom upstairs found the defendart lying °lathe bed with his throat cut, his clothesl being saturated, and the bedclothes and the floor bei'm be- smeared, withblood, and a razorlyine on the ta hie by his side. He was still alive, though bleeding proCusely. Dr. Adamt was sent for and attended to him,and he then became very wild and violent, it being all theoflicers could do to hold him. Mr. Hunt expressed the opi.aion ' that the drunken habits of the defendant's wife .had 'brought on the depression of spirits which caused him ro attempt suielde.—Dr. Adams said the wound extended right across the throat severing the windpipe •completel y through.—Alderman Sutton :It seems almost a miracle he should get better at all.—Dr. Adams said he had never seen such a gash before, and never seen anyone with a like wound get better. In renly to the Bench, the doctor expressed the opinion that the defendant had merely suffered from a momentary suicidal impulse which was not likely to recur. He did not think there was now anything wrong in the defendant's mental con- dition.—Mr. Hunt said he believed the wife had been , kept sway from the house of late,and it would be better if she kept away altogether.—Dr. Adams said he had de- clined to accede to a request that she might have access to him.—Thomas Worsley, aged 19, the defendant's son, said he had no idea as to the cause of his father's at- tempting suicide, except that it was his wife's drinking. —John Worsley, a married man, the defendant's eldest son, said for the last two or three months his father had been very low-spirited through his wife drinking. She had been doing so for eleven or twelve years, and had hardly ever been sober during that time. She would come to the house again if not stopped.—Mr. Hunt said the Workhouse authorities had declined to take the defendant in to be treated, as his was not an Infirmary case. Hence he had had to be watched by a policema n in his bedroom ever since the 18th ult. It was hard for a constable to be penned up in a little bedroom all the time. He had acted as a deterrent to the wife, who had come creating disturbances, but would have to be with- drawn now.—Alderman Sutton asked the defendant whether he felt strong enough to resist the temptation to take his life, and he replied " I will never do it any more, sir."—Alderman Sutton: Supposing your wife annoys you again, would that affect you ?—The defen- dant; No, I should not be bothered with her any more. —He was bound over in his own recognizances of £5, and his two sons were bound over as sureties for him in I the sum of £lO each for his re-appearance if necessary, I and he was ordered to pay 6s. 6d. costs.

At the City of London Registration Court a claim was made for a vote on behalf of Lord Robert Cecil, son of the Marquis of Salisbury, in respect ot certain chambers in the Temple. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1891 RIVER FOYLE DISASTER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19, 1891 RIVER FOYLE DISASTER.
FLOWER SHOW AT CROFT.

SPEECH BY MR. T. W. LEGH, M.P. On'Saturday the annual show in cannection with the Horticultural Society was held in the Board School. Croft. The. membership of the society hav- ing fallen during the year, the entries were some- what under the average. Taking into considera- tion the unfavourable weather which has been ex- perienced lately.the show must be regarded as very satisfactory. Vegetables and fruit were fairly good, and the cut flowers were admirable specimens. Mr. 'R. Harrison and Mr. T. Wilkinson, both of New- ton, discharged the duty of judging the exhibits. The other officials were Messrs. James Shaw, Wm. •Fazakerley, Edward Monks, Henry Green, William Sanderson, Nathan Taylor, jun., John Worthington, and James Green, Committee.; John Sanderson, treasurer; and William C. Savage and John Clough, , secretaries. ' The Rector, in introdueing Mr. Lee' remarked that every horticulturist or florist was, as the apostle put it, working together with God. Mr_ T. W. Legb, M.P., who was cordially received, saidthat it was tortunate that only a few words were expected from him, because he was afraid there were 'few persons who were less qualified than he was to give an opinion upon that exhibition. Still, it did not re- , quire any special knowledge of agriculture orloriculture in order to appreciate the advantages of such an ex- hibition‘as the one being held that day. As an ignorant ,person, he should be inclined to divide it into two parts —the useful and the ornamental. No less illustrious a )person than Mr. Gladstone had called attention recently to the value of the production of vegetables and fruits on a small scale; and he had snecially advocated what was small culture. He considered the suggestion an excellent one, and well worth following. 114 regards the more ornamental portion, by which he meant the pro- duction.oflflowers, it did not require any special intelli- gence to appreciate the beauties of cottage gardens. lEnglish people'were earoneously supposed by many per- sons to beonore, or less, devoid of artistic taste. He was convinced that was a totally wrong impression. He had travelledover mast of the countries in'Europe, and in no country were to be found villages which would ap- proach in beauty and care the villages innglish agri- cultural districts. (Hear, hear.) More time and trouble were expended in making gardens attractive in this country than was the case in any other, ,and the'circumstance was greatly te 'the credit of the-English. The advantages of such an exhibition as the present weretapparent. In the first place, such an exhibition afforded a welcome break in what was pro- hably a somewhat monotonous existence. Many of the villagers, no doubt, looked forward to ,it with pleasure, and retained pleasant recollecticns of it after it was over In the second place, it encouraged a healthy spirit of , competition, which, in the words of Mr. Gladstone, was • an excellent thing for all of us," especially when it was a competition of the friendly character he saw. that day. •On the whole, it must be admitted that slower shows , were of much service, and he trusted it might • long be the aim of the residents of Croft to maintain such an ; excellent exhibition. (Applause.) He had been asked topropose a vote of thanks to the judges, and he did so with very great pleasuse, because as far as his .experi- .eneewent, judging appeared to be a somewhat thankless takk. It was absolutely impossible to satisfy everybody but in the faces around, he was unable to disoover any -signs of discontent. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Captain Withington seconded the vote,. and it was ac- , 'corded, and acknowledged.

EIGHTEEN LIVES LOST. The number drowned in the collisicn on the River Foyle has been brought up to eighteen, the bodies of two men who were thought to have escaped having been found. The Mayor of London- derry has called a town's meeting to start a subscription list for the benefit of the sufferers. At half-past six o'clock on Saturday evening the last of the boats of the grappling party arrived at Derry, having five bodies on board. The scene at the quay was most impressive, a vast crowd looking on whilst the remains were being wrapped in rugs and borne to the mortuary. It is stated that several of the victims had got within a few strokes of the shore. Francis M'Keever, the owner of the steam launch, was brought before the magistrates on Saturday morning on a charge of causing the deaths by mismanagement. He was remanded, but admitted to bail. An inquest was held in the course of the day at which a verdict of "Accidental drowning" was returned. Mr. Graerne Hunter, a Scotch gentleman, who had brought about 150 men to work at Londonderry Quay during a strike of local quay labourers, took twenty-three men and his two children down the river for an excursion on Friday evening. Rith them was Francis M'Keever, a ferryman, who owned the launch. They had gone several miles, and were returning about eight o'clock, when Messrs. Steel and Bentnie's steamer Albatross came into collision with the craft. The launch, it appears came bow on to the steamer, struck her sponsor, and shortly afterwards sank. The captain of the Albatross lowered boats and picked.up a number of men. Several others swam ashore, and one man named Herbert Smith, of Belfast, brougnt with him one of Mr. Graeme Hunter's children. The other was lost. The river was com- paratively narrow at the place, but the night, though cloudless and starry, was very dark. Mr. Graeme Hunter says : I was in the stern with a little girl on each knee. Mr. M'Keever himself was at the [helm, and one of his men was keeping a look-out. We had lights out, I am perfectly sure of that. The crash was the first warning I got. I dashed forward through my men, and a glance showed me that we were sink- ing. The launch's boats were clean stoved in, and the water was rushing in. All was excitement, and I knew the seconds were precious. I feared we might get into the steamer's paddles, which I could now see clearly. I called to M'Keever, and our engines were backed,in the hope that we might reach the shore before she sank. My men divided my thoughts with my little girls. I called to those near the bows to follow me astern to which I ran catching up my little girls. I handed one to Mearns, and the ether to another of my men, both of whom I knew could swim well. Each jumped from the sinking boat, and. made for the shore, and I turned to look after my men. A second later we were all in the water, and the launch was gone. I can swim, but knew some of my men coald not. When I came to the surface I found myself in the centre of a struggling crowd. The two men nearest me were sinking, and I seised one with each arm and kept myself and them afloat with my legs. The boat from the Albatross was coming quickly towards us,when I felt myself seized below the water. *I had given myself up for lost, andl was actually being pulled down, when my hair, short as it was, was grabbed by a stout hand, and a -second later I was hauled into the Albatross's boat with my two men. All this time the rescue work was going on all around us, and we did all men could do. The tneu of the Albatross could not have done more." Herbert Smith, Belfast, the man who saved Mr. Hunter's child, gives the following narrative : " We were coming home nicely. Keath, of Dublin, was stand- ing besides-the funnel playing the accordian, when sud- denly he -shouted 'Help! help! murder! Look at the steamer.' I.shouted Hold your tongue, you fool.' But the words were hardly out of my mouth when a crash came. Even then I didn't know how serious it was. Mr. Hunter rushed forward past me and immediately rushed bank. I ran after him. I was beside the children, and I said. " Mr. Hunter, you will want somebody to look after the kids.' He said, ;Yes Smith, will you take one ?' I said, Yes sir.' Wm. Mearns, of Volga-et., Belfast, was near me. Mr. Hunter said, • Bill, will you take one'? 'I want to see about the men.' Poor Bill said, • Certainiy, sir, I can get her ashore.' The poor wee things were clinging to each other wildly, and each one screamed, • Take me to my mether.' We had to pull them asunder, Bill and me'; and, ,just then, the water came over the gunwale; and when she was sinking Mearns jumped. The same minute my little one clasped me. I went dawn over the neok first, and then came up and held the diild as high over my head as I could. Before jumping,.l shouted, Billi.jump for your life.' When I got to the surface three men were on one side of me, and two our the other. I had to knock two off me, and another -shouted. Keep back, men; don't you see he has got •child r They then left me,and I was ashore before I'knew. When I reached the beach I was totally exhameted, but someone came, and the little child lam so proud of -saving was soon in Mr. Corscaden's kitchen."
A. LODGING HOUSE PANDEMONIUM.

At the Magistrates' Court, Warrington, on Tues- day, John Rourke, Wm. Coleman, Michael Stan- ton, and James Long, were charged with using on the previous day threatening language to Alfred Bruchemite, keeper of the •model lodging-house, Friar's-Green, who is a Frenchman; and James Kelly was charged with assaulting P.C. Clarke on the same occasion, Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution. He stated that the landlord stopped them from playing at cards in the lodging-house on Sunday afternoon, and as the result thy com- menced a disturbance and continued creating an uproar till Monday, keeping the whole neighbour- hood awake all Sunday night by singing and shout- ing as hard as they could. Mr. Browne detailed their violence and threats towards the complainant, and said he had to be continually sending for the police.—Mr. Bruchemite said on Sunday there were 74 lodgers in his house. On Sunday afternoon, five of them, the prisoners, were playing at cards, when he stopped them. They kept him 'up till half- past two next morning,shouting and singing, and he had to get the assistance of P.C. Hardy to quieten them. He got- them out, and after dinner they came back, as he was hanging up some pictures, and with an oath about his nationality threatened violence to him. He had a hammer in his hand, and said he would use it to the first man that touched him. He then escaped from them. They were like mad devils. He had to send for policemen all day long, and hide himself. P.C. Clarke came and Kelly struck him and knocked him down and Stanton took a running kick at him, as he was rising and was on his knees. The others picked half bricks up and threw them at witness driving him out of the house. He was in bodily fear of the men,and most of the lodgers left,there being only 30 there on Monday night.—John Murray, assistant to Mr. Brurchemite, corroborated. He said Rourke threatened both of them, saying he would do three months for them. Witness had to hide himself. A woman working in the house said, Long threatened to kill Bruchemite.—P.C. Clarke said Kelly struck him with the fist,and Stanton came at him with a kick when Mr. Bruchemite knocked him down. Three of the men threatened to kill him. All of the prisoners were drunk except Kelly. They were all locked up.—Bruche- mite said the men seemed to have formed themselves into a ring. They beat several men on Saturday, and there was blood all over the kitchen. Rourke was stripped to the waist fighting. On another occasion three men were lying with their heads bleeding on the table, all through the gang "slaughtering all round," and nobody dare stop them.—Kelly was sent to jail for a month's hard labour and said "Thank you, sir ;" and the other men were bound over in the sum of £lO each for six months ; in default 14 days each.
PROSECUTION OF A WARRINGTON
PUBLICAN.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, Minnie Tonks, landlady of the Ben's Paw Inn, Buttermarket-st., was charged with keeping her house open for the supply of liquor during illegal hours at 10.20 p.m., on the 6th inst., and John Dun- bobbin, painter, 35, Cairo-st., was charged with aiding and abetting. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, ap- peared for the defence. P.C. Smith said he was on duty in plain clothes in Buttermarket-st., at the time mentioned, and saw Dunbobbin leaving the house by the entry, with a half gallon jar in his possession. Witness told Sergeant Rowbottom who followed Dunbobbin up Sankey-st., and called him ,by name. lie then passed the jar to a companion. The Sergeant asked Dunbobbin wheie he got it from and he replied, after some hesitation, that he paid for it at the Bear's Paw at a quarter to 10, and left it till he came back from the Hop Pole, at 10.20. The Sergeant took him and his companion, Robert Littlewood, back to the house, and the landlady confirmed his statement. There was no hesitation on the part of Mrs. Tonks in telling him.—Mr. Jenkins in cross-examining the witness at this point told him he need not look at Mr. Hunt for instruc- tions.—The Mayor said he thought Smith was giving very good evidence—Smith (to Mr. Jenkins) : I think it is very unfair of you to say that, because I am speaking fairly, I am speaking as much for Mrs. Tonks as I can. —Mr. Jenkins -: I don't want you to say that ; I have a complete answer, I don't want any favours.—The Mayor: I was just thinking that it is a long time since I beard an officer make such a splendid statement of a case.—P.C. Rowbotham corroborated as to the part taken by him in the matter. The jar had been placed in a recess among some empty ginger beer bottles outside the door for the defendant to call for, and the house was opened to give him the jar.—Mr. Jenkins maintained that there was no case against his clients who had paid for the liquid at a quarter to ten and merely called for it afterwards, and pointed out that the Licensing Act of 1874 allowed this to be done.—Mrs. Tonks and her little daughter gave evidence supporting her solicitor's statement. The for- mer said she had lived at the house 11 years, and there had been no complaint against it.—Robert Littlewood confirmed their testimony.— the Bench dismissed the cases, on the ground urged by Mr. Jenkins, though the Mayor remarked that the fact of this being the law would lead to a deal of trouble.—Mr. Hunt: They have not all such good characters as Mrs. Tonks.—The Mayor complimented the police officers highly on the way in which they had given their evidence, and Mr. Jenkins concurred in his opinion.—The Mayor commended the officers also for their alertness in the matter, and though admitting that Mrs. Tonks had conducted her house well advised her not to sail so near the edge of the law in future.—Mr. Hunt • I don't think she'll do it again.
Mr. Gladstone has definitely informed :the Mayor of Newcastle that he will visit that city in connection with •the sitting of the National Liberal Federation.

THE SHIP CANAL. j DOWN A IIAYDOCK COAL PIT.
THE NVEAVER SECTION COMPLETED.

With the completion of a second section of the Ship Canal the shareholders of the Company may look forward with some confidence to the days of profit-earning. Before the end of the present month the salt boats of the Weaver Navigation will depend no longer on Mersey tides, but will sail securely into the canal at NV eston Point, and pass through the gates at Eastham into the deep navig- channel of the river, and so to their port of destin- ation. On this traffic, or on a considerable portion of it, tolls will be levied, which will pass into the exchequer of the Company. Since the Eastham section was opened two or three months ago the attention of the engineers has in a large measure been centred on the adjoining Ince section. This length covers a distance of seven miles, and owing to the soft, marshy character of much of the soil through which it passes, it has been necessary to pay close attention to the pitching of the banks. The work was declared finished on Saturday, and to all outward appearance it is a most olid and satisfactory performance. On Monday the letting in of the waters began, a depth of over two feet beidg registered towards the close of the afternoon. The full measurement of 26 feet will soon be reached, and any surplus water which may then come in will pass away through the tidal openings into the Mersey estuary. There was none of the excitement on Monday which attended the comple- tion of the Eastham section. In the presence simply of a few workmen. Mr. Jones, the agent of the section, lifted a sluice (much after the fashion of turning a tap), and then :through a huge pipe the water poured from the full Eastham section in- to the empty Ince section. The proceeding was of the simplest character. Between the two sections there is a neck of land eight or ten yards in width. Piercing the soil is a pipe ninety feet long and four feet in diameter, one end of it being in the Eastham waters and the other emerging some ten or twelve feet above the bed of the Ince portion. By means of the sluice the quantity of water entering from the Eastham side of the dam can be nicely regulated. Mr. Jones lifted the sluice just so high as to admit half the flow of water which the pipe would carry. Out at the Inca end it hurried in a fine stream into a wooden trough, which carried it without much violence into the bed of the canal. In three and a half hours a depth of eighteen inches was measured, and at four o'clock in the afternoon the depth was two feet. By Wednesday morning there was about ten feet of waterin the cutting and the full depth of 26 feet is ex- pected to be reached to-day (Saturday). It should be mentioned that in certain portions of the section there has been a depth of seven feet of water for some time, and this water has been confined by two small cross dams, which will be swept away by the dredger when the whole length is filled to its proper measurement. The importance of the opening of the Weaver section cannot be over estimated. In the first place it will relieve a large quantity of plant and many men who will be transferred to Runcorn and other sections higher up where the work is very difficult and a little backward. But a greater advantage will be that a portion of the canal will be open for moneymaking if not profitmaking. Nearly twelve miles, or one-third of the whole length of the canal will be in use. For some months past the im- mense Marsh Lock, previously described has been ready for transferring traffic from the Weaver Canal to the Ship Canal and in the course of a few weeks the salt and chemical traffic from Winsford, Northwich and Weston will be able to proceed by this means on to Liverpool at all states of the tide. Besides the Canal passes along the front of Weston Point Dock and while the river wall is being constructed the traffic from the docks can be con- ducted through the canal and Marsh Lock.

TILE WEAVER :JAND THE SHIP CANAL. Further operations will be entered upon at the end of the present week, and these, it is expected, will be com- pleted before the 29th inst. The object in view is to connect the Weaver Canal with the Ship Canal. The point of connection is at Weston Marsh, and the method of it is the fine system of locks which have here been built. Between the locks and the canal there is the channel of the Weaver, which the dredgers are making deep—a work which is practically finished. Between the channel,again,and the canal there is a dam or neck of land some eight-or ten yards wide. When the water in the canal is at the full depth of 26ft. the dredgers now in the Weaver channel will cut the dam away. This done, they will pass down the canal to Ellestnere Port and assist in clearing the neck of land which divides the Ince and Eastham sections. There will then be a clear stretch of water from the gates at Eastham straight to the locks at Weston Marsh, and eleven miles, or about one-third the length of the canal, will be opened for traffic. The most difficult part of the whole task of the canal engine- ers will then have been accomplished. The point marked "A" on the Parliamentary plans will have been reached, and the Company will be at liberty to make all possible progress—a thing they are yet expressly debarred from— on the adjoining Runcorn section. On the virtual accom- plishment of this important portion of the undertaking the engineers of the Company deserve warm congratula- tion. Apart from the great engineering features of the canal, such as the locks at Eastham and the sluices at the mouth of the Weaver—a remarkable monument in mas- onry—they have had to meet and overcome many grave difficulties. A very considerable portion of the Canal is built on land snatched from the sea. In the absence of the tides a deep foundation of piling has had to be laid on which to construct sea walls. The inland portions also have in places given the engineers no small amount of anxiety. It may be interesting to indicate the character of the troubles which faced the workers on the Ince section. From Ellesmere Port to the river Gowy which passes in a syphon deep under the Canal to dis- charge itself into the Mersey), there was a tolerably easy cutting through hard clay. From this point to Ince, however, the soil consists of soft marsh clay and peat, and it was necessary continuously to guard against the occurence of slips. For a long distance after this point a clean cutting had to be made through the hard red rock, and as the surface was hilly there is a•straight wall at one point not less than seventy fee!; high. After the rock there was more marsh clay to contend with, and finally a long stretch of shifting sand. As a consequence of having to deal with soil of this sort, the slopes of the Ince section have had to be made very flat, being in the worst places only one foot vertical to four feet horizontal. In its completed state nothing could look more substan- tial than this section. There has been no niggardliness in the use of masonry and in some places of brick. As an extra strengthening fascine work, such as we see in the canals of the Low Countries, has been introduced. The strong cording of willows in the banks is quite a feature of this portion of the work, and in summers to come their greenness will pleasantly break the monotony of stone walls. During the course of Monday morning the operations at Ellesmere Port were witnesses by Mr. W. H. Topham, the experienced manager of works, who has had over- sight of great engineering enterprises in different parts of the world ; Mr. Price, the chief agent, and Mr. Fitzgibbon, the resident engineer of the section. Mr. Topham and Mr. Price also made a passing examination of the work from the mouth of the Weaver to Latchford .
BY LEX.

I have long experienced a desire to invade the mystic depths of one of the coal pits in the Haydock district, but from various reasons, probably a feeling of reluctance to quit the light, or my inability to secure an opportune occasion, I have, during my thirteen years of residence in this gigantic colliery district, been unable to satisfy my curiosity. Whenever I have given expression to such wish, I have been met with the discouraging remark "Not for worlds, would Igo down." " Why ?" I natur- ally asked. " Oh ! I prefer to remain on terra firma in old England," and again they have said : "I don't like swinging over a hole, suspended by a rope." Still I thought I would like to explore the depths from which we obtain one of the articles necessary to our comfort. Last Saturday afternoon the opportunity for doing so presented itself, in the shape of two lady friends, who came from a distance, and who like myself, had long wished to descend a mine. accordingly set about obtaining the necessary permit, which I am bound to say, owing to the extreme kindness of Mr. Sewart, the assistant manager of Messrs. Evans and Co's. mines, was readily forthcoming. As a further proof of this gentleman's obliging disposition he very generously offered to accompany us down the pit and afford us every information in his power. I selected New Boston No. 2 nit, as being the driest, cleanest and perhaps from my point of view the safest, though Mr. Sewart said if I had left the choice to him he would have taken us down the Wood Pit. Bearing in mind, however, th dreadful explosion which took place in that pit in 1878, I preferred giving the scene of that disaster a very wide berth. I might mention in passing that, Mr. Sewart told us, that a week or two ago, they found an Old lamp near the site of the explosion. But to get on. By arrangement, myself and lady friends met Mr. Sewart at the pit, and found every- thing ready for our convenience. The first oper- ation we had to undergo, was the "turning out" process, which to the uninitiated I may say means the clearing out of your pockets such things as matches, pipes and tobacco. These being left be- hind and having suitably attired ourselves for the descent, we proceeded to the cage, and having pre- viously been supplied with lamps, we stepped in; another manager, Mr. Makinson, occupying the top deck of the cage. At a signal given, we began to d scend, but doubtless out of consideration for our feelings, the engineman, let us down very lightly indeed, and we -did not experience any of those sensations which it is said acccmpany a first des- cent.

We were quickly at the bottom, the cage resting over what is called the dib hole. We stepped out of the cage, but for aught we knew, we might have been in some unfathomable depths, so dense was the darkness. After a stay of a few minutes,objects became a little more distinct, and with the aid of our lamps, and a little floundering, we were able to proceed. Turning a corner to tile left, we walked a short distance along an arched tunnel, and pre- sently found ourselves at the uuderlooker's office. Entering, we were asked to be seated until we be- came accustomed to the darkness "which could be felt," and straightway made ourselves comfortable. The office was fitted up with roughly made seats along each side, in the centre being a square table, and we were told that it was in this place where the firemen partook of their meals, and made their reports as to the condition of the workings. In order to allay any uneasiness which might affect us, as to the probability of an explosion, Mr. Sewart produced the report book, showing the fireman's entry for the previous day, in which he reported the aosence of gas, and that the pit was safe. Many of the mysteries of the working of the pit were divulged to us whilst resting in the office. From a small cupboard Mr. Makinson produced a neat little electric battery, which he stated was used in connection with the firing of shots. The charge, which consists of roburite, is lodged in the hole which has already been prepared in the coal, and attached to it is a detonator,secured to the end of a piece of wire. To the end of this is attached what is called a cable, which is a piece of enciosed wire, 50 yards long. This is again attached to the electric battery, and when all is clear, and every- body at a safe distance, one turn of the battery handle sends a current of electricity along the wire and the shot is exploded, removing perhaps several tons of coal. To practically explain the process, Mr. Sewart placed a detonator outside the office, and closing the door, fixed the wire to the battery, and exploded it, a loud report being the result. We had now got pretty well accustomed to the gloom, and leaving the office, we proceeded on a long tramp of nearly a mile to a working al- most under Garswood Park. On the way we had leisure to admire the grand specimen of en- gineering in the construction of the spacious arched road, and the many branches from the main way. Passing along, we were able to keep in an upright position, and so far suffered no inconvenience. Simplicity in working seemed to be the predominant feature, and nothing could be more simple than the method of lowering wagons , loaded with coal down what is called the "jib." To a train of wagons is attached a wire rope, which revolves on a drum, the other end of the rope being attached to a train of empty wagons, so that the weight of the loaded trucks down the incline pulls the empty ones up. In this there is, no doubt, a certain amount of danger, owing to the narrowness of the road, but to obviaLe the possibility of any- body being crushed by the passing wagons, refuge ; holes are provided on each side of the road, into which a man can take shelter until the wagons have passed. We had not much time, however, to minutely explore every object of interest, as Mr. Makinson, who acted as leader, kept us fairly on the march, aryl after passing through several places where the roof was thickly studded with props, we reached the first working in No. 3 district. Here , what are called "faults" were pointed out, and ex- plained to us, after which we vowed never arin tg grumble if we found a little "bass" amongst out ; coal.
Our experiences from this point onward, were quite the reverse of comfortable, and although we- many times wondered how we were to get along, Mr. Sewart said that VMS nothing—that_ pit was

more a show pit. I could not herp wondering if that was a show pit, what the other pits were like. For above a hundred yards we were coMpelled to walk with bent heads, being reminded many times to keep one eye on the ground and another on the roof, and we should be all right. Again we came in a kirly lofty passage, and again for sore.: dis- tance we had almost to go on our hands and knees, until I wondered if I should ever be able to walk straight again. Arrived at another working the ladies were allowed to take a pick, and dig from the side a memento, in the shape of a lump of coal, which they afterwards carefully treasured. We now took another turning, along a narrow gulley, until we were brought to a standstill by an air jib, through which Mr. Makinson crawled. There was not above 18 inches of space, but to get on with our ramble, we had to shuffle through this narrow open- ing as best we could. With sundry mishaps, we managed to get safely to the other side. On we i went, n the same recumbent position for what seemed an interminable length of time, our way being at last nearly blocked by a large quantity of slag which had fallen from the roof. We however clambered over this, and made for the furnaces, which remiVed one of the place which is said to exist still further below the earth. Here the ladies assisted to "fire up," and we then continued our journey to the stables, where the stud of 13 ponies, were comfortably enjoying their meal, and we soon afterwards reached the bottom of the shaft, pre- pared to again view the light of day. Stepping into the cage, at a given signal we were- speedily at the top, and breathed a sigh of relief, that we could again become natural. To conclude cur visit, we inspected the lamp room, and found there several hundreds of lamps in a beautifully clean condition. Here every man who works in the P ' it is supplied with a lamp, which after being lighted is fastened, and secured by a rivet, stamped on one end "R" and on the other "E," and after being so rivetted it is impossible for the collier to open them. From this pit which is 240 yards deep labout 750 tons of coal per day is obtained, and it gives employment to 200 colliers, day wagemen and boys, besides several girls who work on the brow.. I must again exprets my thanks for the kindness of' Mr. Sewart and Mr. Makinson, in so generously accompanying us, and for their very lucid ex- planations.

div.head: AT RUNCORN.
div.p: AT RUNCORN.

great progress is being made at the Bridgewater Lock intende 1 to admit vessels from the river into Runcorn Docks. Work is proceeding night and day, between tides, but theprocess of making the concrete foundations and walls is one requiring the exercise of great care and judgment and to an outsider it will seem to rise slowly but surely. Piling operations are also being carried on for the cqnstruction of the river wall and the lock for the Widnes traffic is beginning to wear a somewhat finished appearance. Higher up at the Old Quay steam navvies are tearing up the soil in an endeavour to cut the canal to a depth of 60 feet, which is required at this point. The most striking features between Weston Point and Latchford are the deviation railways and the high- level bridges. This work is going pn very satisfac- torily. The spoil banks are already bttilt, and in places the slopes are now covered with grass. The bridges, carried in a single span a splendid height above the water level of the canal, are in a forward state. With all their timber supports they are even to-day imposing struc: tures. A low-level swing bridge at Moore Lane is almost ready for use, operations being conducted from a neat red-brick bydraulic house. The 29th inst. is provisionally fixed for the passage of the first boats from the Weaver Navigation to the Ship Canal.

div.head: VYRNWY WATER SCHEME.
div.p: THE VYRNWY WATER SCHEME.
ANOTHER STOPPAGE.

There was a rumour in Liverpool, on Wednesday, that the supply of water from Vyrnwy to Liverpool had ceased. It seems that for about two days there has been an enormous amount of fresh water in the river, and at Fidler's Ferry this has caused the formation of a " bank" over the pipes, which has prevented a diver from getting near them in order to rectify leakages. Somehow or another these leakages in the pipe will occur and it is practically safe to say that the services of a diver have very seldom since the pipe was laid been dispensed with. With regard to the work appertaining to the per- manent scheme, it may be mentioned that up to Thurs- day night the boring shield had been driven to a distance oil7Bft. from the Lancashire side of the river, and that 112 rings of ironwork have been finished. 'There are at present'about 40 men engaged at the crossing works, of whom about 20 live on the works. The remainder have their quarters at Penketh, Widnes, and Runcorn. On Thursday morning Mr. John Barry, water engineer, proceeded to Norton Reservoir for the purpose of super- intending the turning on of the Vyrnwy supply. Norton is the " balancing reservoir" on the Vyrnwf aqueduct nearest to Fidler's Ferry, where diving operations at the temporary crossing are stated to be proceeding satisfac- torily. After the defects in the pipe line across the river have been thoroughly remedied, several days will elapse before the full supply. is again flowing into Prescot.
