The conversion of Mrs. BESAITT to a Theosophy belief in Theosophy has caused special on Trial.

attention to be dram to this new religion, or, perhaps we. Silt Mild say, new form of religion, for it is claimeathat "Theosophy istfthe root-truth that lies at the basis of every great religion: It is not Spiritualism as it is ordinarily 'understood, and yet it hafe much in eommon with it in its thought transference., manifestations, and precipitations. Mrs. BEsAvr professes to have. received letters from the Great Brotherhood— letters ,which bring news from the invisible world, .1 and conveyed not in the ordinary wayby post but by some pcocess of" precipitation" which nobody but a Theosophist can possibly understand. It seems te us that Mrs. BESINT having explained co, much should explain morn—that is if she can. She has set herself to the task of: advocating; Theosophy, and has come to the, conclusion: that "the race has reached a* stage in its evolution at which it is fit to. acoire and! utilise the Hidden Wisdom." Thi,„ being the case,. it is tantalising—not to say absurd r—to cut off the revelation just where the interest commencen. What is the use of telling people - anything at all about " precipitr.ted" letters,unless , she is prepared to lay bare all tad- evidence she*, can produce,. as a means of enforcing conviction P 7 Any person/is in a. position to say„ as Shakespeare:, has it, that he can "call spirits. -from the vastY. deep ; r but the. 'location of questions is—" Will. they come when, he doth gall on them ?" Mrs-i. Itzsaarr, a few years ago, would havnbeen the firsti to scorn tho pretensions to Hidden Wisdom, or. occult powers,of any person who was not prepared. to give evidence,of their possession.; and she would; have been acting then as a rational being. 3,41-85. 11FAANT seema,to.have changed h3r.:.position ; but there is no.-evidence as yet of her- having become more rational..

The demand of the hard-headed! •British puhiic in these matters is" Give us facts,, and we will do our own, reasoning. upon them," and, it is with he object of gettingat the facts that Mr. Stuart C LERLAND. has offered "to give one thousand pounds to .any charity to. be- agreed uponeif a manifesta- tion ' claimed tobe supernatural can be produced in my' presence and that of a committee of salen, tific experts which 'cannot prove to the satiafac- tion of the • said committee to be explicabla on purely mundane ,principles." This is a daring Ichallenge, and;theissue is a clear one; but it, is as well to note that, even if Mr. CI: MUDIRLAND flails to explain "How.it is done," it will by no means fol- low that there has been a demetistration of mira- culous powers,. may simply mean that Mr. CIIMTMELAND not so well up irt'the mysteries of conjuring as he believes himself to bA. would'J be another thing of course if the experts were le6, to conclude that such manifestations as they may.l witness are •beyond any known means ofdproduc- tion. Even,that would not settle anything, but it' would send; people inquiring into Theosophy in the, belief that there might be "something in it!! For, instance, if Colonel DFSSMOND., were by "taking thought" to "remove a piano from one end efts, drawing-room to another " without being in contact with it,, or without any ether person or7thing operating upon it—that, if attested *3l scientific men,would set people thinking. And yet it is rto more than the Colonelhas, accozding to his statement, accomplished in Poolla, close to .Madras.. Indeed, he says "there is nothing ! mysterious in this "—meaning we suppose. that it 'is a mere trifle compared with what can be done by an out-and-out Theosophist when his mindis —so to, speak—in good form. What a ?ity it is by-the-by, the Ship, Canal navvies cannot be con- verted into thorough-going Theosochists ! It would be so much pleasanter removing tons of earth by force cf mind rather than, by fotee of muscle. However there is this to. be saW for Colonel DESMOISD that his. courage is apparently equal to his conviction, for he has accepted, Mr. CITNEBERLAND challenge., Ile says:— "I am, either an honest roan,.a knave% or a fool, and I should be a coward; to fear to attempt what I have never yet failed to accomplish. I. will there- fore accept Mr. Stuart Oumberland's challenge upon these terms:. A committee of gentlemen to be agreed upon as ludges ; I to demonstrate the possession of powers unexplainable upon any scientific or materialistic principle or theory. If I succeed, Mr. Stuart Cumberland to pay a thousand pounds to the said committee, to be distributed as they may think fit among the 'metropolitan charities. If I fail, I pay the like amount for the like purpose." There is nothing now to do but arrange for a suit- able committee, and suitable time, and place; and then,—well "We shall see what we shall see.'

TENNYSON tells us that " the Technical Instruction, thoughts of men are widened with the process of the suns" ; but the process is an exceedingly slow one, especially when it relates to matters of education. A Technical Institute is amongst the things that have been needed in Warrington for many years, and there has been no lack of suggestion that something should be done ; but until recently it looked as if the town would have to wait for one for a long long time. The matter was discussed during the Jubilee Year, and there was a respectable minor- ity who were in favour of the Jubilee being cele- brated by the foundation of an Institute. as might be deemed necessary; and Mr. CHARLES MADELEY, Secretary of the Committee, wrote and published a pamphlet on the subject with a view to stimulate thought and action. But there was no break in the somewhat dreary prospect until it was found that County Councils were to be en-- trusted with a considerable sum for the pur- pose of promoting technical instruction. This was particularly good news for County Boroughs, which could act immediately; but not having risen to the dignity of a County Borough, Warrington had to wait and wait, until the Lancashire County Council could say definitely what sum would be granted. It seemed at one. time that this delay would be fatal to anything being done this year; but happily the local Com- mittee had made all the preliminary preparations; and, assured of a grant of over £6OO, they are now in a posilion to commence operations. A capable - body of teachers has been engaged, and classes are being formed with the object of commencing work immediately. Syllabus and entrance forms are to be hr.d at the Museum and Library; and students would do well to give in their names forth- with, so that no time may be, lost, and the COM- mittee may know what to dein the way of making provision for tuition in the higher branches of instruction.

It will be seen that Evening Classes-will be the rule,thus permitting of the attendance of the young of both sexes who may be otherwise occupied dur- - ing.the day. A fee of five shillings for each class, ;for thersession, is the basis of charging, with a ;reduction to students taking two • or three related übjecta. For cookin and dressmaking the• charge is five shillings each, for al course of twelve lessons.. We are glad to see that such an excellent opportunity is being afforded gith• of acquiring knowledge of a kind which will be of service to them through life. Many of them will be willing in die time to make-some inferior creature happy, and they. cannot too soon learn that one of the ' quickest ways to man's heart is through his stomach. Besides, good cookery is-the highest economy. What would- be " waste ". becomes ".a • taste when properly utilised. And so with dressmaking.;-. • the young woman whoicen cut out- and use. her needle will dress better,. and at less cost than, her companion who has no skill in thexewmatters. Woman has -hitherto been somewhat neglected in matters educational, • but sha- has, a distinct place in • the syllabus • ,of the Wilrringt OM Technical Institute; and it ici-ta be hoped there will be no leek of .female studentm. Most of the subjects to be taught. can of course be taken by girls as- well as boys; and it would be- a good sign if the new departure resulted in something like friendly, rivalry be- - tween the uexesin a hundred familieain Warring- • ton. Very- muck,. it neei hardly be said„ depends ,upon parental. ancl many of them havait in their power to make or-mar the future of their children by giving, or neeecting to give, a right impulse •at the right time.. Having this, in raind, it only ..remains to be said that there can be no better training for those, who are leaving„. or have re- - wetly left the elementary schooll than that which -is, afforded at4a Technical Institute.

The idea had got abro ad that our Transat- • lantic cousins. had. taken possession. of a special field in this department a literature, and that. they would keep it to thero;elves.. But it is evi-. • dent from results that Messrs. MACMILLAJS and Co.. rightly gauged the public ta2to and their own powers to meet it. "The English Illustrated Magazine" presented itself as a marvel of cheapness • —the quality, taken. into account---from its first • appearance in 1883‘ It instantly secured a high place in the affections of all 107er5 of high-art in illustration, and it has held that place ever since. We have before us the volume forth() current year, and, comparing it with the earlier issues, it is gratifying, to observe the steady improvement which has-been made from year 'to year. It is.not too much tosay that nothing in, any magazine has . been published which is finer than the illustrations , by Mr.G:.Rein, R_S.A.,of the -article on Edinburgh by Mrs. OLIPHANT. , The monthly session in connection. with No. 1, Convention (South-west Lancashire) Was held at Orford Barracks on Saturday, commencing at 345 p.m. The session was presidedover by Bro. Colour- Sergeant T. Mantle, C.0.T., and was attended by 93 representatives and visitors from, Warrington, Sankey Bridges, Widnes, Earlestown, Asbton-in- Makertield, S. Helens,. Peasley cross, Handley,. Wigan, Bootle, and Livsrpool. The official reports_ mentioned visit of the van to the district covered by the Convention lodges,, and the.excellenti results. obtained. The Convention secretary recommended lodge secretaries to send reports of weekly meetings. to the press a little oftener. Hcfwas glad to see the excellent name for business the Convention had earned, both inside. and outside the South-west Lancashire district% and hoped it would be retained. The Treasurer reported a szall balance in hand., Bro. Clarke, P.C.C.T. (Earlestown), was deputed. to. complete arrangements for the new lodge at Downall Green.. Bros. Mantle, C.5i;1.T., Roberts, C.. Co., and Kean, C. Sec., were appointed in a similar- capacity for Penketh. The 4 Morning Star "Lodge (Peasley Cross) was, on application, admitted to affiliation with the Convention.. For next sessions which will be held at Peasley Cross on October 10th,, it was decided that Bro. Clarke should read a paper on "Aggressive Temperance Work," to be followed by a. discussion. Bro. R. Skaife (St. Helena), C.S.J.T., read an admirable paper on "juvenile Templary," which elicited a mild discussion and a vote of thanks. The session was closed in the usual form at 6.25 p.m., after which a substantial tea was partaken of. At 7.15 p.m. a public meeting was held, presided over by Councillor Dixon, whose opening address, urging all members to be firm to their pledges and asking non-members to give up drink at once, was well received. Addresses by Bro. R. W. Kirkus, D. Lucas (Liverpool), and Bro. Skaife (St. Helens), and songs, readings, and recitations brought a very interesting day's work to a close at 9.30 p.m. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canasta, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner " Office, by Cunard, Guion, American. The inhabitants of Winmarleigh-st., Warrington, object to circus tents being pitched occasionally in their neighbourhood. It is a nuisance to them. But they must have something to give variety to existence. Why not petition the Sanitary Com- mittee for an Intercepting Depot?

What next? At the Bootle Revision court twoinstances have,come to light of men who lodged with their wives, the gray mare being apparently very much the better horse. Living in this style is little better than having to say, in the words of the song—" My lodging's on the cold,cold ground."

The" Daily News "says :—" There has been an increase of late in the direct shipments of Egypt- ian cotton to America." This is very much like carrying coals to Newcastle; but the explanation is that cotton grown in Egypt is superior to the cotton produced in the United States, and very much superior to cotton from India.

The adage—" Take care of the pence and the pounds will take care of themselves" has been admirably illustrated in the case of the money raised for the building of the Buttermarket-st. Catholic Church, Warrington. Of £lO,OOO ob- tained by the late Father Hall, it is stated that as much as £3,000 was raised by penny suoscrip- Cons.

The Jingo section of the Parisian populace have been raising a shindy because " Lohengrin," the work of Wagner, a German, was being performed at the Opera House. It is true Wagner said un- pleasant things about the French ; but he is dead, and Frenchmen ought to be above such petty spite. However, the mischief-makers have been firmly dealt with and compelled to knuckle under.

A special correspondent of "The Trade Union- ist" is writing a series of articles on the chemical trade of St. Helens ; and, if half of what he states is true, more stringent regulations ought to be framei immediately for the protection of the health and the lives of the workers. The Govern- ment Inspector, whose report is quoted, is im- pr9ssed as we have been with t!e large number of fatalities which occur every year.

It is stated with regard to the Alkali Union that there are upwards of 153 stamps impressed on the conveyances, agreements, and other documents kept with the records of the company in London, representing payments to the Government by the company of more than £30,500. This heavy pay- ment is on the face of it a good thing for the National Exchequer; but it will have to be got back in the course of business.

Big trusts don't do big things for nought. In America they have run prices up from 10 to 50 per cent. • and in England the price of salt has been largely increased. The formation of trusts needs careful watching in this country, for, if reports are true they have resulted in the United States in a terrible grinding of the faces of the poor. It is the trust-mongers who are at the present plundering the people by means of the McKinley Act. And they call it Protection !

Here is a suggestive item of news :—" The arrangement for Adelina Patti's American tour is that she is to get £l,OOO for each night's singing, and also a share in the profits which remain. "Tis a mad world, my masters." One woman gets as much in a night for singing as another will get ins life-time for sewing—and the latter must work her fingers to the bone! There's something awfully wrong ; but how to right it? "There's the rub."

"On horror's head horrors accumulate." At Bolton, on Wednesday night, seventeen dress- makers were working at Constantine Brothers', when they suddenly threw up the windows, shout- ing "Fire !" and "Murder !" A crowd of 2,000 assembled, and broke through the plate-glass win- dows to the rescue. The fire brigade arrived, but there was no trace of fire or assailant. The • girls asserted that they saw a ghost. What can it have been P Not murder evidently. Perhaps it was a case of" manifestation" on the part of a mouse.

What is this about the Army and Navy? Haven't we been told by a hundred Tory orators that there never was such a Government as the present for looking after our fighting forces? And here is Lord Charles Beresford, an authority on the subject—and a Tory to hoot—gravely stating, in a letter to the Tories of North Kensington,that "he is of opinion that on the outbreak of war, we should be placed at the greatest disadvantage from the want of a system of action in conjunction with both branches." What does it all mean?

Lord Tennyson had something to say about the fleet when the Liberals were in power. How would it be to revive a stanza by way of back- ing up Lord Charles Beresford ? Thus: You, you that have had the ordering of the fleet, If you should only compass her disgrace, When all men starve, the wild mob's million feet Will kick you from your place,
Ifut then too late, too late. No, its never "too late" to kick out a Tory Government; but bide a wee; the General Elec- tion cannot be far off!

Southport will he a hundred years old next year, and it is suggested that it centenary should be, celebrated by an exhibition—a great musical ex- hibition. It is not a bad note to strike—" linked sweetness long drawn out." There would, of course, be a special building and a feast of good things at the Winter Gardens. But there is al- ways something good there ; and the New Opera House, which has just been opened in connection with the Gardens, is stated to be one of the prettiest in the Kingdom.

Our racy contributor "Turn 0' Dick 0' Bob's has received an interesting letter from Mr. Glad- stone, who shows that the Lancashire Dialect has come within his wide observation. As the ex- Premier refers to the word " stow " it will be of interest to mention the use to which the late Mr. McMinnies once put the word. He was a master in the niceties of "broad Lanky " ; and some suggestion having been made by the present writer as to-his easing off in political work, he replied "Yes, lam like an old horse going up hill. You mustn't put too big a load on or I shall 'stow.'"

Notwithstanding difficulties as to transfer of licenses, it would seem that the Blackpool Eiffel Tower Company have decided to proceed with the work. At the statutory meeting of the Company, on Wednesday, it was stated that Sir Matthew White Ridley, M.P., has consented to lay the foundation stone of the Tower on the 25th inst. When the Tower has been erected, and a third pier—one at South Shore—has been constructed, the promenade at Blackpool will be one of the liveliest places in the kingdom during the summer season. But all the best goods will be in the shop window ; there is nothing behind.

The question of a Truant School was under con- sideration at Widnes, on Tuesday, it being resolved that the seal of the Board. be attached to a petition to the County Council favour of their provid- ing such accommodation. Dean Finegan could not see the use of such schools; but experience is in favour of them. They relieve the ordinary schools of the most troublesome children; and the truants being brought together can be subject to more rigid discipline than they would otherwise receive. They are well looked after ;and in many cases prevented from drifting into habits which end in crime. There ought to be a Truant or Indus- trial Day School in every town of over 30,000 inhabitants.

---------- FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENTS AT WIGAN. On Thursday, James Robinson, boatman, stationed at Gathurst Bridge, was walking along the Lanca- shire and Yorkshire Railway near Douglas Bank siding, Wigan, when he was knocked down by a ballast train. When found he was dead.—Another man, at present unknown, was killed near the same place later in the day. He was caught by an ex- press train and cut to pieces. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Saßkey-St.. Warrington.—Ae'vt.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS RUNCORN. The autumn session will commence on Thursday next, when the Rev. C. F. Aked of Liverpool, will deliver a lecture on " Marcus Aurelius and his times, or the early days of christianity." Admission is free.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. On Wednesday, before Mr. J. Handley and Mr. H. Reynolds, Richard Johnson was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, Charles Wright 23. 6d. including costs and Margaret Hancock ss. and costs, for being drunk. On Thursday for a like offence Richard Morgan was fined ss. and costs. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.--Advt.

ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL, RUNCORN. Special services were held at this place of worship on Sunday, when the Rev. Evan Williams, of Albany, Australia, and formerly pastor of the Runcorn Church, for 20 years, preached to crowded congregations. In the course of his morning service Mr. Williams alluded in feeling terms to the happy time he had spent in their midst and he said he was pleased to be amongst them once more. '

A POLISH WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES. Dominic Dovitch and Charles Martin Kevitch, Poles were again brought before the Wtdnes Bench, on Thurs- day, to answer a charge of causing grievous bodily harm to Ann Swimen of Hope-st., on the 6th inst. Mr. Knowles appeared for Kevitch. The facts of the case have been previously reported and the Bench after hear- ing witnesses committed both prisoners for trial. The woman is still in a very weak state. _ .
UMBRELLAS RECOVER-i:D.—J. and W. PurroN, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
ALLEGED iWIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES.

An old man named John Hayes, was brougiat before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday, on a charge of neglecting to support his wife, who wag an inmate of Whiston Workhouse.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the prisoner and offered on his behalf to pay the Guardians the cost of his wife's maintenance in the Workhou4e and also to find a home for her. Mr. A. F. Mann, clerk to the Guardians accepted the offer and the case was with- drawn.

div.head: BRUNSWICK RAMBLING CLUB, RUNCORN.
div.p: BRUNSWICK RAMBLING CLUB, RUNCORN.

A social evening was held in Brunswick school on Monday evening to conclude the season of the Rambling Club. Upwards of N sat down to a capital tea, pro- vided by Misses Crosby and Miss Littler, and afterwards there was a short entertainment consisting of songs by Miss Eden, Miss Minnie Cullis, and Mr. Ben Crosby, a reading by Mr. Thomas Riley, a recitation by Mr. J. Ellison and a violin solo by -Master Porah. Afterwards fruit was handed round and the rest of the evening was spent in games. BISSINETTES.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger. 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.— Advt.

div.head: CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THE CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.

The four days bazaar in connection with St. Edwards Roman Catholic Church, Runcorn, was brought to a conclusion on Saturday,when Mr. J. Morrison of Widnes performed the opening ceremony. The attendance was much better than on the previous days and business was brisk. Mr. Thos. Clegg, auctioneer in the evening sold a number of articles by auction and it was announced that a sale by auction would take place shortly. Mr. Smith of Preston, sent a donation of £5 and Mr. Bancroft Cooke of Liverpool, who should have opened the bazaar, on Thursday forwarded two guineas. ACCIDENTAL DEATH OF AN INFANT AT DITTON. On Tuesday, an inquiry was held at the New Inn, Ditton, before Mr. W. T. Husband, concerning the death of a child which occurred on the 13th inst.—Sarah B. Mather said the deceased baby was her child, and was one month old. She went'with her husband to bed about twelve o'clock on the night of the 12th inst , but the child had then been in bed sometime. At five o'clock the following morning, she gave the child nourishment, and about two hours afterwards she awoke and found it dead. It was not insured. The jury returned a verdict to the effect, that the deeeased child was found dead in bed and that it came by its death accidentally. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A RAILWAY OFFICIAL AT DITTON.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A RAILWAY OFFICIAL AT DITTON.

Before Mr. Buchan and Mr. J. Stone, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, James Muller, Davies-street, Dit- ton, was summoned for obstructing a servant of the London and North-Western Railway Company while in the execution of his duty. Mr. Preston, solicitor, prose- cuted, and said this was a most serious case. On Sun- day the 23rd ult., the defendant went up to the booking office at Ditton Junction, pushed before three persons who had been at the ticket window before him,and then smashed the window. When Thomas Cook, the booking clerk interfered, the defendant assaulted him and tore his coat in the struggle, which took place. The defen- dant who pleaded guilty was sentenced to pay a fine of 40s. and costs or go to gaol for a month.

div.head: NEGLECTFUL FATHER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A NEGLECTFUL FATHER AT RUNCORN.

John Alderson, a middle-aged man, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, charged that he being a person able to work and thereby wholly main- tain his family, neglected so to do, whereby his three children were chargeable to the common fund of the Runcorn Union.—The prisoner said he had not done very well since Whitsuntide.—Mr. Frodsham, collector to the Union, said the prisoner was a labourer, and owed the Union £4 14s for the maintenance of his children. The Guardians had obtained work for him at Runcorn Alkali Works, but in consequence of drink he lost the place. The children had been in the house for two or three years. The prisoner had been sent to prison for neglect. —Mr. C. Reynolds said the prisoner was an able-bodied man and there was no excuse for him. People as poor as the prisoner or poorer, load to keep his children and it was not right.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour. UMBRELLAS RECOVEREIL—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-St., Warrington.—Advt.
RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE._

At the fortnightly meeting the above Order at which there was a good attendance of officers and members. Mr. Thomas Heesom gave a paper on the introduction of the Order of Sons of Temperance into this country. He stated that the Order was introduced into England by a number of temperance sailors, from St. John's, New Brunswick. The first lodge was called the Mariners Division, and was opened in Liverpool in the year 1849. The Grand Division of the Order was instituted in 1851, and the National Division in 1853. Since then the Order has made steady progress and is now one of the leading Temperance Benefit Societies in this country. The Order now has in its ranks the leading temperance workers in the country, including Lord and Lady ;Carlisle, Lord Morpeth, members of Parliament, and ministers of all denominations. After the paper there was a very in- teresting conversation, during which it was stated that the first Bandof Hope formed in Runcorn held its first meeting in Granville-st., School-room, on January 6th, 1852. The following members took part in the meeting: —Messrs. Thomas Cooke, Ed. Key, Daniel Bisbrown, John Jones, Thos. Clarke, L. M. Temperley, Thomas H. Holt, James Bisbrown and John Taylor. A vote of thanks wos passed to Mr. Heesom for his paper. Mr. Wesley Cooke occupied the chair. PRESENTATION TO THE REV. A. H. SANDERSON

div.head: A.K.C. OF RUNCORN.
div.p: A.K.C. OF RUNCORN.

A representative meeting of the parishioners of Holy Trinity Church assembled in the schoolroom, on Tuesday, to take part in a social re-union. After tea an interesting event took place, the curate, the Kev. A. H. Sanderson being presented with a hand- some marble timepiece as a mark of the appreciation and regard on the occasion of his severing his con- nection with Runcorn. The Rev. Dr. Preston made the presentation and observed that he felt as though he were losing a brother, but he could not blame Mr. Sanderson for seeking a more remunera- tive post than his present one. He denied himself for the good of others and he did not hesitate to put his hand in his pocket and give largely in charity. The presentation was then made amid applause.— Mr. Sanderson in acknowledging the unexpected gift, said he had been happy in the performance of his duty and he was thankful that he had commenced his clerical career in Trinity parish. Addresses were also delivered by Messrs. W. J. Cunningham, R. Kilcross and H. Hankinson.

div.head: UTE EXAMINER, SATURDAY., SEPTEMBER 19, 1891.
div.p: UTE EXAMINER, SATURDAY., SEPTEMBER 19, 1891.

WIDNES CYCLE CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP. The race for the championship of this club took place on Thursday. Eight members competed, and an exciting race resulted in J. V. Swift (300 yards) coming in first; T. H. Jones (captain 150 yards be- hind scratch) 2 ; and T. Coupe (scratch), 3. The distance was 44- MIDDLEWICH AND NORTHWICH SHOW. The annual show of the Middlewich and Nort h- wich Agricultural Society was held on Wednesday, at Middlewich, and waQ largely attended. There was an increase of about 60 in the entries as com- pared with last year;the improvement being chiefly in the light-horse c! asses. SHOCKING FATALITY TO A BOY AT WESTON. On Tuesday an inquest was held at the Royal Oak Inn, Weston, on the body of a boy named Percy Flannigan, aged 11 years, who died on Monday from injuries received on the sth inst. The boy was searching for "sand martins" on the edge of a quarry, overbalanced himself, and fell a depth of 45 feet, causing concussion of the brain. A verdict of " Accidental Death" was recorded.

WARRINGTON C/lESS As will be seen from our advertisement columns, this club will commence its third season at the Farmers' Stores, Bewsey-st., on Tuesday next, at 7.30 p.m., with a friendly match amongst the mem- bers. Entries will be received for a club tourna- ment which is to be commenced forthwith. The club has again entered the Lancashire League Com- petition, and a good list of matches has been arranged. All chess player residing in or near Warrington should attend on Tuesday next.
be thanks of the Board were accorded to the Rev. G. H. Garrett, 8.D., for conducting the examination of the Board's pupil teachers in Biblical knowledge for the year 1891.
FINANCE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts, amounting to £572 3s. 10d. were passed for payment. The receipts for the month amounted to £1,145 188. Bd.

Ratepayer : You will have to come to a pumping scheme at the finish and you may as well come to it at once.—Mr. Grice said they had spent £2,000 at Newton and nothing came out of it.—Mr. Edwards said that there was plenty of water at New- ton,but he was told that the scheme was never meant to succeed, and that was after £1,4-00 had been spent. div.head: RESULT OF LIVERPOOL LICENSING SESSIONS,
div.p: RESULT OF LIVERPOOL LICENSING SESSIONS,

The net result of the late Liverpool Licensing Sessions is that the number of fully-licensed houses has been reduced by twelve, five licenses having been refused by the magistrates, one given up and six not applied for. A reduction of eight has also been made in the wine and beer licenses, so that on the 10th October next, when the old licenses expire and the new ones come into force, no fewer than 20 drink-selling houses will have ceased to be engaged in that trade.
THE LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAMSHIP
COMPANY.

Now that the days are drawing in, and the even- ings dark towards 7 o'clock, the directors of this very successful company, with a view to accommod- ate their numerous passengers who take advantage of the day trips by the St. Tudno, have thoughtfully arranged that this popular steamer shall turn round at Beaumaris and arrive back in Liverpool about 6 o'clock in the evening, and passengers between Menai Bridge, Bangor, and Beaumaris will be carried by the well-known straits steamer Menai. There is no doubt that many people will find it a great advantage to be able to have such a delight- ful sea excursion, and yet arrive back in Liverpool before dark. UMRRELLIS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. BROUGHT UP BY THE TIDE AT RUNCORN.

The body of a man unknown was found in the Mersey, at Runcorn, near the Pierhead, on Thurs- day morning, by a boatman named R. Parr, em- ployed on the flat Bangor. The body was conveyed to the mortuary at the Cemetery. The police des- cribe it as the body of a man 55 years, sft.loin. high, stout built, brown hair and moustache, no whiskers, bald on the top of the head; dressed in bluejacket, dark overall, grey woollen singlet and drawers, red cotton socks, a pair of low shoes (laced). There was nothing in the pockets by which the body could be identified, except a white handled razor, on which was scratched the name L. U. Skipworth.

div.head: BOILER MAKERS' DINNER,
div.p: BOILER MAKERS' DINNER,

The annual dinner in connection with die Newton branch of the United Society of Boiler Makers and Iron Shipbuilders, was held at the Oddfellows Arms, Legli-st., on Saturday evening. About 40 members and friends sat down to an excellent dinner, catered for by Mr. Lythgoe. After dinner, Mr. T. Traverse, president of the branch, occupied the chair, and gave an interesting address on the progress made by combination in trades unionism. The toast "Success to the Boiler Makers' Society," was given by Bro. W. Harrison, a superannuated member, who alluded in appropriate terms to the benefits to be derived from the Society, and urged every young member to become zealous workmen in its interest. A vote of thanks was unanimously accorded the chairman for his services, and he suit- ably replied. The remainder of the evening was spent in singing and dancing, songs being contri- buted at intervals by Messrs. J. Thompson, J. Simner, A. Lockart, P. Crane, and J. Bell. Mr. W. Taylor presided at the piano. Thanks to Mr. Lythgoe for the excellent manner in which he had catered, terminated the proceedings. UMBRELLAS R ECOVERED.—j . and W. DUTTON. • Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHEMICAL WORKER. Joseph Arnold, a chemical labourer, 51 years of age, of 144. Pocket Nook-st., was found dead on some waste land near his home at noon on Monday. The deceased was employed at M`Bryde's works, belonging to the Alkali Union, and on Monday morning complained to the foreman, James Moore, that he felt unwell. He was advised to go home and get to bed, and he left the works for that pur- pose. A lad named Westhead saw him crossing the waste land, walking very slowly, on his way home, and that was the last time he was seen alive. A girl named Lawrence found the body about one o'clock. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday before Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner.—John Taylor, brother-in-law of the deceased, said the deceased hed suffered from influenza mad was attended by Dr. Knowles. The Coroner: There was a rumour that he was " gassed" at the works. Witness: I don't think it was anything of the sort.—The Coroner: You don't think anything connected with his employment has caused his death? No; he was subject to mazy bouts and dizziness.—The Coroner: I don't think I should have held an inquest if that rumour about being " 6aassed " had not got about.— After other evidence hal been given a verdict of "Death from natural causes" was returned. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND, Warrington, —Advt.
WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Rev. J. Clarke,Rev. Dean Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, and Mr. S, Quinn with Mr. G. H. Danby (clerk).
DISTRICT EDUCATION.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing August (4 weeks) there were 141 applications for payment of fees, which were recommended to be paid in 136 cases. 261 persons appeared before the Committee for contravention of the Education Act and 53 were pro- secuted before the magistrates, 52 of whom were con- v :cted. A report of the work of the Committee during the past year was presented. The cases summoned before the Committee were 4,180; last year, 4,446; per- sons summoned before the Committtee, 1,783 ; last year, 1740; for offences, 2,104; last year, 2,442 ; 719 persons made application for payment of school fees in 2,076 cases, and the fees were recommended to be paid in 1874 cases. Last year the numbers were respectively 597, 2,004, 1,806. 284 persons were prosecuted and 272 fined as compared with 405 and 364 respectively. Six children had been committed to Industrial schools and there were now 25 in such institutions; as compared with 31 last year. The average number on the rolls was 6,547.8,the average attendance 5401.8,and the percentage 82.4. The percentage of attendance last year was 84.—Father Clarke moved the adoption of the report and the Clerk explained that the number of prosecutions had been re- duced because the attendance ~fficers had now instruc- tions to see the father before a summons was taken out and in a great many cases the fathers took upon them- selves to see that the children attended school. This ' accounted for the fewer prosecutions.—The Chairman : A very desirable change.—Dean Finegan remarked that the attendance at school appeared to have fallen off with the prosecutions.—Father Clarke said the decrease in the attendance was due to sickness.—The report was adopted.

A TRUANT SCHOOL WANTED. On the recommendation of the District Education Com- mittee, the seal of the Board was affixed to a petition to the County Council of Lancashire, urging them to pro- vide truant school accommodation for the County .—Dean Finegan did not oppos9 the petition,but he said he failed to see any advantage in a truant school. He seldom saw that boys sent to truant schools and reformatories come back better than they went. They could scarcely hope to make a bad boy good by mixing him with 200 boys as bad as himself.—Father Clarke saida truant: school was needed.

RESIGNATIONS. The School Management Committee recommended that the resignations of the Misses A. A. Strong, Jessie., Poul- son, A. C. Davies, A. Jamieson, be accepted and that Miss Clegg be appointed head mistress of the junior boys' department of the Simms Cross School(vice Miss Strong), at a salary of £lO5 per annum.—Dean Finegan moved the adoption of the minutes and said the Committee had acted on a principle of giving such situations as Miss Strong's to one who bad had a college training. Some of th best teachers, however, had not had such a train- ing —The minutes were passed.

div.head: PENNY FEE,
div.p: THE PENNY FEE,

The Clerk said he had written to the Education De- partment with reference to the proposed charge of id. in the schools and the department replied that if the managers accepted the fee grant they will be at liberty to charge any such fees for the whole or any portion of the children over three and under 15 years of age as will not make the average rate of fees charged for such children for the year exceed 2s. 11d. in Simms Cross school, 2s. 10d. in Warrington-road school, and 3s. 02d. in West Bank School. If from any accident or miscal- culation the fees actually charged are found :at ithe end of the school year to have exceeded the maximum allow- able under the Act, and the department are satisfied there has been a reasonable excuse for such excess, the case will be dealt with under section 1 (2)of the Act, i.e. the fee grant will be reduced by a sum equal to the ex- , 1 eess.
TONIC SOL-FA CELEBRATION AT RUNCORN.

In celebration of the Tonic Sol-Fa Jubilee, a de- monstration arranged by the Sol-Faists of the town took place in Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday evening, ana the building was crowded to excess. Mr. James Pritchard, chairman of the School Board, occupied the chair, and he was supported on his right by Mr. J. Spencer Curwen, F.R.A.M.,president of the Tonic Sol-Fa College ; and on his left by Mr. Robert Griffiths, G. and L.T.S.C., secretary to the College. Rising behind the platform was a gallery, holding a juvenile choir of 180 voices, who per- formed the first part of the programme. They sang several songs in a very clever manner, and the audience would not be satisfied until they had thrice heard "The Fire Brigade." The singing from hand signs was testimony to the careful training of the children, and the exercises they went through charmed the crowded auditory. The second part of the programme was filled by an adult choir of 100 voices. That rendered " Rejoice ye sons of song," and theprize Jubilee Ode "The spirit of song," with a power and harmony they showed Tonic Sol-Fa was capable of the best musical ex- pression. The " ear exercise " was a remarkable test of the musical ability of the choir. Mr. liallord played on the piano the four parts of a psalm tune,and the members of the choir wrote down the music as he proceeded and then immediately gave a capital rendering of the same. The sight test was an oqually, if not more, difficult, exercise. A piece of music specially composed by Mr. Raiford (" Blow, blow, thou winter wind ") was placed in the hands of thc, choir, who had never previously seen the copy and without being allowed a moment to study the composition, they sang it without hesitation and with tunefulness and expression. The performance throughout was a testimony to the energy. perseverance and training of Mr. John Halford, G.T.S.C., who was the conductor. In the course of the evening brief speeches were made. The Chairman said they were celebrating that evening the jubilee of the tonic sol fa system of singing, and this event had aroused a great amount of interest in the country. The celebration commenced with a festival in St. Paul's Cathedral, London, and afterwards an im- mense gathering was held in the Crystal Palace. Since then the celebration had been carried on in provincial towns by demonstrations of this character, and he was glad to find that Runcorn was not behind hand in this matter—(hear, hear)—but that they were locally celeb- rating this interesting jubilee. He believed they were indebted to the inventive faculties of the ladies for the origination of the system of tonic sol fa, that was in the person of Miss Glover, of Norwich, and it was after- wards adopted for public use by the late Rev. John Curwen—(Applause)—the father of the gentleman who was present that evening. The primary object of the system had been to teach music to the people, and no doubt we were greatly indebted to tonic sol fa for the prevalance of music amongst the people at the present I day in comparison with what prevailed some years ago. By this system music had been carried into every village and almost every home in the country and had vastly improved the congregational singing in all our places of worship. (Hear, hear.) What it had done for us locally they had an example in the concert and entertainment provided that evening. Tonic sol fa was not only a musi- cal, but also a great educational movement. (Hear, hear.) According to the returns of the Education De- partment, no less than three million of children were taught music by this system—(applause)—and it was generally believed that before many years had elapsed this system would prevail in all schools throughout the land. He trusted that that this local celebration would be worthy of the great occasion. (Applause.) Mr. Curwen said their object that night was to demon- strate the value of tonic sol-fatand the best way of doing so was not by talking but by doing something, and the musical exercises the choirs had performed formed a more powerful argument for the system than the most eloquent speech. He congratulated Mr. Holford upon the fresh- ness and tunefulness of the singing. The chairman said it was a popular system; it was also a scientific system; and if they wanted to go from tonic sol-fa to a higher class of music what was learned in tonic sol-fa would be a shining light through their path of musical study into harmony and composition. (Applause.) For this reason it had been approved by the highest authorities both musicians and scientific men. It was adopted in 83 per cent. of the elementary schools in England, Scotland and Wales. Their system had done a great deal to improve congregational singing and to improve choirs, and they would do more if the churches would only let them. (Hear, hear.) Supposing the churches and chapels had the advantages of tonic sol-fa classes he ventured to say that congregational singing which was so much desired and talked about would come very soon. He hoped they had done something that night to spread tonic sol fa in Runcorn. (Applause.) Mr. Griffiths said they were there that evening to show their sympathy with the good work which Mr. Flalford was doing in that town (applause) and to do what they could to strengthen the hands of one who worked so generously, so thoroughly and so educationally as their friend Mr. Raiford did. (Applause.) The object the solfaists set out with 50 years ago was to make England a singing nation, and that was their object to-day. The improvement in that town was very great but they ex- pected a hundred times more in the next 50 years. He advocated classes being formed in connection with the Sunday schools, and said they had plenty of capable men ready and willing to give lessons for nothing. He urged all who could to attend Mr. Halford's singing classes, which would shortly commence. Mr. Clifford Le Couteur ably accompanied the choir on the piano. The proceedings concluded with the singing of the Hallelujah chorus.

div.head: PROPOSED WATER SCHEME FOR
div.p: THE PROPOSED WATER SCHEME FOR

Fit ODSTIAM. RATEPAYERS' MEETING. On Thursday evening a meeting of the ratepayers called by the Overseers was held in Frodsham Town Hall, for the purpose of considering the proposed water scheme for the township. There was a large attendance and Mr. Thomas Davies was voted to the chair. Mr. James Edwards prefaced his remarks by thanking the ratepayers for electing him a guardian and said he hoped their trust would never be misplaced. Nothing, he added, should be wanted on his part to merit their confidence. As to the water scheme, he had given notice that at the next meeting of the Rural Sanitary Authority he should move that the resolution approving of the scheme be rescinded. For the benefit of those who did not know what the scheme: was, he might state that it was a boring 300 feet deep in a field adjoining the gas works, and when they had got water it was to be pumped up to a height of 225 feet in a reservoir near the Vicarage. He contended that it was a most absurd, ridiculous and costly scheme, and if carried cut meant a large increase in the rates. At the present time the rates of the township amounted to no less that 3s. Bd. in the £ per annum, and if this scheme were carried out according to the estimates it would mean an increase of ad. in the L. It had gone forth from Mr. Thomas, he believed, on the authority of Mr. Timmins, that the cost of the scheme would be 2 per thousand gallons. No- thing more fallacious ever went forth. The total cost would be £3,600 and interest at 5 percent., sinking fund included, to be repaid in a certain number of years, would be £lBO per annum. There a man would be re- quired to superintend an eight horse power gas engine, and putting him down at 30s. per week would be £7B pewinnum. Then there would be at the very least a cohliumption of 500,000 cubic feet of gas, which at 4s. per thousand feet would make £52 for the year, mak- ing a total of £3lO per annum, which on the rateable value of the township meant an extra 6d. on the rates. It was for the ratepayers to decide whether they would accept this expensive scheme. He was not against a water scheme, but he wanted one that would not be a burden to the ratepayers, but which would help to lessen the rates. In a situation like that of Frodsham, nearly on the bend of a river, with high lying lands above, if they could not get water without pumping, it was a poor look out. He pointed out that the scheme was only adopted by the votes of the Lordship and of two el-officio members and said the ratepayers of the Lordship were looking forward to this scheme being passed, and they wanted the township to bear all the expense, and that when it was nicely settled, they would say" Give us a little drop of your water." (Laughter.) —Mr. W. Yond said he noticed Mr. Timmins was pre- sent,would he please explain the scheme.—Mr. T. Tim- mins said his brAher Mr. Walter Timmins had drawn thescheme out, and he was prepared to go into it at any time with Mr. Edwards who was off the mark altog,ethor. —Mr. Yond asked had Mr. Edwards another scheme to lay before them. (Hear, hear.) If they could get water

div.head: I dream't I dwelt in a marble hall With the girl in the Gainsboro' bat; You tickle me and I tickle you And what can be nicer than that.
div.p: I dream't I dwelt in a marble hall With the girl in the Gainsboro' bat; You tickle me and I tickle you And what can be nicer than that.

(Loud laughter.) Mr. E. Ashworth said they had had gravitation schemes enough, and the present plans ought to be passed and carried out.—Mr. P. Riley seconded this suggestion. Mr. Edwards had nothing to propose in the place of the pre- sent scheme, and it was time they had water.—Mr. Edwards said it was not his place to suggest a scheme. He asked them to reject this scheme as a costly and in comprehensible scheme.—Mr. Proud said the lordship ought to join the township in this matter and he sug- gested that a water district should be formed,and a com- prehensive scheme carried out so that they should not want another scheme in ten years time.—Mr. Edwards favoured this idea.—Mr. A. Rigby seconded Mr. Proud's suggestion.—Mr. Hutehinson moved and Mr. Tickle seconded that the present scheme be rescinded.—A rate- payer remarked that if this scheme were carried out the township could sell water to the Lordship, but Mr. Ed- wards said they would have no power to supply the Lordship.—Mr. Kydd strongly supported the present scheme, which was the only feasible scheme proposed.— Mr. Proud then handed in his resolution as follows: That this meeting of the ratepayers of Frodsham town- ship recognises the want of water in both the township and the Lordship and suggests to the Rural Sanitary Authority that before proceeding with the present scheme the Guardians memorialise the iiocal Government to sanction the formation of a separate district including portions of the township and Lordship for the purposes of water supply.—Dr. Robinson said it was no use pass- ing such a resolution, as the members of the Lordship would not join in the scheme. He proposed that the , scheme be carried out subject to a water district being formed and marked out by a boundary line. If the Lordship were added the scheme would cost another £3,ooo.—Mr. Edwards: Why don't the Gas Company take it up.—Dr. Robinson : Because the scheme was esti- mated at £B,OOO, and they could not see their way to go on with it. If all the inhabitants had taken water and there had been no bad debts it would only kave paid five per cent.—ln answer to the ratepayers, Dr. Robinson said a two inch boring on the Marsh yielded 39,000 gal- lons in 24 hours and the temperature was 51 degrees. The water was good but a little hard.—The discussion continued and Mr. Yond shouted they were continually moving and moving but nothing was being passed. Were they a lot of lunatics and fools to let people pass things as they wanted. (Laughter and applause.)—Dr. I Robinson's motion was then put and lost by a large majority ; there were no voters for the motion rescinding the scheme entirely, and Mr. Proud's motion was carried without a dissentient voice.—A vote of thanks to the I Chairman concluded the meeting.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The annual meeting of this Committee was held on Wednesday afternoon. Present Rev. Canon Wood, Messrs. W. Hankinson, S. Taylor, W. M. Sowerby, T. Riley and J. D. Jones (secretary). On the motion of Canon Wood, seconded by Mr. Taylor, Mr. Riley was unanimously elected chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. W. Handley was unanimously elected vice-chairman on the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Hankinson. The Secretary reported that the receipts for the month amountea to £39 18s. 2d. and after paying the accounts there was a balance of £34 19s. 2d. The books issued during the month had been theology 29, philosophy 7, science 56, history 142, poetry 12, fiction 1,396, miscellaneous 151, total 1,793, decrease 73. Thirty-five volumes had been consulted in the reference department. —The Secretary said Mr. Handley with considerable trouble had ascertained the dates of various Acts of Parliament of local interest, which it was thought the library ought to possess. Seven of the Acts referred to the river Weaver, four to the Bridgewater Canal, one to the Trent and Mersey, one Runcorn and Weston Canal, and the Upper Mersey Navigation Acts.—The Secretary was instructed to as- certain the costs of obtaining these Acts.—. The Book Selection Committee recommended the purchase of 96 volumes at a cost of £l9 15s. At the conclusion of the proceedings a vote of thanks was accerded to Canon Wood for his services during the past year.

div.head: RE-OPENING OF PADGATE WESLEYAN
div.p: RE-OPENING OF PADGATE WESLEYAN
CHAPEL

On Thursday afternoon, the Rev. J. H. Siloll, of Manchester, preached, in the Padgate Wesleyan Chapel, before a good congregation, the first of a series of special sermons to be delivered in connec- tion with the re-opening of the building, after extensive repairs by which it has been much beautified. The rev, gentleman selected for his text Eph. 111., 14., " For this cause 1 bow my knees with the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Subse- quently a tea meeting was held in the school adjoining the chapel, about 150 persons partaking' of it. In the evening, Mr. Sholl preached before a large congregation from the sth and 6th verses of the Ist chapter of Revelations, "And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness and the first begotton of the dead, and the prince of kings of the earth. Unto Him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in His own blood, and hath made us kings and priests unto God and His Father; to Him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen." The preacher delivered a most earnest and forcible discourse, and at the close in appealing for liberality in the collection said that building was one of the loveliest little chapels he had ever seen. It was a grand thing when they had spent a considerable amount of thought and anxiety and money in the erection or renovation of a place of worship and were satisfied with the work that was done. He had been in some chapels where ' they had spent their money and work, and after months or years the work had been done and every- body was disappointed. The Rev. J. Gunnell, super- intendent minister, and the Revs. A. Freeman and T. Ross were present at the tea and services, and the Rev. J. Gunnell took part of the duties in con- nection therewith. Miss Bennett presided at the organ in the afternoon, and Mr. Wright, of Man- chester, in the evening : and on the latter occasion the choir sang the anthem " will lift up mine eyes." The collections, which were taken by several young ladies of the congregation, were very hard- some, these with the proceeds of the tea, it being I announced by the Rev. J. Gunnell, amounting to about £35.

div.head: SPORTS AT ORFORD BARRACKS.
div.p: SPORTS AT ORFORD BARRACKS.

The annual sports of the Bth and 40th Regimen- tal District took place at Orford Barracks on Thurs- day. The sports as usual attracted a large number of outsiders, who were rewarded by seeing a good day's sport. The events were well contested, prizes to the value of about £2O in, cash being given awn. The mile race-eight times round the course -which was open to the volunteers and police of Warrington, was won by James Massey, who is well known in Warrington as a long distance runner. He conceded his opponents a lap start but ran in fully twenty yards ahead of the second man, Private Turner, Drummer Murphy just managing to get third place. Massey has now won this race for a good many years. Colonel A. C. Twentyman, C.B. Major C. Linton, and Major Stone were the stewards, Captain Synge, Captain Griffiths, Captain E. Manion and Captain S. L. Cotton, the judges, and Lieutenant F. A. Dudgeon the starter. The following are the results :-Flat race, 100 yards, Ist. Lance Sergeant Jones ; 2nd, Private Hough; 3rd, Private Turner. Putting the shot, with a follow, Ist, Private Kelly (27ft. 9in.) ; 2nd, Private Waldron (25ft. sin.) Flat race, 100 yards, Ist. Lance Sergeant Jones; 2nd, Sergeant Wilks (Army Pay: Department) ; 3rd, Sergeant Hunt. High jump, Private Collester and Private Read, dead heat, the height being 4ft. sin. Half-mile race. Ist, Private Wilson; 2nd, Corporal surly; 3rd, Private Kelly. Handicap race, 100 yards (for boys between eleven and fourteen years of age), Ist. F. Rice ; 2nd, Jolley ; 3rd. W. Powner. Hurdle race, 120 yards, Ist, Ser- geapt Wilks ; 2nd Private Hough ; 3rd Private Reardon. Handicap race. 80 yards, (for boys between eight and eleven years of age), Ist,gged race, C. Fryer; 2nd, T. Day ; 3rd, S. Chamberlain. Three-le 100 yards, Ist, Privates Jackson and Linaker ; 2nd Privates Jackson and Smith. Flat race, 440 yards Ist, PriVate Wilson; 2nd Private Turner ; 3rd, Private Read. Egg and spoon race, 100 yards. Ist, Private Stafford : 2nd Private Line- ker. Veterans race, 100 yards, Ist, Sergeant Fryer ; 2nd Colour-Sergeant Geary. Old soldiers race, 100 yards, Ist, Private Watts ; 2nd, Private Percival. Handi- cap Race, 100 yards (for girls between eleven and four- teen years of age), Ist, M. Geary ; 2nd, F. Geary ; 3rd, E. Chamberlain. Combination race (run 100 yards, walk 100 yards and hop 50), Ist, Private Murphy ; 2nd, Private Wynne. Bucket race, 100 yards, Ist, Private Wynne; 2nd, Private Wright. Sack race, Ist, Private Dunbobbin ; 2nd, Private Whelan. Tilting at the bucket, Ist, Privates Mills and Owens; 2nd Privates Linnaker and Henry. Handicap race, 80 yards (for girls between eight and eleven years of age) Ist, Martha Geary ;' 2nd, A. Peachy- 3rd, A. Dunbobbin. Clog dance, prizes divided between Blundell and Shannon. Mile race, Ist, James Massey :2nd, Private Turner • 3rd, Drummer Murphy. Monkey race, Jones and Dolphin (Dead heat). Obstacle race, Ist, Private White ; 2nd, Private Henry ; 3rd, Private Larkin.

WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART SKETCHING cLuri; During the week the marks have been awarded by Mr. R. Glazier,art master of the Technical School Manchester, to the members of the Vacation Sketch- ing Club in connection with the Warrington School, of Art. A very satisfactory collection was submit- ted,and there was a great improvement in the work as compared with that of previous years. The general public will have an opportunity of inspect- ing the works at the annual exhibition of students' work held in December at the school. The follow- ing is a list of marks and list of special prizes awarded :—Advanced Section: Maximum number of marks 100; Miss Constance Broadbent, 63, Miss Mary Burgess, 58, Mr. Charles E. Jones, 55. Ele- mentary section: Miss Florence Birtles, 20, Mr. Leonard Newcombe, 19, Miss Helen Cooper,lB, ICES Jeans, 18. Special competition: Best study from life (Mr. J. Rylands, J.P.) awarded to Miss Con- stance Broadbent ; best study of flowers (Mr. R. Garnett, J.P.), Miss Annie Chrimes ; best set of sketches in black and white, (Mr. Thomas Birtles), Mr. Charles E. Jones; best landscape in oil or watercolour, Miss Mary Burgess; best set of archi- tectural sketches, Mr. Charles E. Jones; best archi- tectural sketch of whole or distinct feature of a building (to be within ,five miles of :Warrington), Mr. Oswald Garside ; best outdoor study, not a pic- ture, Miss Mary Burgess; special prize for elemen- tary section, Mr. Leonard Newcombe. THE EDUCATION ACT AND WARRING- TON SCHOOLS. In a circular issued to the parents of the children in Wycliffe day school, the Rev. J. Yonge, writing on behalf of the managers, says the acceptance of the Government free grant " will not enable us to do more than reduce existing fees. We hope the time is not far distant when National education will be entirely free. Meanwhile, from October 5, we propose to charge the following reduced fees— Upper school, standards 1. to 111.-2 d. per child; upper school, standards IV. to VIII.-3d. per child; Infants school, Id. These fees are to include books, which from the date named, with all other school neeessaries,will be provided with out further charge." The Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) writing on be- half of the managers to the parents of children in the Parish Church day schools, says" The managers are very desirous to give parents the full benefit of the Act, only securing themselves against loss. They have, therefore, after much consideration, decided upon the following scale, which is in all leases 2d., and in some 3d. a week less than at pre- sent, and in a school year of 46 weeks, such as ours will henceforth be, saves the parent the whole amount granted by the Act, viz., 10s. a year on each child. The following is the scale which will come into force on the first Monday of October, in all the schools, the charge for books being left as at pre- sent :—Mount Schools: Upper girls. Standards 111. and under, 4d.; IV. and over, 6d.; Girls: Standard 111. and under, id.; IV. and over, 2d.; Infants: One penny. Church-st. School: Boys. Standards 111. and under, 2d.; IV. and over, 3d.; Infants, one penny. Smith-st. School: Girls, one Penny. The holidays in future will be as follows :—Two weeks at Christmas, one week at Easter, three weeks in the summer. The summer holidays will begin on the Saturday before Walking Day." The Rector also urges upon parents the importance of a careful and wise use of the money now saved to them by the fee grant. He suggest the parochial penny bank as one of the best ways of investing small sums.—Mr. J. J. Crosfield, the hon. sec., of the People's College has also issued a circular in which he says that the acceptance of the grant enables a reduction to be made in the school fees, and from Monday, October the sth, the following scale will be charged :—lnfants, id. per week ; standard 1., 2d. ; 11., 3d.; 111., 3d.: IV., 4d.; V., 5d.; VI., 5d.: VII. 6d. _

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
COMING EVRNTS.
Special services will be held at Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-road, to-morrow. The preacher will be the Rev. J. Yonge. There will be special music and anthems, and collections for the Church funds.

The Rev. J. Monro Gibson, B.D.' of London, mod- erator of the Presbyterian Church of England, will preach in St. John's Presbyterian Church, Wiu- wick-st., on Wednesday evening. There will be a special collection. THE REV. H. GIBSON-SMITH.
The Rev. 11. Gibson-Smith, M.A., late second master of the Warrington Grammar School, will commence his duties as Rector of Halewood on Sun- day next.

METHODIST SPECIAL SERVICES. On Monday and Tuesday evenings the first two of a series of special services were conducted at the Friars' Green Independent Methodist Chapel, by Mr. R. B. Woods, Connexional evangelist, formerly of Warrington. The services have also been con- tinued during the week.

div.head: FIRE AT A SANKEY FARM.
div.p: FIRE AT A SANKEY FARM.

The Warrington Fire Brigade were called, on Sat- urday afternoon, to a fire on the farm of Mr. W. J. Houghton, Sankey, and succeeded in saving a large quantity of hay. The loss is estimated at £B4. The fire is supposed to have been caused by an incen- diary.

div.head: SUCCESS OF A WARRINGTON CYCLIST.
div.p: SUCCESS OF A WARRINGTON CYCLIST.

At the Weaste and District Oddfellows' Athletic Sports, commenced on Saturday, and brought to a conclusion on Monday. the first prize in the two miles bicycle handicap was carried off by Mr. W. H. Bellian, captain of the Warrington Cycling Club who had 170 yards start. Mr. Bellian was third in the one mile bicycle handicap.

1.0.G.T. PICNIC TO FRODSHAM. The members of the Order residing in Orford Barracks, with 26 children, proceeded to Frodsham on Tuesday, for their annual picnic. The party left Bank Quay Station at 10.25, and arrived at Mersey View pleasure grounds about 11,15 a.m. Swing- boats, donkey rides, refreshments, &c., occupied the time till 7.52., when the party returned to Warring- ton, having spent a most enjoyable day. The arrangements were in the hands of Colour-Sergeant Mantle and Mrs. Mantle.

PEERS' ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY. This society held another ballot meeting at the offices, 19, King-street, on Tuesday. Mr. Birchall (the president) occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance of members. Mrs. R. Anderton, Miss Winstanley, and Mr. H. Hoult were appointed scrutineers to conduct the ballot proceedings, which resulted in No. 6 being drawn, and this being held by Mr. Thomas J. Hulse, for five shares, he became entitled to the use of £5OO free of interest for 16i years. A vote of thanks to the chairman and scrutineers concluded the business.

WARRINGTON V. SWINTON. These football teams will meet this aftPrnoon on the Wilderspe, ground. Both clubs will put their strongesl combination in thetield, the follow- ing being tho players selected; Warrington: fail back, Boscow ; three-quarters, Lawless, Barnes, and Evans; half backs,J. T. Bate and J. Bate; forwards, Ashton, Fair Turner, Berry, E. Dillon, Randles, Donoghue, J. Jolley, Holmes, Nevins. Swinton: Full back, Murray ; three-quarters, Valentine, Marsh, and W. Winterbottom ; half backs, Bumby, and Brockbank ; forwards, Rothwell, Wall, Walker, Hallam, A. Sharples, E. Sharples, Evans, Chapman, and Hotchkiss. FUNERAL OF Mn. SAMUEL GASHELL.

The remains of Mr. Samuel Gaskell, of Latchford, whose death we recorded last week were interred in the Parish Church yard, Grappenhall, on Tues- day. The Rev. B. B. Prescott, of Christ Church, Latchford, and the Rev. J. Stephens, Godley, con- ducted the burial service. A large number of friends and,relatives followed the body to the grave, in- cluding Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. Broadbent, Dr. Starkey Smith, Mr. Rose, Mr. George Dakin, the Dlisses Massey, Mr. Millington, Mr. E. Aukland, Mr. Moore, &c. The coffin, which was of fumed oak, with brass mountings, bore the following inscrip- tion .—" Samuel Gaskell, born November 29, 1829, entered into rest, September 11, 1891." Many beautiful wreaths were sent by friends. WARRINGTON TRADES UNIONISM AND MUNICIPAL REPRESENTATION. A special meeting of the members of the Warring Trades Council was held, on Tuesday night, for the purpose of selecting two labour candidates for .the Warrington Corporation in the approaching election. The president, Mr. Crelly, ocntipied the chair. Mr. Malkin, secretary for the Warrington Ironworker's Union, was selected for Howley Ward, and Mr. John Price, (Win wick-street) secretary of No. 5 of the Federated Union, which includes navvies, gen- eral labourers, and others, for Latchford Ward. It has since been discovered that Mr. Price on account of not:baying resided in the town for the prescribed period, is not qualified to act as a Town Councillor. A new candidate will therefore be selected in his place by the Trades Council in the course of a few days.

div.head: NEW WELSH CHURCH.
div.p: THE NEW WELSH CHURCH.
We are pleased to bear that Mr. It Davies, Bod- londeb, Bangor, has sent a donation of £lOO towards the new Welsh Church to be built in Crosfield-street. A LURRY BACKED THROUGH A SHOP WINDOW.

On Wednesday morning, a lurry belonging to Mr. John Dunn, greengrocer, of Ea.lestown, was accidentally backed through the plate-glass window of Messrs. Henry Milling and Company, Limited, grocers, Horsemarket--at. The window was insured.

div.head: RECENT 'Bus ACCIDENT.
div.p: THE RECENT 'Bus ACCIDENT.

We are pleased to state that we learnt on inquiry late last night that Mr. Mc.Nair, of 56 Legllt., who was so severely injured through a bus in which he was riding being collided with, is recovering. His case has necessitated most careful treatment on the
part, of his medical man, Dr. Joseph. THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE.

The programme of classes for the ensuing session for this institute was issued on Monday. The teaching staff has been strengthened by the addition of Mr. J. Bolton, who will give instruction in book- keeping, and Mr. Woodheaa will take a class in agriculture. A number of scholarships, tenable at the classes of the Institute next year, are to be awarded to students who obtain first-class certific- ates in the examinations at the end of the season. The commercial classes commence on the :29th inst. Other classes commence on Tuesday evening. Programmes and entrance forms can be had at the Museum lending department.

EXCURSION TO LLANGOLLEN. The annual excursion of the employes of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son ( Warrington and Burton), Limited, took place on Saturday, Llangollen having been selected. The party from Warrington left the Central Station at 720, for Liverpool. No time was lost in reaching Birkenhead Station, where they entered the train which was due at Llangollen at 10 25. After luncheon at the Royal Hotel, Llan- gollen, the party started in waggonettes and pio- ceeded to Vale Crucis Abbey, the Horse Shoe Palls, and Glandyfrdwy, returning to Llangollen, and thence to Plas Newydd, the residence of Kr. G. H. Rcbertson. The party afterwards returned to the Royal Hotel, Llangollen, where an excellent dinner was served. The train left Llangollen shortly before eight o'clock, and Warrington was safely reached in good time. The excursion was a most enjoyable one.

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S TOTAL ABSTINENCE SOCIETY.
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S TOTAL ABSTINENCE SOCIETY.

On Sunday morning a meeting was held in con- nection with the above-named, on the ground behind Bewsey-st., after which an adjournment was made to the Public Hall, where a meeting took place under the presidency of Mr. William Tharme, railway missionary, of Liverpool. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman, Mr. McTeane, Miss Bol- land, and Mr. John Price, of Winwick-street. An- other meeting was hold in the afternoon, Mr. Thos. Roff, of Latchford, presiding, and addresses were given by him, Mr. Pemberton, Messrs. McTeane, W. itoberts, J. H. Warlow, & Councillor Dixon. A third meeting took place in the evening when Mr. W. Tharme was chairman, and delivered the first annual sermon in connection with the society. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman and an- other; and a duet was contributed by Mr. F. Wil- liams and Mr. Cooke, and a solo by Mrs. M. Tilley, and Mr. Thomas Marshall. INTERESTING PRESENTATION AT WINWICK.

On Tuesday night the congregation of the Winwick Parish Church assembled in the school- room to witness a presentation which was about to be made to Mr. J. Kerfoot, organist on his giving up that position. Canon Penrhyn spoke of the long services of Mr. Kerfoot, and the various changes which he had seen in the church. He said that Mr. Kerioot had served under three different rectors. He called upon Mrs. Comber of Middleton Hall, to make the presentation, which consisted of an illuminated address and a copy of Hymns Ancient and Modern. Mr. Kerfoot, in responding, thanked all who had taken part in that presentation, and then gave an interesting account oT how be had come to be organist of Winwick, some M years ago. On sitting down he was warmly cheered. A pro- gramme of songs was then gone through by the members of the choir and others in a capital _ _ _ _
manner. The presents were greatly admired b'y all as they were passed round the room for inspection.. The meeting closed with the singing of "Auld Lang Syne " and " God save the Queen.'

div.head: EMPIRE THEATRE OF VARIETIES.
div.p: EMPIRE THEATRE OF VARIETIES.

This theatre presents this week a most pleasing array of talent, which in no way detracts from the high reputation it as earned as a caterer for the public amusement. Miss Ethel Etherdo, serio-comic and burlesque actress,still charms the audiences with her delightful singing and dancing, and the Merry Muriels continue to appear, and with the introduc- tion of new jokes and conundrums are as diverting as ever. Deutcher and Schnider, the clever juvenile artistes, still make abundant applause and merri- ment by their bright songs and stirring dances with the comical acrobatic variations thrown in. Mr. Herbert Sinclair, a fine baritone, sings with much animation and fervour and with refreshing natural- ness; and Pat Connor the Irish vocal comedian, delights all, bringing down tte house by his render- ing of a clever song which forms a pasquinade upon the amours of Parnell. Bon-Bon and Artino, comical gymnasts, comedians, and grotesque boxers, are a most amusing pair; and their feats for skill, and strength on the trapeze are remarkable. Mr. Harry Russell the" Tyrolean vocalist and dancer," is another acquisition to the company; and adds new flavour to the programme by his choice renderings. A capital programme is promised for next week. HEALTH AND WEATHER OF WARRINGTON.

For week ending Saturday,llth Sept., 1891,which was the 37th of the cuirent year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Births: War- rington, 43; Latchford, 2; total 45. Deaths: War- rington, 19; Latchford, 4; total 23. The excess of births over deaths was 22. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 22.56 per 1,000 against 16.62, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 15.6 the corresponding week of last year. The death- rate from the seven chief zymotic disesases was equal to 4.9 per 1,000, against 2.43, the average rate of the four previous weeks, and against 3.12 the corresponding week of 1890. The ages of mortality were- 0 to 1, 11 ; 1 to 5, 6 ; 5 to 15,1 ; 15 to 25, ; 25 to 60, 1•, 60 upwards, 4; total 23. The deaths included-4 from measles, 1 from croup, 1 from diarrhcea, 2 from old age, 4 from brain disease, 1 from lung disease, 1 from liver disease. No cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week. Meteorology—The mean temperature was 60.35 Fah., and therefore 4.38 higher than preceding week. The maximum temperature 81 F., was re- ported on the 11th and 12th inst., and the mini- 1311M temperature 46 F., on the 7th inst. The rain- fall measured .55 inch. The general direction was Southerly, the reading of the Anemometer denoting 1,055 miles.—JoHN H. GORNA.LL, Medical Officer of Health. PROPOSED MEMORIAL AT ST. ALBAN'S CHURCH.

The congregation at St. Alban's Roman Catholic Church, Warrington, are taking steps to establish a memorial to the late Father Hall, who was a very prominent worker in the local Catholic cause. Owing to his instrumentality and dogged persever- ance,tbe Catholics of his time were enabled to make much progress. It is to Father Hall that they were largely indebted for the beautiful Cemetery provided for them in the town. Ile obtained for the Catholic inmates otthe workhouse the privilege of attending service at St. Alban's. He was a benefactor to the Church of St. Mary, Buttermarket-street, and it is related of him that he collected over .E. 3,000 in pen- nies alone, and that altogether he succeeded in raising some £lO,OOO for this work during the time that he was engaged at St. Alban's.. It is expected that the movement will very readily be taken up by the Catholics of the town generally. It has been decided that the memorial shall take the form of new altar rails for the sanctuary at St. Alban's, the estimated cost of which is about £lOO. The deci- sion was come to at a large meeting of the congre- gation, held on Sunday night,in the schools attached to the mission. There were present amongst many others, including the principal members of the con- gregation, the following persons :—Fathers Feeney, Cody, and Turner, who delivered addresses, and Messrs. G. Cavanagh, J. Marsh, E. Whitchurch, Connolly, Brooks, and J. Speakman.
The silver bullion taken from Valparaiso to Monte Video by H.M.S. Espiegle, has arrived at Southampton, on board the Moselle, and will be conveyed to the Bank of England.
