div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
" HIGH TIMES " IN THE POLICE CELLS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday on the case of Thomas McGarry, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Irlam-st. on Saturday night, being heard, the constable proving the case said he had to bring the man to the police station, and he was very noisy in his cell. The Chief Constable said this disorder in the cells was very much on the increase on Saturday night especially. Prisoners when they got in indulged in all sorts of jollifications and bad language and uproar, and it must be stopped. He would not press the case against the present prisoner, as he did not think he had been there before, but it must be understood this sort of thing could not be allowed at the police station either on Saturday or any other night.—The prisoner was fined ss.
A BRUTAL SON HUNTS HIS MOTHER WITH A KNIFE.

John Carroll, fireman, was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, with assaulting Mary Carroll, his mother, in Bakehouse Yard, on Saturday night.—The complainant said the defendant was drunk and ran her up to the top of the street with a table knife she produced, and added" He used the knife to myself with both kicks and blows. This is not the first time he has used this. He used this on his dead father."—The defendant said he might have been mad drunk, but he never did the like of that.—P.C. Wood deposed to going into the complainant's house on hearing the defendant making a disturbance there, and seeing him strike his mother.—The defendant: She wants to break my heart and send me out of the country altogether. I never used a, knife.—He was sent to prison for 14 days with hard labour.
A STRANGE EXCUSE FOR DRUNKENNESS-PUBLICANS' BOTTLING BUSINESS AFTER HOURS.

At the'magistrates- court, Warrington, on Wednesday, George Leckwood, who described himself as a Yorkshire- man, was charged with being drunk at 12 30 that morn- ing, in Bewsey-road—P C. Rylatt proved the case.—The defendant said he had been" wild" with the tic the night before and that to relieve the pain he had taken four sixpennyworths of whisky in 20 minutes at the Three Pigeons, hardly knowing what he was doing. He thought the waiter ought to be brought up for supplying him with so much, when he was in that state.—P.C. Rylatt said he had to bring the prisoner to the lock-up in a hand cart. He observed nothing to show that the man was suffering in the way described.—Mr. John Fairclough, one of the magistrates, said a case of a publican serving a man with four sixpennyworths in 20 minutes was one in which enauiry ought to be made.—Mr. Hunt said there were plenty of places in which after hours publicans did a bottling business every night, especially Friday, Saturday, and Monday nights.—The prisoner was fined 55.

THEFT OF VESTS FROM A DRAPER'S. Thomas Barton, Ship Canal labourer, was charged with stealing, the previous morning, from the shop of Anthony Bradley, 108 Bridge-st., three men's vests, value 1.55. 11d., his property. The Chief Constable said the complainant came to Warrington on Saturday last, and had been lodging on Friars Green and Town Hill. About ten minutes past eleven on Tuesday morning he was seen by a man named John Nolan to go to the complain- ant's door and cut the strings that held two men's vests, and walk away with them. Nolan informed Mr. Brad- ley, and his assistant, Herbert Roden, followed the pri- soner and took the vests from him, also started P.C. Turner in pursuit of him. Turner came up with him near the cricket ground, the man running away as soon as he saw the constable. The prisoner said he knew what Turner had come for, and would go with him. Roden met them and handed the two vests to Turner, and subsequently discovered at the shop that a white moleskin vest had also been stolen. This the prisoner was found to be wearing. He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour.

THE SEVEN SLEEPERS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday, Michael Brannon, labourer,of Warrington, James Walsh, of Wigan, Joseph Furnival, of Warrington, Daniel Crosby, of no settled abode, Wm. Berry, of Oldham,Jas. Kirkham, of no settled abode, and John Murphy, of St. Helens,were charged with being found sleeping in a shed at Arpley and near Bank Quay Station, between three and four o'clock that morning. Inspector Spinks said that morning about three o'clock he heard that several dinners had been stolen from the chemical works. He examined the neighbourhood, and the prisoners were found sleeping in the shed. They had twopence among them. A representative from the works made an un- sworn statement. He said the men coming to sleep in the shed was a very great nuisance to the works. The employes frequently had tobacco and their dinsers stolen. —Mr. Hunt said the prisoners were rogues on circuit from place to place.—The Chairman remarked that Cros- by now made his 68th appearance. Mr. Hunt might find him a job at the bridewell, as he seemed very fond of it.—The prisoners were all sent to jail for 7 days hard labour each, except Crosby and Furnival, who both having a previous record against them, were sent for 14 ilays each.

A JUVENILE INCORRIGIBLE. At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, Elizabeth Bate, milliner, Cobden-st., was charged with neglecting to send her brother Alfred Bate, of whom she was the guardian, his parents being dead, regularly to school. It was proved that the lad was quite incorrigible, and Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, said the boy had been twice convicted for stealing, therefore could not be sent to the Clio. Police-Sergeant Cox said seven keys of greengrocer? stores had been found on the bey. Sergeant Monaghan said his sister locked him in the house, but he got out through the bedroom windows,and sometimes when he could not get his clothes got out of the house without them. His sister,in reply to Mr. Garnett, who was on the bench. said she sent him every Sunday to Academy-st., Mission Sunday School. Her brothers who lived with her had done all they could with him without avail. She thought he wanted to be sent away. Mr. Garnett: I think if he were to have six strokes of the birch rod every two or three days it would do him good. —The Magistrates' Clerk (to the sister) : Are you will- ing he should be birched ?—The Sister: He has been birched.—Mr. Garnett repeated his question, but she made no reply.—The Magistrates' Clerk : She does not seem willing.—The Chairman (Mr. Guest) : You must either pay a fine or the boy shall be birched. A fine of ss. Was imposed. A previous fine of that amount hAd not bees paid by the defendant.

INDECENT CONDUCT TO CHTLDREN. Edward Fitzgerald, an unmarried labourer, lodging in Priestlev-street, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, -on Monday, with indecent conduct towards Lydia Yates, :vied 14, of 41 Bewsey-st., and Ellen Bur- don, of 3 School-brow, in Bank Park, on Saturday afternoon, also with assaulting Joseph Topping, an assist- ant park-keeper on the same occasion. The children gave evidence as to the offence, and said he had also insulted some young women, and Topping stated that on the for- rner complaining to him he went to look for the prisoner and found him behind some bushes,upon which he seized him, and the man then dealt him a violent blow with a can he carried. He was drunk at the time. The pri- soner said he was all black with the blows Topping gave him with his stick and Alderman Sutton told him if he was he richly deserted to he, but Topping said he did not strike him.—Ffe wis sent to gaol for a month's hard labour.—Thomas Usher, a young man, of 9, Morris's Court, and whose mother repeated the evidence to him, lie being deaf, was charged with indecent conduct to a

child named Rose Wooton, aged six years of Porter-st., at the Theatre R0y2.1 on Saturday night, also with assaulting her mother on her upbraiding him with the alleged offence. The prisoner denied his guilt, and his mother said he had had a drop of drink that night. He was fined 10s. including costs for the assault on the mother, but the magistrates dismissed the other charge.
A TASTE FOR RAW CABBAGE.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, seven lads ranging from 8 to 14 years of age, named James Morris, Daniel Morris, Alfred Brown, Thomas Stockton, John Connolly, John Woods, and Thomas Ireland were charged with having stolen cabbages belonging to Mr. John Welsby, from a field. They all pleaded guilty. On last Sunday afternoox P.S. Taylor and another constable were going past the field and they saw the lads go in to it and pull the cabbage. The officer added that the lads told him that they had pulled the cabbages to eat them. The mothers of the lads who were present all asserted with a good deal of indignant emphasis that their lads had no need to eat raw cabbage as they had had good dinners at home. Dr. Gornall said he was sorry he could not order the lads to be birched. A fine of ss. would be im- posed in each case.
A DIVIDED HOUSEHOLD: THE SON BEATS THE FATHER AND THE HUSBAND THE WIFE.

Thomas Farrington, who is about 18 or 19 years of age, was charged yesterday morning at the borough police court,with assaulting his father, Wm. Farrington. The latter, who appeared with a considerable amount of plaster on his face, said his son came home about mid- night on Sunday and began beating a younger brother. Witness,who was in bed, came downstairs in his shirt, to protect his younger son. Ile pris®ner then assaulted and threw a fender iron at him,which, striking his face, cut it severely. Mrs. Farrington, the mother of the pri- soner, who had a black eye, gave evidence in favour of her son. She said he was not drunk and it was only half- past nine o'clock when he came home at night. Because he was not in regular work she dare not give him any- thing to eat when her husband is about, and on Sunday night the younger son shouted upstairs to his father that the prisoner was getting some bread. The father came downstairs and began to abuse the prisoner, and this led to the assault. On Monday, her husband, after taking a warrant out against her son, assaulted her and gave her the black eve. Inspector Spinks informed the bench that he knew this family. They lived a wretched life, which was, he thought, mainly due to the wife who was continually jangling, and did not keep the house clean. The prisoner was bound over in £5 to keep the peace for six months.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Mr. Robert
Garnett.

RAILWAY Tuss-rs.—John Carney, a recruit from Orford Barracks, who had until recently been employed as a, collier at St. Helens, was charged on remand with hav- ing stolen from the London and North-Western Railway Station 115 scarves and 40 expired railway passes, the scarves being valued at 40s. and the passes at 55.—Mr. Preston appeared for the Railway Company. He said that a commercial traveller, who owned the scarves, gave them in charge of a man named Hamlet to take to the station, but how the other man get hold of them was a mystery to him. One of the Sergeants at the Barracks had seen the prisoner with the articles in Battersby-lane on the night in question, which was the 7th inst. The prisoner was at the time under the influence of drink.— The Bench decided to send him to prison for three months with hard labour.

DRUNKENNESS.—John McDonald was ordered to pay 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on Friar's- green, on Friday afternoon.—For a like offence in Pin- ners'-brow, on Friday, Patrick Mitchell was fined 2s. 6d. —John Burns, for being drunk and disorderly in Jolley's yard, on Friday night, was fined ss.—Bodelia Smith was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermar- ket-street, on Friday night; and Robert Hayes was charged with a similar offence in Wilderspool-road, on Saturday morning. They were each fined ss. and costs. BREACHES OF THE PEACE. —Kate Pownall, Bridget Lanelly, Ann Floy, and Ann Cowley were charged with committing a breach of the peace in Warburton-street, on Tuesday afternoon. They were fined ss. and costs each —For a like offence in Ship-yard, Bridget Costello, Ellen Higgins, Elizabeth Higgins, and Bridget Dogherty were ordered to pay ss. each. STONE THROWING.—AIfred Floy, Benjamin Jaundice, William Jaundice, and Patrick Lanelly, were summoned for throwing stones in Warburton-street, on Tuesday, to the danger of passengers. The Jaundices were discharged. The other defendants, who pleaded not guilty, were ordered to receive six strokes of the birch rod, by per- mission of their respective parents, and the Bench gave instructions that the two younger boys should watch the operation. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), and Aldermen Sutton and Wright. _

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY —Samuel Gandy- for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday last and assaulting P.C. Bell, was sent to jail for 14 days with hard labour.--Thomas Gleeson, from Manchester, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the same street on Saturday night. Inspector Bowen,who proved the case said the man had an open knife in his hand and got hold of a woman and dragged her from her husband. He went into a butcher's shop also and frightened a woman there.—The first-mentioned woman gave cor- roborative evidence, but said the man did not threaten her.—The defendant said he was cutting tobacco with the knife.—The Chairman said such conduct was abomin- able.—The Inspector said he saw the defendant going about with his knife open in Winwick-st., the same night and made him put it up.—Robert Disdale in Scotland- road, on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Sarah Crooks, in Tanner's-lane, at half-past 11, on Sunday night, who according to the prosecuting constable had acted like a mad woman, ss.—John Edwardsin Bridge-st., soon after midnight on Monday morning, ss.—Bridget Healey, in Ashton's-yard, on Saturday week, dismissed with a caution.—Patrick Mahar, in St. James-st., on the 7th inst., ss. and costs.—Walter Warburton, in Winwick-st. ss.—John Crooks, in the same street, on the 7th inst. ss.

DRUNII.—John Smith, drunk in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night. Alderman Sutton, on hearing that the defendant was a wooden-legged man, asked jocularly "Was the wooden leg drunk ?" (Laughter.) Fined 25. 6d.—Frederick Kelly was charged with being drunk in Knutsford-road. A p-,lice officer had found him asleep in the road, and woke him and got him away, but later on found him asleep in the same road. He therefore took him to the lockup. He had an empty bottle, that had contained spirits, in his pocket. The Bench fined him 55., Alderman Sutton remarking that that would pay for his lodgings on Saturday night. FURIOUS DRIVING.—AIfred Lee, carter, 74, Atherton- st. was fined 105. and costs for furious driving in Cliurch-st., on the 4th inst. FIGFITING.—John Hennessy, labourer, of Cropper's- brow, and Simon Scott, a Londoner, employed in the town, were bound over in the sum of £5 each to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay Costs. HAVING A CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Walter Birmingham, of Friar's-lane, for having his chimney on fire, on the sth inst, had to pay costs. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest (chairman) E. M. Crosfield, and R. Garnett.

ABSENCE FROM MILITIA TRAINING.—Thos. Flannery, of 14, Percival's-fold, was charged with being absent from the training of the 3rd South Lancashire militia regiment, in 1887. The prisoner had subsequently enlisted in the line under the name of Lowrey, and been discharged as constitutionally unfit for service. 40., or seven days. THEFT OF AN EGG Box.—Thos. McGuinness, of St. Helens, was charged with stealing the previous day an egg box from premises off Mersey-st. the property of Wm. Fairless, corn dealer. P.S. Chantler said, when in plain clothes he saw the prisoner coming away with the box, which he dropped on seeing him; and he said Mr. Fairless had Given him permission to take it, which proved to be false. He was sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour.

DESERTION FROM THE ARMY.—Thomas Larkin, charged with deserting from the Scotch Guards, stationed at Newry, was sent to Strangeways gaol to await an escort. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.—David Plinston, Back Aikin-street, drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Bridge-st., on Monday night, was fined 10s., and 3s. 6d. costa.

INDECENT BEHAVIOUR.—Mary France,married woman, for indecent conduct on Monday night, in Buttermarket street, she having been convicted of like behaviour in October, 1890, was sent to gaol for two months without hard labour.—Mary O'Reilly for indecency the same night, she having been convicted of the like conduct in June last, was sent to prison for the same period, with hard labour.

&nom. CASFS.—John Bennett, forgeman, of Pier- point-st ~ was summoned in respect of his son's non- attendance at school. The boy, Mr. Riley said,had been twice birched for his truancy. The father was fined ss. and informed that on the next offence the lad would be sent to the Clio.—Michael Cain, labourer, was charged with respect to his child. The father, Mr. Riley said, lived close to the Roman Catholic School. The lad be- longed to Orford-lane, which had been the first to adopt the free education system,and yet the lad did not go. 2s. 6d.—Price Edwards, stove maker, Manchester-lane, 2s. 6d.—James Henson, glass cutter, Ashton-st., who ex- changed some rather strong recriminations with Mr. Riley was fined IN.—James Gleeve,file forger,Lythgoes- lane, ss.—ratrick Lennerdy, brewer's man, Warburton- st.. Win. Lawrensen, forgeman, Bewsey-road, John McDonald, Ship Yard, Seth Travis, painter, School Brow, James Ward, labourer, Friars Green, and Edwin Stacey, forgeman, Bank Quay, ss. each.—Mrs. Stacey said the Bank Quay School was supposed now to be a free school, but the schoolmistress wanted the same sum as before. Mary Owen, labourer, Fennell-st., 2s. 6d.— Warrants were ordered for Michael Connor and Moses Williams. - -

.• THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Capt. Ridgway and Councillor John Fairclough. AN ABSENTEE FROM SCHOOL.—MOSeS Williams, forge- man, appeared on rem and charged with not send- ing his two boys regularly to school. Mr. Riley stated that this was the defendant's 18th appearance on charges of keeping his children from school. An order was made for one of the boys to be sent to St. Anne's vdustrial
school,and a similar order was made as to the other, sub- ject to there being a vacancy, which was not certain. Famy.—Before Alderman Sutton and Dr. Gornall.

ALLEGED THREATS.—Martha Hickey, a young married woman, was charged with having used threats towards Martha Lee, but the case was dismissed. Mr. A.Browne appeared for the defendant. INDECENCy.—Elizabeth Hunt was committed for 14 days hard labour for indecent behaviour, in Catherine- street. Catherine Smith and Thomas Jackson were charged with indecency in a field off Gorsey-Lane ; Smith I was sent to gaol for a month, and Jackson was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. AN UNPAID GAS BILL.—At the instance of the Gas Department of the Warrington Corporation, an order for distraint was made against John Wiley for an unpaid gas accoußt of £8 is. 2d. THE MAINTENANCE OF PARENTS.—On the application of Mr. Shearer orders were made upon the following persons to pay the sums named in support of their parents who had become chargeable to the Warrington Union :—Thomas Birchall, is. a week ; Joseph Green, is. a week; William Holt and Alfred Holt, is. a week each ; Thomas Isherwood, is. 6d. a week ; Henry Reaney, 2s. a week; John Wadsworth is. 6d. a week. A MIDNIGHT FLITTING.—Wm. Holbrook was fined 20s. and costs or one month's imprisonment for not having paid rent for a house due to Frederick John Carlyle. It was stated that the defendant, who did not appear,had made a midnight flitting, and had afterwards been sum- moned in respect of 16s. rent due. The case had been adjourned a fortnight to allow of the payment of the sum claimed but complainant had never seen defendant during the fortnight. Consequently the fine mentioned was imposed.

div.p: THE MTNER. SATURDA Y, SEPTEMBER 19, 1891.
WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs (chairman) and W. J. Bleckley. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Matthew Foy, on the 30th ult., at Croft, 2s. 6d. and costs.—Jacob Wood, on the 7th inst., at Poulton, 2s. 6d. and costs.—Joseph Thomas, at Penketh on the sth inst., 2s. 6d. and costs.—James Chambers and Martin Callon, in Dale-st.,Sankey Bridges, on the 30th ult., 2s. 6d. and costs each.

DRUNK IN CHARGE OF HORSES AND CARTS.—Charles Harrison, miller, drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Poulton, on the 9th inst. 2s. 6d. and costs.—Jacob Wood, drunk in charge of a horse and cart at Padgate, on the 9th inst., is. and costs._

FIGHTING.—Thomas Kelson, was charged with fighting at Penketh, on the previous Wednesday night. The case was adjourned till October 7th. ILLEGAL WErGHTS AND MEASURES.—Annie Litttlewood confectioner and second-hand clothes dealer, Sankey, was charged with having in her possession on the 31st ult., a pair of scales which were unjust and unstamped, and also certain unjust weights. Inspector Spencer said there were a Vb. weight 11 drachms out of balance and unstamped, a 11b. weight 2 drachms light and un- stamped, and a lb. weight a drachm light. The defen- dant pleaded that she had only been a month in business, and did not know the weights were faulty. The cases were dismissed.—Charles Humphreys,licensed victualler, of Sankey, was charged with having in his possession four gill wine measures one a quarter of a gill light, and the other three nearly a quarter light. Inspector Spencer proved the case. The defendant pleaded that he had been absent from his business, through illness, nearly 12 months, and his brother had been in charge, and must have changed the measures. He (the defen- dant) had been in business 31 years, and this was the first time he had been charged. He was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Refore Mr. C. Reynolds and Dr. Steele. TRMPORARY AIITHORITY.—Peter Brown was granted temporary authority to sell at the Rutters Vaults, Bruns- wick-street, under the license lately held by Sarah Friss.

AN OFFENDING BICYCLE RlDER.—George Bailey, of Grove-street, St. Helens, was fined is., and costs 9s. 6d. for riding his bicycle on the footpath at Sutton. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence Wm. Price, Thomas Murphy, and John Corcoran were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs. John Johnson and Ann Parkes were fined 10s. and costs for a like offence. John Harris and Ellen Coffey were fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—CharIes Whittle was fined is. and costs for obstructing the footpath in Bridge-st.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Birchall.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Birchall.
DRUNKENNESS.—John Hazgerty, no fixed abode, James Darsey, Sankey-street ; and Annie Dooley,no fixed abode, were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
MIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. J. Birchall and Mr. J. Stone.

DRUNK AND DISORDERL. Y-:—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Catherine Burns, Major Cross-st., Peter Ford, Walmsley-st., Mary Cosgrove, Greenfell-st., and Thos. Jackson, Wilmere-lane.—Mary Pitt, Bedford-st., and James Walsh, Lunt's Heath, were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for creating a breach of the peace.—Jos. Hamp- son, of Alforde-at., was dealt with in a like manner for using threats to James Williams,of Widnes Alkali Works. The offence was committed eighteen months ago,when the prisoner absconded. MORE COAL STEALERS.—AIice Drury, 10, Sankey-street and S. A. Bates, 24, Sankey-street, were brought up on remand charged with stealing a quantity of coal belong- ing to the United Alkali Company from the yard of Messrs. Craskell, Deacon and Co. The prisoners pleaded guilty and were each fined 10s. or seven days. ASSAULT ON A MOTHER-IN-LAW.---Mary A. Noon, of Nelson-street, was charged on remand with assaulting her mother-in-law, Mary Noon, by striking her on the head with a clog. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. CASES TOO COMKON.—Rosa A. Mooney, Nelson-st., was summoned by Bridget Tansey of the same street, for wilfully breaking three panes of glass, and also with using defamatory language to Mrs. Tansey. The case was proved, and the Bench said these kind of cases were too common. The defendant would be fined 10s. and must pay the damage Bs. 6d., and also be bound over to keep the peace for three months.—Mary Dunn, of Travis-pt., was summoned for assaulting Mary Mc- Laughlin and also using abusive language to her. The evidence showed that the woman had been much ill- treated, and a fine of 20s. and costs was imposed.

div.head: FIRE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.
div.p: FIRE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.

DAMAGES .£2,000. About 4 o'clock,on Sunday afternoon,several boys saw smoke issuing from the windows at the rear of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn, and they immediately informed P.S. Gosling who was in the locality. The fire bell was also rung. The Sergeant accompanied by several constables promptly made for the side door which they smashed in, and on entering the building they saw the organ loft in one mass of flames. The heat was scorching. willing hands commenced the removal of cushions, carpets, books, &c., and others attempted to restrain the progress of the fire, but it had attained such a hold that all their efforts were fruitless. Superin- tendent Large arrived in a few minutes and directed the efforts of his men. At length, half an hour after the alarm was given, the brigade arrived on the scene, under the command of Mr. W. Brown, who acted in the absence of Mr. Robert Wright, the superintendent and Mr. William Wright, the deputy, who were unfor- tunately away from home. In the meantime the flames had spread from the organ chamber to other parts of the building, the woodwork being of pitchpine, and in a short time the upper portion of the building was one circle of flame, and the windows burst with a loud report. The brigade attached their hose to the hydrants with dispatch, and were soon pouring an immense volume of water on the burning mass. Aided by a number of helpers they worked with a will and in a space of about half an hour they had got the fire partly under control, but it was not completely extinguished until seven o'clock. The ceiling fell about half-past five with a tremendous crash, and several of the firemen were buried beneath the debris, but they were quickly extricated. One named John Plant was brought out suffering from a dreadful gash in the cheek, and another named William Corker was overcome by the heat, dust and smoke, but was not otherwise injured and after a rest in the church- yard he returned to his work. A man named Peter Crogan, who had no connection with the brigade, was also partly suffocated and was carried to his home on the ambulance stretcher. The interior of the edifice was almost entirely destroyed. Not one vestige of the organ, which was recently repaired at a cost of £6O, remains. The building was erected in 1835 at a cost of £6,000, but since that time several hundreds of pounds had been spent in altering and improving the sitting accommodation and in generally renovating the place. The damage done is estimated at £2,000, and the building was insured for £3,000 in the General Life and Fire Assurance Company. How the 'fire arose is a question that cannot be answered, and probably will always remain a mystery. Sunday had been set apart for the choir sermons and the Rev. Samuel Yates, of Spalding, in Lincolnshire, who was formerly pastor of the chapel, had preached in the morning. In the afternoon the members of the choir had a practice for the evening service and they did not leave until ten minutes to four. A quarter of an hour later the organ loft was in flames. The day was very hot and no fire was being used in the building but the organist had used a gas jet at the organ, though this had been turned completely out before the instrument was closed. The members of Bethesda Con- gregation have the sympathy of the other religious denominations in the town in their great loss, and at several of the places of worship on Sunday evening the officiating ministers made sympathic references to the event.

Sir Edmund Lechmere, M.P. for Worcestershire, has been selected as the Unionist candidate for South Wor- cestershire, now represented by Sir Richard Temple. At Wolverhampton, on Thursday,a borJkmaker, named Ball, alias Chippy Norton, was fined £2), for using a stand at Dunstall Park races. Two other bookmakers were fined £5 each.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

DOUGLAS (ISLE OF MAN) V. WARRINGTON .—Played at Douglas, on Saturday. As might have been expected the Warrington men proved too powerful for the home team and won easily by 3 goals and 3 tries to nothing. Both teams worked hard, but the weather was unpleasantly warm for the game. WARRINGTON V. ISLE OF MAN.—The Warringtonians, continuing their tour, encountered a team selected by the Manx Union on Monday, at Belle Vue, Douglas. A capital attendance was recorded,and in splendid weather the visitors soon adopted the aggressive. James Bate scored during the first ma, whilst Evans and Fair Tur- ner augmented the score during the second portion, Barnes converting one. Final result :—Warrington, 1-2-6 ; Isle of Man, nil. MILL-LANE STAR V. ST MARTS.—This match was played on Saturday afternoon, on the Star ground, in fine weather. Pemberton kicked off for the star and the home team attached, a minor resulting. Directly after- wards H. Dardy received a pass and after a good run scored a try for the Star. A second try was scored by F. Howell and a third by W. Rider for the Star. Banner put in some splendid kicking for the home team. Score : Star, 3 tries, 2 minors ;St. Mary's, 1 try, 1 minor. WARRINGTON STAR V. ECCLESTON Rovens (ST. HELENS).—The above match took place on Saturday, on the Star field. The home team started, and ere long from some loose play, Walmsley got over. Soon after Clare followed suit. Half time score : Star 3 tries, 2 minors, to nil. In the second half the home team again pressed and just before call of time Lawless got over, the kick at goal being a failure. Final result Warrington, Star 4 tries, 3 minors; Eccleston Rovers, 1 try, 1 minor. WIDNES ST. MARY'S V. WEST LElGlL—Played at Widnes on Saturday. The home team kicked off, but West Leigh attacked, taking advantage of some erratic passing by St. Mary's. A spirited attack by the home team cul- minated in Mason scoring a try. Cook failed at goal. ' St. Mary's now showed greatly improved combination, some really fine passing taking play from one end of the field to the other. A combined rush by the visitors ended in J. Jiles scoring a try, Sinclair kicking a goal. Mid- field exchanges were for some time the order of play,but Howard put the home team on the attack once more, Mason scoring a second try, which remained unconverted. Half-time score :—West Leigh 1 goal, Widnes St. Mary's 2 tries. Final result :—Widnes St. Mary's 1 goal, 2 tries, 1 minor, West Leigh, 1 goal, 1 try. FRODSHAM V. DINGLE.—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday. Both teams started without their full complement, Frodsham playing 14 and Dingle 13 men. The home team were short of Parker, r. Rogers, Clough, M. Rogers, and Brown. The visitors kicked off, and Frodsham at once began to press. From a kick by the visitors' full back, Peacock secured, and after a good run half the length of the field, scored near the touch line. Darlington made a good attempt at the plaae, the ball hitting the post. After this, the play ruled more even, but the home forwards, with a nice dribble, took the ball no the field and W. Rogers scored, the kick at goal failing. From the drop out, Sutton got hold, and dropped a neat goal. Then Hayes scored and the whistle blew for half time, with the score Frodsham 1 goal (dropped), 3 tries and 3 minors to nil. The home full back now arrived, but the Frodsham captain, T. Darlington, in order to equalize numbers, consented to allow him to play for the visitors. From some pretty passing by the home halves, T. Darlington scored, but the kick at goal again failed. Then T. Darlington, Goodall, and F. Darlington scored in rapid succession, the goal kick failing in each instance, and " time " arrived with the score Frodsham 1 goal (dropped) 7 tries and 3 minors to Dingle nil. RUNCORN V. MR. H. H. BAINBRIDGE'S MANCHESTER TEADL—The opening game of the season was played on Saturday on the Irwell-lane ground. The weather was totally unfit for the winter sport, the great heat making play disagreeable. On the home side Crompton and Williams were absent,whilst the visitors were not a very strong lot, the paincipal player being Molyneux, of the Manchester club. A game of two 30's was started by the District team, when after a series of scrimmages it soon became apparent that the home team were going to have things much their own way. Faulkner was first to score after an effort by Pendlebury. The game had not been in progress long ere Faulkner again got over the line,Houghton narrowly missing the goal. Buck having again put the ball into play, the visitors made a raid to the home end, Molyneux, Buck and Wardley being very prominent. This was smartly neutralized, for Davies picked up, ran strongly, and finished by throwing to Abrams, when Faulkner,Gayter,and Hamp son carried the ball over the District line, the latter scor- ng the point, and Faulkner kicking a goal. Evans and Abrams by short passing got the ball to Davies, who eluded all opposition, going behind the posts, the try at goal failing. Immediataly after the drop out, Davies forced his way behind the line, Faulkner being successful in :the goal kick. At this point the District team seemed completely routed and they were never once dangerous. The scoring on the part of the home team continued, a forward rush over the line was completed by Riley scoring, Faulkner kicking another goal. Pendlebury got a wide pass, and after a race got over at the corner flag. This brought the welcome interval with a score of 3 goals and 4 tries in favour of Runcorn—to nil. After a brief rest, Faulkner set the ball going and scoring soon began. Lee after a series of exchanges in which several forwards were prom- inent, scored a good try, but no goal resulted. After this, Davies ran in three times in succession. Faulkner coming to the front in the goal kicking line, being suc- cessful in placing the goals. Final result:—Runcorn, six goals, five tries ; Nanchester District nothing. Teams Runcorn: S. Houghton, back; T. H. Davies, W. Faulk- ner, and George Pendlebury, three-quarter backs • S. Abrams and W. E. Evans, half-backs ;R. Dolan,P. J. Gayter, George Lee, 0. Hughes, H. May, W. Shaw, A. Hampson, and J. Davies, forwards. Manchester Dis- trict: C. Wardley, back; Dawson, Webster, and Buck, three-quarter backs; Molyneaux and Hollingsworth, half-backs; Parlane, Abbey, Webster, Tomlinson, White- head, Hickey, Grange, Ibbotson, and Bainbridge, for- wards. EARLESTOWN V. RUNCORN " A."—The Earlestown club opened their new ground under very favourable circum- stances, both as regards weather and spectators, on Saturday, when they encountered the " A " string of the redoubtable Runcorn club. The Runcorn men were on the ground in good time, but the Earlestown team were very dilatory in putting in an appearance,and when they did step on to the field they were two men short, and another delay took place in finding substitutes. This was rather bad for a start, but owing to the presence of the Earlestown band, the time passed pleasantly enough. The Runcorn team however were very impatient, and with half-an-hour's late start they agreed upon twenty minutes' play each way. Earlestown lost the toss, and Runcorn elected to defend the lower goal, with the sun at their backs. Earlestown kicked off, and the ball was quickly returned by Runcorn. From a scrimmage, Run- corn picked up, but they lost possession and Earlestown crossed the visitors' 25. A quick return was made, and the ball went into touch. From throw in the ball became dead. Some smart play afterwards took place and Run- corn registered the first point, a minor. Play was then confined within the home 25, and several scrimmages en- sued, Runcorn showing their superiority by the smartness with which they secured the ball, they on nearly every occasion being successful in getting it clear, owing principally to the faulty play on the part of the home forwards. After some smart exchanges, in which Carson nearly broke away, Gayter, for Runcorn, secured a try. The kick at goal was taken by Booth and proved successful. The game then stand- ing Runcorn 1 goal, 3 minors, to nil. Half time was immediately called and after crossing over, play was again transferred to the home 25. Some misunder- standing arose as to a foul, and a change of referees took place. On play being recommenced,Harrison got hold and made a gallant effort to get over the line, but was pulled up when nearly successful. The ball was again carried to the home 25 by a smart bit of passing, and Robinson ultimately crossed the line a second time. Booth again took the kick, but he shot a little wide. From a high kick by Williams the ball travelled over the Runcornline but Watkins was unable to touch down, and it was returned into play. Some loose play took place, but Runcorn maintained the upper hand, Earlestown being at no time dangerous, owing to a lack of combination. When the whistle sounded the game stood, Runcorn, 1 goal, 1 try, 3 minors ; Earlestown, 1 minor.—Teams— Earlestown: Back, Carson; three-quarter backs, A. Williams, Melia, Taylor; half backs, Slinn, A. P. Watkins; forwards, H. Watkins, Sherrington, Clarke, Reyes, Collier' Harrison, Ashton, Schofield, Lees. Run- corn : Back, Robinson; three-quarters, Webb, Booth, Antrobus ; half backs, Hollinsworth, Robinson ; for- fards, Evans, Coleshall, Massey, Rees, Eccles, Gayter, Taylor, Stubbs and Derbyshire. WARRINGTON A V. RUNCORN A.—These local rivals met on Monday evening, at Wilderspool, and mucluin- terest was added to the encounter owing to the visltbrs having the assistance of several first team men. Run- corn winning the toss, took advantageof a slight breeze, and while hostilities were proceeding about midfield, a pass from Lally to Daniels enabled the latter to run to the 25 flag. A free kick to the visitors nullified the advantage, and forced Warrington back to their own half. Lally got away splendidly, and Daniels enhanced the position. A kick by Robinson found the combatants vieine. with one another, in neutral territory, and after a stiff struggle the Runcorn men got away to the home line. Lally relievEd ; and some strong work by Buckley, Lawless, and Tears improved matters. Barnes, Buckley, Davies. and Russell dribbled splendidly to midfield, and Lawless and Russell carried the leather to the visitors' goal. Lally fairly roused the spectators by the manner in which he scored a grand try, but no goal resulted. A mull let the visitors in, and Davies ultimately dodged over at the corner. Potts afterwards dribbled grandly to his opponents' quarters, and the game ruled fast and furious. Cawley was at this stage hurt, but Davies saved a rush finely, Sampson replied to a kick, and Potts took the oval grandly to the further end of the field. A rush of the home for- wards harrassed the Runcorn defence, until a

kick released the position. Lawless was here conspicu- ous, and some very exciting tussles were witnessed. The Runcorn forwards came away to the centre line, but Robinson had to save. A rush was the next item of interest by Warburton, Russell, and Buckley. Lawless spoiled a fine run by a wild pass, and half time arrived with the score level. On re-commencing, fast play characterized the opening movements. A huge punt by Webster gave the Warringtonians a distinct advantage, but eventually a spell of passing,in which Crompton was , the chief factor, gave the Cheshire men a footing in the home 25. Lally was applauded for some smart play, but Potts was a trifle erratic, and failed at an exciting movement. The miniature home half back got clear away from a pack opposite the grand stand, but some kicking by Crompton eventually forced a minor. The drop-out saw the game at half way, Gayter, Stubbs, and Antrobus for Runcorn, Davies and Buckley for Warrington, showing up alternately. A forward rush, headed by Russell, took the game near the visitors' posts, and a moment later the " Wirepullers " were pulled up on the line. Daniels spoiled a good chance by dropping at goal, a performance that was ridiculed by the large crowd. With the minors equal, Runcorn dropped out, and some short passing by the visitors ter- minated in Robinson scoring. Russell shone on the restart, and the homesters redoubled their energies, but Runcorn forced another minor. Darkness was fast creeping on, and the last stages of the game were only witnessed with difficulty. Davies was instru- mental in Warriagton gaining a final footing in the Run- corn 25, and although Tlaornley confidently claimed a try, a minor was the only award, and an enjoyable game ended—Runcorn, 0-2-2, Warrington 0-1-3. Warrington: Sampson, back; Webster, Potts, Daniels, three-quarter backs ; Lawless and Lally, half backs; Davies, Thornley Barnes, Molyneux' Buckley, Teare, Rowlands, Russell, and Warburton. Runcorn : T. Robinson, back; Caw- ' ley Crompton, Davies, three-quarter backs; G. Robin- - , son and Booth, half backs ; Massey. Reas, Evans, Derby- shire, Antrobus, Gayter, Taylor, Webb, and Stubbs, for- wards.

WARRINGTON" A" v. TRANDIERE WANDERERS.—The opening of the legitimate season, so far as Warrington is concerned, was begun on Saturday when the above teams met on the Wilderspool enclosure. The opening of the match was witnessed by a large crowd, and Ruth dribbled well at the opening, but Daniels, intercepting a pass, ran splendidly three parts the length of the ground being stopped by Snape. Some strong work by the visitors' forwards showed they meant business, but any advantage gained by Heden's punt was nullified by off-side play. A fine piece of work then roused the enthusiasm of the spectators. It was started by Buckley and the leather passed through the hands of Bailey, Thornley, and Mather, the last named scoring a try. Following the drop out, Thornley picked up smartly, and threw to Mather, who was only pulled up on the line, where, after Potts had almost scored, Barnes did the trick, and Sampson placed a goal. The Wanderers then pressed their attentions on the home goal, through the Warrington back delaying his kicking powers, and the result of smart play by Heden and Hancock caused the warfare to hover about the Warrington line. A fine relief was effected by Daniels and Thornley, and a really splendid bout of passing, between Mather Potts, and Webster, enabled the latter to run in beautifully. A grand goal followed from Sampson's kick. While the game was fluctuating in the neighbour- hood of the centre line, Lawless threw to Webster, who effected a tall punt, but the off-side play of some of the homesters caused a rapid retirement to their quarter flag. Davies, Warburton, and Teare were instrumental in re- gaining the lost ground, tut Jones, showing his dribbling powers, transferred the game to the Warrington line, where disaster was averted. The visitors had a fine chance of scoring at this stage, but failed at the essential moment, and half-time arrived with Warrington 2-1-0 to nil. After the usual council of war had taken place, the game was prosecuted with vigour, notwithstanding the great heat, and Tranmere attacked strongly. The im- minent danger to the goal was eventually relieved by Davies, Rowlands, and Molyneaux, and Lawless supple- mented matters by a run and kick. A tall punt by Mather was badly mulled, and Bailey seizing the leather threw beautifully across to Webster,who ran in strongly near the corner flag. After the drop-out D. Buckley showed his great ability by the way in which he fielded, and passed the ball to Mather, who was floored on the line. The success which had attended the Warrington- ians seemed to follow their efforts,for Lawless ran right to the line before being stopped. Then the Wanderers started to liven up, a splendid dribble by Garnhan carrying play to midfield. Davies, Rowlands, Barnes, and Teare were here promimmt by some sterling work, amidst a lot of rough and tumble encounters. Heden then ran in fine style, and a lot of somewhat indiscriminate passing amongst the visiting forwards almost resulted in a tang- ible point. The game continued to be rather rough, and I after Bailey, Lawless, and Buckley had effected a relief, H. Heden foiled the home halves, but after getting right away, was quickly overhauled by Webster, and from a wild throw Heaton got possession and secured the coveted try, no goal resulting. Strong forward play made matters very warm for the homesters, but Samp- son eventually ran the ball out to neutral territory. In the loose, Thornley. Barnes, and Buckley took the ball to the quarter flag, and after some exciting encounters, a smart bit of work resulted in Rowlands dashing over the line. This was not the lastltenr, for Lawless got away and secured a capital try, but the place again failed. From the kick out Teare showed up prominently, but ultimately the whistle blew leaving Warrington winners by 24-0 to 0-1-0.

div.head: CHARGE OF WIFE MURDER.
div.p: CHARGE OF WIFE MURDER.

The adjourned inquest was held at Bath, on Monday, concerning the death of Hannah Bainton, wife of a mason, who has been remanded by the magistrates on the charge of murdering the deceased by throwing her into the river Avon on Tuesday last. Additional evi- dence having been given, a verdict of wilful murder against the man was returned.

div.head: SIR C. RUSSELL AT DONCASTER.
div.p: SIR C. RUSSELL AT DONCASTER.

Sir Charles Russell was the principal speaker at a Liberal demonstration, held at Doncaster, on Monday night. Responding to a resolution expressing confi- dence in Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party, he said that people were beginning to understand the Irish ques- tion, which was the principle of governing according to popular will. Liberals trusted the people, and the his- tory of the world recorded no instance of people having power to act under their own will having made a mis- take. Referring to the House of Lords, Sir Charles said he did not want any reformation which would make it stronger so long as it was non-representative in character. *

div.head: LORD EGERTON'S BIGOTRY.
div.p: LORD EGERTON'S BIGOTRY.

The "Daily News" says :—Lord Egerton of Tat- ton has been challenged to explain, or if possible to disavow, his responsibility for a curious form of agreement setting forth the conditions on which he proposed to sell a site, and subscribe £4OO for cer- tain church schools in Heaton Chapel, near Man- chester. These conditions were considered, even by Lord Egerton's fellow Churchmen, so alien to the spirit of the times, so intolerant to Nonconformists, and so inctaisistent with the conditions of school life under the Education Act, that the rector of the par- ish concerned has publicly announced the refusal of Lord Tatton's subscription, and the purchase of a site from another landowner. The agreement sub- mitted to the school managers provided that by a mortgage deed the return of the .E4OO should be secured in the event of the school coming under the control of a school Board "or any other statutory body appointed to control or supervise education," or in the event of the Church of England being dis- established, or in case the school should be " used for the education of the children of persons not be- longing to the Church of England." The Committee were not even to be excused from returning the money if legislation compelled them to deviate from Lord Egerton's requirements. It was in these con- ditions that the school managers at Heaton Chapel resolved to do without Lord Egerton's land and gift, or rather loan.
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.
A WIDNES MAN KILLED.

About half-past two o'clock, on Thursday after- noon,a shocking accident occurred in the St. Helens Chemical Works, belonging to the United Alkali Company, by which a man named William Beswick, was killed, and two men, named Gaffney and Caunce, were injured. For some time the works have not been in use, and a number of men have been engaged pulling down certain buildings. The three men, under the superintendence of a man named Pennington, were assisting to de- molish a large wooden structure, on which had been placed six large pans used in Weldon's pro- cess. The structure which was forty feet high, forty long, and fourteen feet wide had stood while the pans were taken off, but on Thursday, without any warning whatever, suddenly collapsed. Beswick and Gaffney, who were on the top, were thrown to the ground, and whilst falling were struck with the timbers. Caunce was workinc, on the ground, and when he heard the crash ran, but was caught c.n the back and thrown forward. He however only sustained slight injuires to his right arm. Two hand ambulances were quickly on the spot from the police office, and Gaffney, who bad one arm broken and injuries to the head was removed to Providence Hospital. Beswick was with difficulty got from under the fallen debris, and taken to his lodgings in Langtree-st. The affair has caused a great sensation in the works and neighbour- hood. The cause of the accident is supposed to have been the rotten state of the timber, it having been com- pletely eaten by acid. The deceased man Beswick re- sided at Crompton's Cross, Appleton, and was in the employ of a contractor named Burton, also of Widnes. While working in St. Helens he had lodged, as stated, in Langtree-st.

Total THE FAMINE IN RUSSIA.

According to accounts from the Russian frontier, it is not only the provinces where the crops have failed that are afflicted with famine, but also the districts bordering thereon. In the Government of Orel things are well- nigh desperate. The population has been decimated by hunger and disease. Bread is literally fought for. Transports of rye bread, flour, and salt are attacked and plundered on the road to their destination by the fam- ished peasants and labourers, even when escorted by soldiers. There have been frequent sanguinary collisionS between the troops and the people, who on such occa- sions freely use their knives. The Relief Committees are inefficiently organised. M. Pobedonoszew has installed special Committees under the auspices of the Holy Synod, but they confine themselves to assisting the monasteries and the small clergy. Since famine has broken out the prisons have filled rapidly. The lower classes find they are better provided for in gaol than outside, and many of them commit petty offences in order to get a few weeks' imprisonment. At Jelisowetgrad the number of prisoners is seventy per cent. of the population. At Nischni-Novgorod it has been found necessary to construct temporary sheds for the accommodation of criminals, as the prisons are all overcrowded.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

NEWTON V. WARRINGTON (2ND ELEVEN).—PIayed at Newton on Saturday. Newton won the toss, and were first represented by Hindley and Lister. The latter, who showed a liking for hitting, was soon taken in the long field, one for eight. Hindley, Halliday, and Cooke all played a careful game, and the score slowly reached 44 ere the fourth wicket fell. The next wicket added 14 runs, but on Smith changing ends, three more wickets quickly fell to his bowling—nine for 69. Owing to an error in fielding the last wicket added nine more runs, the total finally reading 78. The visitors had 70 minutes to obtain the requisite number of runs. Bell and Adam- son being the first pair to represent Warrington, and runs came at a rare pace, chiefly from Bell's bat,3B being notched ere the second wicket fell. Smith hit out when- ever opportunity presented itself,and Dunbobbin played carefully, although the visitors wanted the runs and had plenty of wickets in hand, and within 15 minutes of drawing time, it seemed doubtful whether the runs would be obtaieed. Wanting five runs to win, Smith was badly run out for a grandly hit 27, and within three minutes of time Wallington, Bullivant, and Spinks all risked their wickets to obtain the runs, the visitors just winning on the point of time with three wickets in hand. THE CHOLERA ON BRITISH WARSHIPS.

Fifteen deaths from cholera have occurred on board the British warships at Bombay. On Monday, however, only one fresh case appeared. The vessels affected are the Marathem and Redbreast, and not the Blanche,as at first reported.
HEAVY DAMAGES FOR BREACH OF PROMISE.

The London Sheriff's Court, on Thursday, awarded £l,OOO damages, for breach of promise, to Mary Jane Benson, of Haggingfield, Essex, the defendant being Sidney Casbourne, described as a Government clerk,liv- ing at Norwood. Counsel stated that about a thousand letters passed between the parties during their engage- ment.

div.head: MINER SHOT DEAD.
div.p: A MINER SHOT DEAD.

On Thursday, at Coseley, near Dudley, the coroner's jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against Samuel Whitehouse, a volunteer. It is alleged that he shot dead a miner named Elwell as the latter was leaving his house, which is a long distance from the rifle range. White- house admitted that on returning from the range he fired twice in the direction of the miner's home.

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN QUEBEC.
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN QUEBEC.
200 PERSONS HOMELESS.

On Sunday evening a fire broke out in a private house in Eyre Blanc, a suburb of Quebec, and spread with such rapidity that before it could be checked thirty dwelling houses had been burnt to the ground. The dre has ren- dered two hundred persons homeless, but temporary shelter has been found for them. A man has been ar- rested on suspicion of wilfully causing the fire.

div.head: MR. DE COBAIN AGAIN.
div.p: MR. DE COBAIN AGAIN.

The "Pall Mall Gazette" of Thursday puplishes an in- terview between a correspondent and Mr. De Cobain at Boulogne. In this interview Mr. De Cobain swore he was as innocent of the charges brought against him as a new born babe, and that they were the result of a con- spiracy by members of the high Tory party in the North of Ireland, whose names he could not give with- out his solicitor's permission. The information he pos- sessed would dumbfound England and all Europe.
CROSSFIRING.

The hearing of the charge against a man named Allen of exposing to public view an indecent print was con- cluded at Belfast on Thursday. This is the case in which some remarkable statements were made on Wednesday in reference to Mr. de Cobain's case. On Thursday several witnesses were examined, including Mr. de Co- bain's solicitor, and in the end Allen was discharged.

CADDIS WORMS AND THEIR HABlTS.—Amongst the almost endless number of objects of interest which meet the eye of the searcher after brook and river treasures few will be found to reward his investigations more richly, or open up a wider field for study and reflection, than the genus of xieuropterous insects (Phryganea), to which the so- called caddis-fly belongs. A vast number of species have been described by naturalists as inhabiting the rivers and brooks of England. Some of these families of insects are comparatively local, whilst others appear to be common wherever suitable conditions for their sustenance and support are met with. Not only do the perfect insects or flies of different species vary in colour, tint, etc., but the larvas, who are accomplished builders in their way, adopt a style of architecture in accordance with the customs of the family to which the constructor belongs. P. fluviacornis, for example, from the moment he quits the egg dropped by the parent fly to the still deeps of the brook pool, turns his attention to the collection of tiny fresh-water shells and minute particles of shell-like substances. These, by a process allied to that by which the silkworm forma its cocoon, are, so to speak, spun together. The glutinous filaments of web, as they are given off by the insect, adapt themselves to every Inequality of the substance to be secured at the point intended to be next the chamber or tube, in which, when smoothly and evenly lined, the indus- trious and deft worm will find an abiding place. Shell after shell and particle after particle are thus added step by step to the structure, and as the caddis-worm grows so he increases the bulk of his building materials, turning them with his ready claws until they are in a position to suit his require- ments. But whilst we admire his contructive talent and skilful selection, truth compels us to state that P. fluviacornis is most dishonest and un- scrupulous in his building operations. What should we say of a powerful potentate who, to build for himself a splendid mansion, seized on the dwelling- houses of other people, carried them off bodily, turned them upside down with the inhabitants in them, and then cemented one on the other until the tyrant's stronghold was complete Such con- duct, although highly reprehensive in the potentate, Is most interesting and curious in a caddis-worm, who is perfectly indifferent as to whether the fresh- water mollusk fixed on for building purposes is in his castle or not. If he is, he simply has to travel from place to plaoe at the will of his captor; if not, the empty shell is taken immediate possession of, just as any other stray substance would be.—From Cassell's Fopular Educator. WELLINGTON IN DIFFICULTY.—A French officer tells an amusing anecdote. It was at the time when the French army stood before Torres Vedras, separated from the British camp by a number of vineyards in which there were a few caves con- taining wine. The soldiers of both armies drank fraternally from these stores without ever coming into conflict. One day, however, a French sergeant was captured in one of the caves by some English soldiers, who took him into their camp and con- ducted him to the Duke of Wellington. After a few questions the sergeant was ordered to leave, but would not stir. "Go along," said the General. No movement, but the brusque reply, "General, your soldiers had no right to make me their prisoner." "And how is that?" "Hose is that? It is in this way. The cave being neutral ground, they had no more right to capture me than I had to capture them. They took advantage of my Isolation. Soldiers ought to have more manners among themselves." "Was that the way you were taken prisoner ?" "Yes, General." "Very well, you shall dine with ray attendants and go where you came from." But the Frenchman still refused to move an inch. "Have you not heard what I said, sergeant ?" "Oh, yes, General, I have heard it all, but I do not wish to go with your attendant." "And why not?" "Because no French soldier ever eats with domestic servants." Lord Wellington, with a bow and a sign of astiont, took the hint, ordered another 4‘ couvert " to be laid at his own table, and invited the French sergeant to dinner. A GIPSY TRICIL—The feat known by the gip- sies as "the great secret" is performed by Inducing some woman of largely magnified faith— say some decent farmer's wife—to believe that there is hiaden in the house a magic treasure, which can only be made to come to hand by de- positing in the cellar another treasure, to which it will come by natural affinity or attraction. "For gold, as you sees, my dearie, grows gold, and so if you ties up all your money in a pocket-handkerchief and leaves it, you'll find it doubled. And wasn't there the Squire's lady, and didn't she draw two hundred gold guineas out of the ground when they'd laid in an old grave—and only one guinea she gave me for all my trouble; and I hope you'll do better by the poor old gipsy, my dearie." The gold and all the spoons are tied up—for, as the enchantress observes, there may be silver too—and she solemnly repeats over it certain magical rhymes. The next day the gipsy comes to see how the charm is working. Could anyone look under the cloak she might find another bundle -precisely resembling the one containing the treasure. She looks at the precious deposit, repeats her rhyme again and departs, after carefully charging the housewife that the bundle must not be touched or spoken about for three weeks. "Every word you tell about it, my dearie, will be a guinea gone away." Sometimes she exacts an oath on the Bible that nothing shall be said. Back to the farmer's wife never again. After three weeks another extraordinary instance of gross inorednlity appears in the country papers, and is perhaps repeated in the colossal London daily, with a referenoe to the absence of the schoolmaster. There is wailing and shame in the house—perhaps great suffering, for it may be that the savings of years have been swept away. The charm has worked. 0 How PERFORMING ANIMALS ARE TRAINED.— People who go to the circus and see horses, ele- phants, monkeys, and the like perform wonderful tricks must often ask themselves how the animals Are taught to do them. A writer in the Moan, timing interviewed several circus celebrities, under- takes to satisfy their curiosity. M. Loyal, who has been ring-master of the leading Paris circus for 32 years, supplies interesting information concern- ing horses. "The horse," be says, contrary to general belief, "is the most stupid animal on earth. He has only one faculty—memory. You must teach him his exercises with the cavesrn and the long whip. Having forced them into his head, you =lust use the short whip when he resists, and give him a carrot when he obeys. Whips and carrots form the secret of the trainer." With respect to dogs, M. Changsax says their edu- cation is a work of time and patience. Some- times it takes two years. "I use neither sugar nor whip," he informs us. "I take my dog in my hands, talk to him, and try to make him under- stand what he is to do. I perform the tricks my- self, and the dogs follow and imitate me." At present he is showing a carriage dog which per- forms on the single wire. "I made him first of all walk on a plank which was balanced to and fro. The plank was gradually reduced in width every day, and ultimately the dog found himself on a single wire." Strange to say, this dog is Olind. Mr. Changeux says scent is the great quality which enables dogs to perform some tricks. The pig is said to be the most 'difficult animal to train. Tony Grioe, the clown, does not believe in learned pig). They are to be taught only by their weak point—their gluttony. A CENTENARIAN IN A BALLOON.—One of the last persons who went up in Giffard's great captive balloon, when it was exhibited in London, was as old woman, a centenarian. It it said that she was the same who, on losing her son of seventy-five, exclaimed, "I felt sure I never should bring up that child 1" For the last forty years of her life she had been an inmate of Lambeth workhouse, and the master of that establishment, on her hundredth birthday, asking liar what she should like best, rece.ived. for. answer that her greatest remaining desire in life was to ascend in the captive balloon. So the trip was arranged, and she ascended in company with some of her ancient friends. " Adventures above the Clouds," by Frederick Whymper, in "Good Words." div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

I, 1 here are fourteen clubs in the League; only two Satur- days of the season have passed away, and only two of the League clubs remain unbeaten. These are Aston Villa and the Bolton Wanderers, who are respectively placed first and second in the table. All the favourites have been knocked down, but it is long odds against the two named attaining to the eminence of Preston North End in the first year of the estabishment of the League. To go through the whole series of matches without a de- feat was indeed magnificent, and we are not likely to ever see it approached again.

Mr. Rowland Hill, above all other people, must have been wonderfully delighted at the extraordinary success that attended the efforts of the team he got together to visit South Africa. To absolutely win every one of the 19 matches taken part in and only have one try scored against them, is an achievement that will stand as a record for a long time to come. The British players are now on their way home, and it would be well if, on their arrival in England, an effort could be made to pit M'Lagan's team against a strong south of England or England fifteen.

It will be satisfactory to supporters of football in Warrington to know that Mr. Warren, the secretary of the local club, has been elected a member of the Lanca- shire Rugby Football Union. The annual meeting of the Union was held on Monday night, at the Grand Hotel, Manchester. Mr. A. N. Hornby presided, and there was a crowded attendance of delegates. The balance sheet was passed. The balance in hand was £293 12s. 7d., the amount of gate receipts Laying come to £1,380 18s. 3d. The following is a full list of the officers elected : President, A. N. Hornby ; vice-presidents, F. A. Grover, and R. Walker; hon. secretary and treasurer, J. H. Payne ; past president, J. M'Laren ; past vice-presidents, E. Kewley and W. Brierley ; committee—north division, J. M. Mawson, (Barrow) ; south, W. H. Bleackley, (Manchester) ; A. M, Crooke, (Free Wanderers) ; J. nig- son, (Salford) ; J. E. Warren,(Warrington) ; north-east, E. Healey, (Rochdale Hornets) ; W. Lees, (Mossley) ; J. Saville, (Oldham) ; north-west, J. W. Clegg, (Wigan) ; T. Deane, (Broughton) ; J. Mills, (Swinton) ; and J. Robertson, (Broughton Rangers). The referees' com- mittee appointed where Messrs. J. M'Laren,F. A. Grover, AM. Crooke, and J. Robertson.

The Warrington Club opened its list of engagements in a successful fashion on Saturday, the first team win- ning easily in the Isle of Man, alid the "A" team notching a decisive victory over Tranmere Wanderers. 'rhe " A" team is again displaying all its old smartness and combination. Tranmere are a sturdy lot of players but, except in sheer weight and strength, they were no match for their well-trained and lively opponents.

Runcorn paid a high compliment to the prowess of the Warrington" A" team when they thought it necessary to pit against them, on Monday evening, such players as Crompton and Davies and others who have won a name in Cheshire county football. It was hardly to be expected that the Warringtonians could hold their own against such a team as this, but with a shade of luck they might easily have made a draw, if they had not won, instead of being a try to the bad. The game was just such a one as spectators enjoy, there being plenty of clever passing, and smart running and dodging on both sides.

Swinton and St. Helens Recs. are worthy foes, but on Saturday the " Lions" just managed to humble the glass-makers on their own ground. This achievement of the Swintonians will give all the more zest to the grand struggle that is to take place to-day between them and Warrington. Remembering their experiences of last year, Swinton will no doubt see the advisability of putting their strongest combination into the field ,and the local men may be relied upon to do their best to win the credit which attaches to a victory over Valentine's famous team.
IMPORTANT LICENSING CASE AT ST. " HELENS. THE OFF-LICENSE QUESTION.

At St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, Edward I Greenough, a grocer and off-license holder in Jub- bit's-lane, Sutton, was summoned for selling beer to be consumed on the highway adjoining his pre- mises. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the defendant, Inspector Steele stated that on the previous Tues- day forenoon he was passing the defendant's house and saw a min named Murray sitting on a seat in front of the house. There were two pint jugs on the seat, and one contained beer. Defendant stood at the door, and in his presence Murray said he had paid for the beer and he had a right to drink it there. He also said that the defendant had let him have the jug for the beer. Defendant said to Murray; "It's all right, drink it up; you need not be afraid," and Murray then drank the beer. Witness spoke to the defendant upon the matter, and .the defendant said the beer had not been consumed on his premises. He added, "This is a public thoroughfare. I hold two licenses— a retail license and a wholesale license, and I can sell a barrel of beer to be consumed on this highway if it should be required. I have done this thing for years. The Superintendent who was here before Mr. Wood saw beer sold and consumed here. He took the opinion of counsel upon it, and he found it was all right. The sergeant who was here before Sergeant Brooks saw the same thing many time, and he never bothered me. The point of law hat been already tried, and it is right according to my license."—The defendant's wife then came up, and made a similar statement in regard to the rights of selling and consuming beer on the thoroughfare in front of the house. Witness said,—" I don't think you have any right to allow beer to be con- sumed here, and I shall report the matter," He then left the house, but returned in about half an hour and agaip found Murray sitting on the seat with two pint jugs. The seat was about. twelve yards from the house on a footpath some three yards from the highway.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, witness said the footpath was well trodden. He did not know it was a private path. He believed Sergeant Brooks had known about the drinking going on. He could not say whether or not Superintendent Johnson was aware of it.—Mr. Swift, for the defence, said there was no dispute as to the facts, and if defend- ant had transgressed the law, he had been transgressing it every day for the last ten years with the knowledge and approval of the police authorities. He maintained that it had not been proved that the beer was consumed on a public highway. The footpath, he submitted, was on private land which had been trespassed upon by the teople of the district, and that fact did not make it a public thoroughfare. He added that• the defendant would do his utmost to prevent the consumption of his beer under such circumstances in future, and the owners ot the land would take steps to close the footpath.— Chief-constable Wood stated that if the defendant would promise not to repeat the offence, and would pay the costs, he would withdraw the summons.—The defendant gave the necessary undertaking, and the summons was withdrawn.

RAILWAY EX'IURSIONISTS AND THEIR
TICKETS.

A case of considerable importance and interest to the travelling public generally and to excursionists in par- ticular was gone into before Alderman Burgess and Mr. Robert Garnett at the Warrington Police Court on Satur- day morning. In connection with the Doncaster Races the Cheshire Lines Committee ran excursion trains from Liverpool to Doncaster on the Bth, 9th, 10th, and 11th tickets back kd: tbssi Tal mosh fepe tuhdtbehaliiysre published shose weree ftnai scrnuekureemwt s bta hwse eser6des being. . at tonhcdpea aor r9cn ctcehoadrs andinrtthht oee th 10th 111., and the 11th IV. Among the excursionists who took advantage of the cheap train on the Bth was Mr. Abraham Solomon, new and antique china merchant, Liverpool, but this gentleman was unable, to return the same day. He arrived at the Central Station, Warring- ton, on Friday night at 9.20, and on being asked for his ticket he tendered the return half of the excur- sion ticket of the Bth and 3s. 9-Id. in cash. This was not accepted. Mr. Percy Davies,solicitor, appeared for the railway committee, and Mr. Arthur Browne de- fended Solomon. Mr. Davies stated that the charge was for travelling from Doncaster to Warrington without paying his fare. After narrating the particulars of the issue and nature of the excursion tickets, Mr. Davies called evidence of the particulars of the charge.—Ben- jamin Higson, foreman, said he refused to receive the 3s. 9-0. and the return half of the excursion ticket. He demanded instead 6s. 9id., the full fare from Doncaster to Liverpool. Witness called Inspector Charles Astbury to the compartment.—Mr. Astbury stated that they had reeeived instructions in effect not to give credit for un- used return halves of tickets out of date. Other gentle- men in the same compartment wih Mr. Solomon, who had also tickets of the Bth inst., paid the full 6s. 9id., but as Mr. Solomon declined to do so, and refused to leave, the inspector called the station constables, who took him from the train. The guard of the train told the offijals that he knew Mr. Solomon, but they nevertheless refused to take his name and address,on the ground that if they had dons so they would have had to have done so all along the train. Mr. Solomon was accordingly taken to the lock-up. About eleven p.m., he sent to the railway sta- tion, and on Inspector Astbury arriving he offered him the full 6s. 91d., so as not to be locked up. The inspector said the matter had gone too far, and declined to receive it. Mr. Davies said there was also a charge of obstruct- ing the railway officials.—Mr.Browne pointed out that as the charge was under the by-law of the committee (by- law 2), the Committee had no power to lock Mr. Solomon up. They ought to have proceeded by summon. Mr. Browne added that there would be an action against the company for assault and imprisonment, and the point of law would be thoroughly tested.—The magistrates, after a private consultation with their deputy clerk (Mr. G. F. F. White), ordered Mr. Solomon to pay the 6s. 91d., and 20s. towards the costs. They recorded no conviction, so that the case was practically dismissed :on payment of £1 6s. nd.

THE COCKNEY AND TAFFY.

Sir,—LastTuesday evening a rare sight was witnessed from the highway bolding from Stockton 'Heath to Stretton. In a garden which has lately been taken 'possession of by a Cockney, and which is situated not far from the road, might have been seen two men very busy gathering pears from a tree. But the tree was high, and the Cockney, who preferred terra firma to the dizsyheights of the pear tree, and whose genius was not behind in suggesting a means for securing the fruit, obtained a handsaw and, scaling the tree, began to cut away the top of it. Taffy in order to secure the safety of the Cockney,suggested, that " Shon " should make fast a rope. "It was be safer, you was know, Shon, and I was hold the rope, and was help you much—yes, indeed Mon." Taffy held the rope, and Cockney worked the saw, and soon down came the top of-the tree with a crash, when there was a regular scramble to get the pears. No one could blame the men for getting the fruit, but the means used were anything but good. For a Cockney it might be excusable. But what should be said of Taffy? And yet pear trees are hardly in the line of one who professes to know more of the nature of horses than trees. But your readers will be both amused and astounded to know that in the latter part of the nine- teenth century, and within three miles of Warrington, -two men, married, and householders, could be found, who would be so far behind the age, as to dream of cutting down the tree in order to obtain the fruit! Yourefze.„ NEMO.
THE LABOUR AND CAPITAL QUESTION.

r,—The solution of this question remains an enigma to those who have hitherto tried to remove the friction between these divided interests. The only way out of the difficulty is the abolition of money and barter, and tubatituting a system of production and distribution under the direction of a universal common-wealth.

The love of money—" the root of all evil," the bone of contextien, and the offspring of selfishness, or the pro- moter of it—is the sole muse of the quarrel between 'labour and capital. To Minds which have not seriously thought it out, this proposition may seem absurd, and impossible to bring about in a system 6,000 years old; but anything that has proved so disastrous to the welfare and happiness of both (so called) rich and poor, can be speedily changed with benefit to all parties. The accumulation of money makes unnecessary and useless labour, and only "robs Teter to pay Paul ;" whereas the work required for a happy life can beperformed in a few hours a day, leaving ample time to devote to the cultivation of the higher life of man.

In a brief 'letter it is impossible to show with What ease this New Order can be brought about And established ; but I shall be pleased to explain the system through the press, ,on a free public platform or by any other means; and shall feel my mission accomplished in healing the 'terrible conditions of suffering and despair to which all .classes are subjected by the slavery of the moneysystem. —Yours, in Love and Truth, WILLIAM H. VON SWARTWOUT,
