div.head: DRINK AND GAMBLING.
div.p: DRINK AND GAMBLING.

Bk.—Through our last licensing session there seems to have been something done by the Warrington temper- ance agitators that has greatly pleased the licensed vic- tuallers and publicans of Warrington and elsewhere. There is one licensed victualler that appears in your paper„foom the Crosby Hotel,Manchester. He says that •one of the witnesses was very badly drilled. He asks, further, "what will Lord Bramwell's opinion be on such mean and cowardly objects?" Sir, I am-not a teetotal- ler myself, so I cannot be one of the agitators. I can- not think that the Rev. J. Yonge and other rev. gentlemen in the town would attempt to do anything to injure any body of men, let them be publicans or what they may, as their aim is for a greater and nobler object. I know from my own experience that drink is one of the greatest curses that this country is possessed of. There is another great evil and that is gambling and betting, and I think Mr. Flood will know that drunken- ness, gambling, and betting are strictly prohibited on licensed premises. In fact he says "in my opinion the publican who knowingly serves intoxicating drinks to any intoxicated man or woman no fine or punishment is too heavy for the offender." I can assure him and Lord Bramwell that there is more gambling allowed in the public-houses in Warrington now than ever was known 'before, as men, women, and youths can go in licensed houses in this town and make bets for principal meet- ings, the some as if they were on the racecourse. On the other hand men and youths can be allowed to go and drink and play dominoes for both drink and money. In some instances the game "kitty" at dominoes has amounted to Bs. or 10s. the game. Two and three shil- hags is a common gain to the one that wins the game. Eir, tny proof of the above facts is that I have gone through it myself, and I fear no contradiction. Had Mr. Drury., the Rev. J. Yonge, and others known the above facts there would have been a different colour on the subject. The sooner gambling is done away with there will be less,' drunkenness, as it is the betting and the gambling that is the instigator of scores going to public- houses and spending their money, instead of taking it tome to their wivti and families. I may say that there

are gentlemen that are tenants of licensed premises that would sacrifice their living and position before they would allow drunkenness and gambling, but lam sorry to say they are in the minority. Without something is done by the police, or the licensed victuallers themselves, to do away with the above evils, Mr. Robert Davies and his friends will have something before them that will not be so easily got over at the next licensing sessions.— Yours truly, Warrington, Sep. 10th, 1891.
A LOOKER-ON.
THE GENERAL ELECTION AND THE LAND AND LIQUOR LAWS.

Sir,—No one at present can positively say when a general election will take place, but everybody knows that it is an event in the near future. The political fac- den now in power will retain their offices and emoluments as long 'as they can, and their opponents of the opposite camp will strain every nerve to oust them and get into their places as soon as possible. It behoves every man, therefore, who loves his country and desires to promote the wellbeing of his fellow citzens to prepare and make himself ready for the coming struggle. Directly Parliament is dissolved, and perhaps before it, the political wire-pullers will come down upon the 'con- stituencies with the swoop of eagles greedy for prey, and scream in the usual fashion to draw a too credulous people into their nets. The Salisburyites will probably asstime the sublime attitude of great education, local government, and land law reformers: while the official meuthpieces of the Grand Old Man will be sure to blow the trumpet of Home Rule for Ireland with stentorian lungs, and at the same time wave their paper guarantees for the unity of the Empire in the faces of the people. And thus the electioneering cries "of Salisbury for ever," and" Gladstone for ever," will be raised and shouted in every constituency in the Kingdom. I take this early opportunity to entreat the working- men electors of Warrington to beware of these selfish and crafty politicians, and to give them a wide berth. Neither my Lord Salisbury nor the Prophet of Hawarden have ever yet seriously attempted to grapple with the gigantic iniquities which lie at the root of nearly all the evils which afflict this country, and, through it, many other nations of the world. Their boasted measures of reform in the past have generally been neither more nor less than expensive but comparatively useless forms of quackery applied to check the ravages of political and social evils whose only cure lies in their extermination. And the class of society to which these politicians belong precludes any reasonable hope that their future legisla- tion will be any better. The two evils which most affect and impoverish the toiling masses of the people of this country are, un- doubtedly unrighteous Land Laws, and an abominable Liquor Traffic. All the other wrongs connected with our social condition pale into insignificance when brought into contrast with the tremendous iniquities of our agrarian and drink laws. And so long as these laws are permitted to disgrace the Statute Book of England, so long will poverty, drunkenness, and crime be the portion of the great bulk of our population. I ask our working- men and women to seriously consider these two things, Land and Liquor,in view of the coming general election. Let them remember and lay it to heart that nearly every acre of the soil of England is owned and held by a few of the descendants of profligate monarchs and their abandoned minions ; and that the farmers must pay these self-constituted landowners extravagant rents for per- mission to till the fields w`iich are the . Divinely given inheritance of the people. In former times the land had to bear the burdens of the State. In return for the broad acres granted to them, the barons had to find soldiers for the army, provide for the ministrations of religion, and maintain the poor. But now this arrange- ment no longer exists. Through a lone and tortuous course of most unjust legislation the noble landowners of Britain managed to relieve themselves of their responsi- bilities, and te place nearly the whole of the cost of the Government of the countrf upon the shoulders of the wage-earning classes of the community. Thus through their selfish,cruel and unjust policy, the governing classes of this country have robbed the peo- ple of their birthright in the land, and given them in exchange a mess of pottage in shape of enormous taxa- tion. And the consequences are fearful to contemplate. The farmers find it hard enough to live and pay their way under ordinary circumstances, but in adverse seasons many of them are driven to the verge of bankruptcy; the position of the agricultural labourers, with their miserable wages and demoralising surroundings, is de- plorable in the extreme; and in times of trade depres- sion how wretched is the state of thousands of our town workers when their wages fail! Having no field or gar- den produce to tide them over the time of difficulty,they must either become paupers or subsist in some way upon the kindness ef friends able and willing to assist them. And all the while Duke this and Marquis that must suffer no diminution in their Rent Rolls. The sufferings of the poor are matters which concern them not so long as funds are forthcoming to enable them to enjoy them- selves at horse racing, grouse and pigeon shooting, gambling, boxing, and the other noble pastimes peculiar to their caste.

_ Working-men of Warrington, do not commit the folly of asking the lord of Hatfield or the man of Hawar- den to reform the land laws-for you. As well might you invite Satan to reprove sin. The only way to amend our agrarian system is to reform it out of existence al- together and restore the land to its rightful owners, the people of England. The noble Marquis and the learned Seer are not the men to do this, seeing that they them- selves are large landowners, and therefore deeply in- terested in the continuation of the present state of things. Out of the people themselves a deliverer must come. Working-men, see to this now and when the elec- tion comes round.
I reserve a few remarks on the Liquor Traffic for next week. Yours faithfully, lONA.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL COURESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL COURESPONDENT.

The fire at Bethesda Chapel rudely broke the quietude of the Sabbath on Sunday last, and threw people into a state of great excitement. At one time there would be about 42,000 persons congre- gated about the burning building,but the police he d not a very difficult task to keep them in order. A gra titying feature of the unfortunate affair is thtt the damage is covered by insurance, and had it not been for the promptitude with which Sergeant •Gosling engaged men to clear away the things which •could be removed, Including a harmonium, the damage would have been very much greater. The worshippers at Bethesda have the sympathy of all the other congregations of the town in their sa d and unfortunate anshap.

It may not be generally known that Bethesda is the oldest chapel in Runcorn and was .built by the late Mr. John Tomkinson, who at ene time owned the Weston Quarries and was a large contractor. Built entirely of stone, the masonry is no less than two feet thick, and it is no ordinary firethat will demolish that substantial pile. To Mr. Tomkinson belongsthe fame of having built that 'noble structure 'St: George's Hall, Liverpool.

Ever since the Runcorn Free Librau Committee ,was formed some nine years ago, Mr. Thomas Riley of Runconn Soap and Alkali Works, has been placed ,upen it as a representative working-man and now , the Committee have done him the honour to make i.him chairman in succession to Canon Wood. it is a ,compliment to working-men that on of their number has:been placed in such a position. It is to be hoped that the duties will weigh ligibtly .upon him.

The ship Canal Company are vigorously pushing ahead with the building of Victoria Bridge, at Hill Brow. he last arch has been built across the Big Pool, and the connection with the new road from Crreenway-road will soon be made. The Bridge is most strongly aed substantially built, and its appearance is from unpleasing. I rather think that although Waterloo Bridge has so many pears start :Victoria Bridge will be finished first.

The tonic sol fa demonstration at Runcorn, on Wednesday evening,was an unqualified success,and I congratulate Mr. Haltord and his band of willing assistants thereon. Tonic sol fa has done much for the musical education of Runcorn,aud if the paople would only take advantage of the facilities offered them, would do still more, The tonic sol fa choir is a local institution deserving of far more support than it obtains, and should en audience like that of Wednesday evening greeZ; them on the occasion of their first concert of the seventh season in a week the members would shout for joy. They deserve to do so for their up-bill fight. Mr. lialford has recently been presented by the Widn6s and Run- corn members of the choir that took part in the Crystal Palace celebration with an admirable por- trait of himself, suitably framed, as a token of res- pect and esteem.

The Frodsham Conservative Club have taken the initiative in preparing a requisition asking Mr. Chas. Reynolds, J.P., to contest the Frodsham Division at the County Council election next spring,as a Liberal Unionist. The requisition has been very numerously signed, but Mr. Reynolds is away from home on a fishing expedition and it has not therefore been yet presented. There could not be a stronger candidate to fight the seat against Mr. Slater Lewis, the pre- sent member, and should he consent to stead a lively and exciting contest will result.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 19. Tql..

In recognition of his services to the Runcorn Foot- ball Club,a testimonial is being got up for Mr. Hugh Hughes, the late late captain " Hughie " as his thousands of admirers familiarly call him. As the captain of the team when they were on the bottom rung of the ladder, and for eight years he had led them on to victory and fame, and there is now na club more widely known, or more highly respected as opponents on the field than that known as the " wearers of the green." At the end of last season Hughie retired, though he still retains his interest in the club, and the event is to be celebrated in a suitable manner shortly. Subscriptions have flowed in most spontaneously, and it is believed that a tes- timonial equal to the occasion will be the result.

Mr. Oppenheim. clerk to Widnes Local Board, has received a communication from the Privy Council informing him that the scheme for granting a charter of incorporation to Widnes would not be settled and approved until early next month. Other formalities will occupy another month, and it is not probable that the charter will be granted before the middle of December.

The United Alkali Company has not hitherto been regarded as a boon and a blessing to the chemical workers of Widnes. Several hundred men have been thrown out of employment through the change in the ownership of the works of the town and through the reduction of the output. There are signs of better times, however. The British Port- land Cement Works, which have been closed for some months, have been purchased by a new com- pany, and work has been re-commenced there. The old Desoto Works (Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Company) are now placed under the control of the Phosphate Alkali and Chlorine Company, Limited, and there is a well authenticated rumour that large copper works are shortly to be built in Widnes by a firm of St. Helens gentlemen, who will trade as the Widnes Smelting and Refining Company, Limited. There should therefore, be no lack of well-paid labour in the town for some time to come.
VIOLENT CONDUCT OF A WIDNES SAILOR.

On Monday afternoon,at Holywell, James Ather- ton, a sailor, of Widnes, was charged with having assaulted J. W. King, captain of the flat John, now laing in Mostyn deeps. The prisoner, it appeared, asked the captain if he might go on the John, and permission being given, he got aboard. No sooner had he done so than he pulled off his jersey, and in- dicating the captain, he said, " I'll kill the swine." He then got into a small boat, in which was the cap- tain,and struck him repeatedly in the face. Atherton was further charged with cutting the mooring rope, and letting the John adrift. The prisoner was not seen actually cutting the rope, but a man on the steam-tug Albert heard the rope splash into the water, and on looking about Atherton was the only person near.—The prisoner said the complainant had caused him to lose his flat in Liverpool, and his family to starve. During the sailors' strike in Liverpool the plaintiff summoned him before Mr. Raffles for assault and intimidation The case of assault was withdrawn, and that of intimidation was adjourned. The present case was a revival of the bitter feeling then existing ; the parties not having met since. For the assault the prisoner WBS fined £4, including costs, and he was given the benefit of the doubt in the second case.—The money was paid by his friends,

Id ne'er strikes 'em as hevin' out to do wi' them, though they may happen ha' helpt to kill some poor crayter th' afte noon or fleet afoore, ayther a parra- shootist or a" fly on the ceiling." Aw ne'er dud pay mi sixpence or shillin' yet to see onybody risk their lives thad rooad, an' after th' cases there's bin i' th . ' pappers this last fortneet ot sooa aw ne:er ; aw corn'd hey a bit o' summat as is excitin beawt id mekkin' widows an' orphans aw'll do beawt, an' ged on as weel as aw con vt footbo' matches till th' politickle meetin's stert. Aw another thing, iv th' merch ov intellect, an' skoo boards is gooin to eddicate us up to Bich exhibitions as these, wod aw say is be— —to em' ! an' yo' con put th' strongest word yo' feel th' place o' thad blank. Aw feel mad enough to say a nowty word when aw COMB to sit deawn ov a neet to read !Ili papper, an' think a bit; yigh, yo' may laugh at th' idea ov me thinkin but aw'm tekken thad way at times. Aw jcnow scoores o' fooak as wod sooner wear sixpence or moore to see a mon kill hissel', nor spend i' th' best . book there or for a seeto' th' grandest picter ever painted, or i toaathri heawrs o' th' best singin' an' playin' ever heeard, an' o' th'time as they're coin sooa they'n a wife an' childer at hooam welly clam'd to deeath. These soort is generally known as "pat- rons," an' they're patterns as isn'd woth copyin'; an' th' " caterers "is woss nor them, a lot. As for th, performer he's o' no consequence; he nobbut does id for brass; he may hey a sick wife, or two aged par- ents to keep, and iv he hed'nd ha' broken his back thad rooad, he mut ha' drunk hiss& to deeath. Ay, to be sure he mut, sooa ne'er mind him. Tawkin' abeawt amusements, aw see there were a meetin' last Monda' o' th' Leith Shoo' Booard, an' they were discussin' as to th' advisability o' teychin' dancin' to th' skollars. There were th' usual argy- ments, an' some on 'em as silly as ever ; yo' know th advocates for jiggin' olez tawk abeawt sich a bible karickter " dancing before the Lord," but they for- ged as hoo dudn'd do id half undrest, wi' ony waistrel's arm reawnd her. An' then they tawk abeawt th' "poetry of motion" as iv thad couldn'd be shown off i' walkin' or skatin,' an' nod i' go' lopin' through a polka. One o' th' speykers tliowt becose th' middle classes were teycht this "art as th' werkin classes should be towt id as weel. Well, aw know nowt abeawt th' middle classes, but, as far as a lot o' th' werkin classes gooa aw know as they'll mek for ony low jerry-shop at hooam, an' for places still lower away fro' hooam, for th' sake ov a dance. When Sunda' skoo' skollars an' Sunda' skoo' teychers do these things, wod a temptation id mon be for them as isn'd as good as them by a long way! Happen id wod be as weel iv th' Leith lasses were towt to mend stockin's, an' use th' mop rag, dish-cleawt, an' scrubbin' brush better, even iv they paid sixpence a week extry for th' course o' lessons.
MR. GLADSTONE AND " TIIM 0' DICK 0' BOB'S,"

In a recent communication, acknowledging the receipt of a copy of " A Blegburn Dickshonary," by "Turn o' Dick o' Bobs," Mr. Gladstone says— " Thank you very much . , for sending me your specimens of a dialect full of interest to me, and which in the south-west of the country I could myself at one time speak in perfection. I think the different parts of the courtry include much variation of speech. The words thrutch (thrust) and stow (of a horse that could not get on) were familar to me ; I do not find them in your book . . . ' In a further communication to the author, Mr. Glad- stone (who had overlooked the two words men- tioned by him) shows himself to be quite an author- ity on the whole matter. The question is, what matter is he not an authority on, from Homeric synchronism to fruit preserving ?

div.head: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

My prophecy in regard to the vacancy on the Newton Board of Commissioners was, it appears, entirely correct. Mr. Peter Thompson. of Bridge-st., was the only candidate before the Board, and as a m Ater of course he was elected a member without opposition. He only takes up Mr. Glover's unex- pired term of twelve months, and in July next year will have to vacate his seat, and stand his chance of an election. lie is a very desirable man for the Earlestown ratepayers, and though he can- not by any stretch of the imagination be called an orator, yet his vote will count one, in any instance where a good vote is required.

Great has been the comment anent the trouble our enterprising sweep brought upon himself at St. Helens. He is a very energetic man, and frequently breaks out in fresh places. Lately he evolved the idea of imitating the itinerant musicians who are said to hail from Italy's sunny clime and bought for himself a span new street piano. Whether he had previously been taking lessons on the instru- ment does not transpire, but a few weeks ago the Earlestown public were startled and amused to see Vieir sweep, pertectly clean, and suitably attired, regaling the inhabitants with selections on a street piano. After deluging us with music which failed to" sooth the savage beast," he started off to explore fresh fields and pastures new, and the first we learn of his peregrinations is that he has been drawn up before "the beak," and fined. I rather think Mr. Carlin will not consider the game worth the candle if he has one or two more experiences of this kind.

I learn that a bad case of scarlet fever has broken out in the town, or properly speaking, perhaps, I should say it has been brought to the town. The afflicted one is a child, daughter of a temporary resident, who is here to-day and gone to-morrow. We cannot blame our sanitary arrangements for zhis, as I believe they are now almost perfect, but the best we can do is to get the case removed out of the awn at once, to the nearest infectious dis- eases hospital, otherwise there is no telling to what alarming extent the disease may spread.

I believe the Committee of the Viaduct Institute intend to extend the subjects taught at the Institute during the coming season. Last year they had a cookery class, but this year they will not only teach young ladies how to cook, but also how to wash starch and iron their brothers', cousins' and Rrospec- five husband's linen. Any young man in search of a wife, must scan the list of prize-winners at the end of the session, and he will not go very much wrong.

div.head: SAD DEATH OF A. WIDNES BOY.
div.p: SAD DEATH OF A. WIDNES BOY.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A SCHOOLMASTER. Yesterlay afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held the adjourned inquest on the body of Alfred Abram, aged 10 years, son of Thomas Abram, flatman, of Pitt-ltreet, who died on Sunday under the circumstances detailed below. Mr. J. W. Knowles represented Mr. J. C. Crawford, headmaster of the National Schools, who it was alleged had struck the boy on the head with a ruler. Superintendent Noblett was also present.—Ann Abram, step-mother of the deceased said he com- menced to be ill three weeks ago that day, and on the following Monday she called in Dr. Hutchinson. He came home from school crying, and said Mr. Crawford had struck him on the side of the head with a ruler. He was attending the National School. The boy had been healthy. He commenced ." rambling "on the Sunday night and that was the reason she called in the docter.—By Mr. Knowles: She had not told Mr. Crawford that the boy only said his teacher struck him.--Thomas Abram, the father, said deceased showed him the place on his head where he was struck. and said it was done at theeehool. He thought he was con- scious at the time. On Monday he went to the school but he could not get any satisfaction, but Mr. Crawford owned to making a mark on his hand —By Mr. Knowles; He had told Mr. Crawford that the boy had come home at different times with marks on his hand and that. was the reason Mr. Crawford made the statement. When he went to the school he asked for the boys teacher as he understoed that he had been struck by the teacher. —By the jury: Ile never examined the boys head. —Dr. Hutchinson who had attendedthe boy up to the time of his death, said he found no indication of injury to the head, whatever, and in his opinion the cause of death was tubercular meningitis. He came to the conclusion thatthe boy was suffering from an organic disease on the occasion of his second visit. He had sent a letter to the registrar saying the teacher had touched the boy on the head with a pencil but there was nothing to show that this lad had anything to do with his illness.—By the ,Coroner, he was certain the disease had not been set up by a blow.—Dr. Chisholm, of Woolton, said he had made a post mortem examination of the body. Dr. O'Keeffe was present and said he was mpresenting Dr. Hutch inson. Dr. Hudson was also present. The witness said there was no sign of .bruises on any part of the body. He described in detail the appearance and condition of the various organs, especially the head, and said everything pointed to death having resulted from inflammation of the membranes of the brain—or tubercular meningitis. To any person suffering from such a serious disease, a blow on the head would hasten death, but he was of opinion that this boy's death was not hastened by a blow.—Mr. Crawford said he had been headmaster at the National schools for 25 years, and during that time there had been no-complaint of ill-usage against him He l'ad never hit bay Abram, nor ever used a ruler for punishment under any cireumstances whatever. An assistant taught the deceased but he held an examination of theelass on the day in question and he had no recollection of even caiaing the boy on the hard on that day.—The Coroner said there were al- legations made by several school boys,and he asked why they had not been called,—Superintendent Nablett said be had thought it unnecessary to warn them after hearing the rssult of the post-mortem. —The jury decided that they would hear those wit- nesses, and the court was adjourned to allow them to be sent for.—Frederick Shepherd, aged 11 years, said on Thursday afternoon two weeks ago, he saw Mr. Crawford strike him twice on the hand, and several times on the back with a cane.—By Mr. Knowles: He did not know that the deceased's name d'd not appear on the register for that Thurs- day morning.—Geo. Wm. Abrams, aged 13, said on , the Friday in question he sayv. Mr. Bingham hit his brother with a ruler for writing crooked. He also saw Mr. Crawford hit him with a cane.—?lr. Knowles showed in cross-examination that the boy had wade several contradictory statements. The ruler was a short flat piece of wood.—Mr. F. Bing- ham pupil teacher denied that he had struck the deceased. He was not allowed to punish boys by the rules of the school.—The jury returned a verdict that " the deceased died from natural causes, and they agreed that Mr. Crawford and the teacher are free from biame•—The Coroner : I agree with you,

div.head: CLAIM OF MR. P. DAVIES.
div.p: CLAIM OF MR. P. DAVIES.

Mr. Longton claimed on behalf of Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington, in respect of his house at Latch- ford. Mr. Humphreys objected that Mr. Davies did not live in the Grappenhall part of the Latchford township, but in that part which was within the Warrington Par- liamentary borough, and that he was on the list for the borough.—The claim was not allowed.

div.head: CLAIM OF A WIDOW.
div.p: CLAIM OF A WIDOW.

Mrs. Laverock, widow of a Warrington tailor, claimed as occupant of a house in New-road, Latchford. Her husband had lived there until the autumn of last year and then died, and she had continued the tenancy.—The Conservative solicitor, who supported the claim, urged that as there was no breach in the tenancy she was en- titled to vote.—Mr. Humphreys said there was a break in the responsibility for rent and rates.—The claim was allowed.
CLAIM BY TWO BROTRBRS.

The Conservatives made a claim on behalf of Albert and Thomas Broady brothers, of the Red Lion Inn, Stockton Heath.—Mr. Longton said the claimants were joint owners of land behind the public-house and lived there together.—The Overseer said they had been more than 12 months previous to last month in occupation of the land.—Mr. Humphreys said they were joint tenants.- -The Overseer, in zeply to the Barrister, said before they took this land Albert was on other land at Stockton Quay which he occupied under Mr. Robert Davies. Since then they had occupied their present farm under Messrs. Greenall. Whitley. and Co.—lt appeared that Albert still held a plot of land under Mr. Davies and another piece jointly with his brother, under Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., and he was rated separately for them, but the joint occupation had not lasted the necessary period. The claim of Albert was therefore allowed, and that of Thomas disallowed. ALDERMAN HARRISON'S CLAIM REJECTED. The Conserv-tive solicitor submitted a claim on be- half of Alderman Harrison, J.P., in respect of a cottage and land adjoining his house at Latchford. Mr. Long- ton stated that ke had sold the land to the Ship Canal Company, and bought it back when they had taken what they wanted. He was at present in Llandudno, and had telegraphed to his sister-in-law to hand him the deeds showing the conveyance of the land which he now produced.—The Revising Barrister asked whether the land was of the clear value of 40s. a year.—Mr. Longton : It is clear £7 value. Mr. Humphreys objected that there was no proof that it was not mortgaged.—The Barrister said he had no doubt it was unmortgaged and of the necessary value,but he must have proper evidence that this was the case.—Mr. Humphreys said Mr. Harri- son's sister-in-law might be the mortgagee.—Mr. Long- ton : She is not the mortgagee.—The claim was dis- allowed in the absence of the evidence desired. DARESBURY. Mr. Lloyd the same day attended at the Daresbury courthouse for the revision of the list of voters for the township of Acton Grange, Antrobus, Daresbury, Hatton, Kekewick, Moore, Newton-by-Daresbury, Preston-0111'4E11, Sevenoaks,Stretton, Walton Inferior, Walton Superior, Whitley Inferior and Whitley Superior. Mr. W. Humphreys appeared for the Liberal, and Mr. , J. H. Dean, of Knutsford, for the Conservatives.
AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER AS REVISING BARRISTER.

In the cow se of the proceedings, the Revising Barrister took occasion to complain to the assistant overseer of Lower Walton (Mr. Joseph Whitfield) that he had failed to send any claims or objections for that township to the Clerk of the Peace.—Mr. Whitfield said he had not published the claims because the persons interested were not entitled to vote.—The Barrister : It is not your business to deal with them. You have been acting as Revising Barrister all by yourself. It so happens you have not done any harm,but you might have done.—Mr. Humphreys: Done some good perhaps. He will get them to improve their claims.

THE OVERSEERS GONE WRONG. Later on his Honour observed that nearly all the over- seers seemed to have gone wrong. He complained that about five of the overseers had reprinted the ownership list, thus incurring unnecessary expense, instead of send- ing the old list.to the Clerk of the Peace. There was nothing else of moment in the proceedings.
6TEI V.B. KING'S LIVERPOOL REGI-
MENT.

The 30th annual Prize Meeting of Newton de- tachment 6th V.B. King's Liverpool Regiment, took place at High field Moss,on Saturday,whe prizes to the value of nearly £4O were competed for, and which are mainly contributed by ladies and gentle- men in the surrounding district, upon whose generous support the success of this very popular meeting greatly depends. The shooting commenced about 11 a.m. and was continuously proceeded with until after 6 p.m., when the failing light necessit- ated the postponement of the recruits competition until Saturday next, the 19th inst. The whole number of entries amounted to over 100, which out of a full strength of 145 N.C. officers and men may be considered as remarkably good. The weather which was very fine and warm was on the whole favourable to good shooting, and the average scores were much above that of previous years. The light in the earlypart of the day somewhat disconcerted a few of the crack shots, particularly so in the General Handicap Prizes, when Private Ernest Nicholson snached the Ist prize, £2, from the hands of a well-known and reputed marksman of the company. Handicapping under any circumstances is not a very pleasant task, but the above result, as well as many others, undoubtedly prove that the handicap committee did their duty in a fair and ex- perienced manner. At the conclusion of the practise the committee and members returned to the Orderly Room, Southworth-road, where the prizes were immedi- ately distributed, and this concluded one of the most successful meetings held on the range. Mrs. Bond as before supplied the refreshments on the range, and in accordance with her reputation gave every satisfaction. A list of prize winners is apended : HANDICA MONEY PRIZES.

div.head: PENR ETH.
div.p: PENR ETH.
PRESENTATION TO A FOREMAN.

An interesting ceremony was witnessed on Wednesday evening. Mr. T. Garnett, who has recently vacated the position he has held for many years as foreman of Messrs. Garnett's cabinet works, was the recipient, at his house, of a testimonial given by Messrs. Garnett's employ6s. The presen- tation took the form of an address and a handsome marble timepiece. Several of the employes spoke of the great satisfaction they had in working under Mr. T. Garnett, and said it was greatly regretted that a connection of so many years standing should have boen so rudely severed. During the time he had been at the cabinet works his relations with the men have always been of a most pleasant and harmonious character. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

A meeting of the members of the Penketh Wes- leyan Mutual Association was held, on Wednesday evening, for the purpose-of arranging a syllabus for the coming session and to transact any other busi- ness. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Gandy. There was a moderate attendance. Mr. T. Gandy in opening the meeting said their object in coming together was to devise some mr Ins of making the meetings more attractive. Mrs. Garnett thought it would be a good thing to have the first Wednesday in each month as a miscellaneous evening. She proposes that the meetings be held on alternative Thursday evenings instead of the weekly meeting on Wednesday evenings. Mr. H. T. Jones seconded. Mr. J. T. Budden proposed as an amendment that the meetings be held as before. Mr. Peers seconded. Upon the motion being put to the vote the amend- ment was carried by 4 votes. A number of names were given in for papers, &c.

div.head: Lr 3131.
div.p: ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—On Sunday anniversary ser- vices were held at the Zion Chapel, Cherry-lane, Lymm. Two sermons were preached by Mr. B. B. Woods, of Pendleton. A collection was made at the close of each service in aid of the chapel funds, and over £5 was real- ised. 'mere was a fair congregation at each service. TEMPERANCE LECTURES.—The temperance mission van, which has been staying at Latchford, yesterday week, proceeded on its journey, and stopped at the Cross, Lymm, remaining there till Monday night. On Saturday Mr. and Mrs. Fiske delivered addresses from the van. The Rev. Charles Clay, 8.A., took the chair. On Sunday lectures were given at the various chapels, and on Monday at Newfield, when the chair was occu- pied by Mr. F. 0. Moston, of Newfield. Much interest was manifested in the proceedings, and many villagers assembled to gether to hear the lectures. _

I FRIENDLY -SOCIETIES' DEMONSTRATION.—The second annual demonstration of the friendly societies' com- prising Oddfellows, Foresters, Druids, &c., took place on Sunday, when members of the various Orders to the number of 259 assembled at the Cross, Lymm, at two o'clock. The procession, to the strains of three brass bands, marched round the mill, up Eagle-brow, by the Nag's Head, and over the Dam Head to the church, where at three o'clock a service was conducted by the Rev. G. W. Guest and Rev. W. G. Knocker. The Rev. F. Wainwright, Vicar of St. John's, Altrincham, preached a sermon appropriate t)the occasion. A collec- tion was taken at the close in aid of the church bells, which, added to that collected at the dedication of the bells on the previous day, amounted to £2O 13s. 4d. TRH NEW BELLS.—Saturday was a red-letter day in the history of the picturesque village of Lymm, as the new bells, eight in number, and the new clock in the tower were dedicated in the presence of a large congre- gation. Several months ago the Bishop of Chester dedi- cated the handsome tower, and the proceedings on Saturday marked the completion of the work in connec- tion with the church, upon which a large sum of money has been expended. The cost of the bells, which are said to be among the finest in Cheshire, is from £BOO to £9OO, and the clock, which is the gift of Miss Fox, cost about £l5O. The bells are from the forndry of Messrs. John Taylor and Co., of Loughborough, and the clock, which strikes the Westminster chimes, has been supplied by Messrs. Potts, of Leeds. Prior to the service, there was a procession of Sunday school children through the village, aiad at the service in the church an appropriate sermon was preached by the Yen Archdeacon Barber, of Chester, in the absence of the Bishop.

LYMM PETTY SESSIONS FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Lister (in the chair), Dr. Brabazon, and Mr. W. Long. A DOG CASE.—Archibald Thomson, farm labourer, ad- mitted allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled on the 30th August at Partington. He was fined 3s. 6d., in- cluding COAL DADIA'at TO CROPS.—Peter Winstanley and Abraham Wilson, young men, who described themselves as fus- tian cutters, admitted damaging potatoes to the amount of ss. in a field at Oughtrington, occupied by John Hugh Simpson, on the 19th August. They were each fined 55., including 2s. 6d. each for the da:nage. "A DISGRACEFUL Row."—Frederick Stone, Ship Canal brickmaker. was summoned for assaulting Charles Alice, who is similarly employed, at Statham, on the sth Sep- tember. Martha Alice summoned Fanny Stone for a similar offence, the latter responded with a cross-sum- mons against Mrs. Alice. The Chairman described the affair as a disgraceful row, and the Stones were bound over to keep the peace for six months in the sum of £lO each. The charge against Alice was dismissed.
Two families, numbering 22 persons, have been mur- dered by brigands near Elizabethpol, in the Russian Caucasus.
One of the Crown witnesses in the De Cobain case, named William Allen, has been apprehended on a charge of exhibiting obscene prints.

THE WORLD-FAMED LORD GEORGE SANGER'S FOUR AMALGAMATED EXHIBITiONS. GREAT CIRCUS, HIPPODROME. AND MENAGERIE, ST. HELENS, FRIDAY, SEPT.' 25TH. WARRINGTON, SATURDAY, SEPT. 2671 x. 250 Horses and Ponies, Herd of Elephants. Flock of , Camels. 20 Carriages of Wild Animals. Wonderful perform- ing Lions and Tigers. Polar Bears. 200 Specimens of Wild Beasts of the rarest description, including the Horse-faced Antelope, the only one in Europe. and the first that has been seen. in any part of the United Kingdom for the last thirty years. There is nothing in any part.of.the globe to compare with LORD GEORGE SANGER'S NEW ENTERPRISE OF 1891. THE CIRCUS DEPARTMENT IS COMPLETE. The Finest Lady and Gentlemen Equestrians the World has ever seen. The Wire Walkers and Ascensionists, and Gymnasts, Acrobats, and Tumblers have been selected from ' allthe principal establishments of Europe and America ; and in conjunction will appear at each performance I A S 'I A, The Woman of the Nile, the Queen of the Crescent, in her Crystal Barge, with those Monsters of Egypt--Crocodiles, Alligators, Serpents, Bm. She will summon them, they will obey her ;she will command them, they will perform. She will then give that EXTRAORDINARY EXHIBITION that can only be realised by seeing for oneself. It is impos- sible for the tongue of man to give the most remote idea of the wonderful exhibition of this exceptional woman, standing as shedoes alone in the world without an equal. TWO POWERFaL BANDS will accompany the Monster Exhibition, and the Great Street Parade with all the Animals and Reptiles open to view free. of charge, and upon the summit of the Royal Carriage will. be seen BRITANNIA AND THE LIVING LION WALLACE. Pasha Lawrence, the Noblest Roman of them all, with his African ,Forest-bred Lions. LORD GEORGE SANGER'S FOUR AMALGAMATED EXHIBITIONS. The Exhibition abounds with Novelty. Grand procession, leaving the grounds at 1 o'clock. Two performarees, at 2 and 7-33. Carriages may be ordered at 4-45 and 10.45 p.m.- —Prices of Advaission--35.,.25„ Ir., and 6d. The Mammoth Marquee, capable of holding 10.000 people •is perfectly Waterproof. Door open One Hour previous to each performance. The Morning Performance is in every respect &motto the Evening. To avoid confusion, no coppers taken at the Entrances. The Exhibition estimated at £150,000, .and notwithstanding, its superiority over anything eve seen, the penny postage and the half-penny post-card llas •brought its exormous revenue to the Treasury, and from that fact the prices cf admission will remain as they were. (signed) LORD GEORGE SANGER. The World's Greatest Showman.

FIRE AT MAIDSTONE. A large turner's shop and several cottages were burned down at Maidstone yesterday. THE "FREEMAN'S JOURNAL." The Press Association is informed ihat Mr. Dwyer Gray has been promised over 16,000 votes at the meeting ot shareholders of the "Freeman's Journal," to be held next Monday. The total number of votes is 25,000. A " NOBLE " BANKRUPT. At the London Bankruptcy Court yesterday, the creditors of Lord Esm6 Stuart Gordon entertained an arrangement under which the debtor's father-in-law, Mr. Brown, provides a sum sufficient to pay not less than 75. 6d. in the 2. EXTRAORDINARY CHARGE. Inquiries are being made at Glasgow concerning an allegation that a coachman responsible for the delivery of the bodies of paupers,at Sandymount Cemetery has been selling them for ss. each for anatomical purposes. Ths coachman has disappeared. A SELF-ACCUSED MURDERER. Yesterday, Herbert Green was charged, on remand, at Westminster, on his own confession, with the murder of his six-year-old daughter, by administering chloro- dyne, and immersing her in the sea, at Brighton, on the sth inst. The prisoner was handed over to the Brighton police. NEWTON SENTENCED TO SIX MONTHS' IMPRISON- MENT. At the Old Bailey, yesterday, Edward Morris Callender Newton, journalist, pleaded guilty to abducting and carnally knowing Lucy Pearman, daughter of a tobacconist living in the Strand, and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The Recorder, in passing sentence, took into account the girl's passionate letters, the fact that had the prisoner waited a few months longer there would have been no crime, and that the Act making the offence criminal had only lately been passed. THE FLOODS IN SPAIN. ROBBING THE DEAD. MADRID, FRIDAY, 11 A.M.-At Consuegra ten miscre- ants have been arrested for robbing :the dead. It has been noticed that since the catastrophe the river Amar- guillo has changed its course. Over a thousand victims have already been buried.

WARCHI AVE SCHOOLS. On Thursday afternoon, the annual treat to the scholars attending the Wargrave day and Sunday sctiools, took place in a field behind the schoolS belonging to Mr. H. Hood-Wright. The children assembled at the school at half-past two, and pro— ceeded to the field, where they enjoyed themselves until about 4 o'clock, when they adjourned t 3 the for tea. After tea they returned to. the field, wnere they indulged in all manner of games until dusk.
